INTRODUCTION
CLAY ON THE
 KOREAN
PENINSULA

People who make pots out of clay have been part of Korea’s history for
thousands of years. In this book we tell a story of shifting centres of
population, changes in belief and ways of living that evolved with time and
politics. Because ceramics are inherently robust and long-lived, they
survive in greater numbers than some other materials. There is abundant
evidence of how ceramics were produced, transported and consumed in pre-
modern Korea. Kilns operated right across the peninsula, some supplying
local needs, others making ritual and ceremonial vessels for royal and elite
customers. Far in the north, at Hoeryeong in Hamgyeong Province near the
Russian border, and right across the land as far south as Busan on the south
coast, just a few hundred kilometres from the Japanese archipelago,
communities of potters made storage jars, drinking cups, dining wares,
vases, bottles and ceramic versions of ritual bronzes. Ceramics were present
everywhere, but because large-scale trade with customers and countries
outside Korea only began with the forced opening of the country in the
1880s, the wider international community initially formed a distorted view
of Korean ceramics. Our aim in this book is to lead interested readers to the
fascinating and copious materials that now exist to develop a more accurate
account of making and using ceramics in Korea.
    The various earthenwares (clay vessels baked at temperatures between
about 700 and 900°C) made during the Neolithic and Bronze ages were fired
in pits, more or less open to the elements, and therefore not able to reach the
higher temperatures required for stoneware and porcelain. These soft-
bodied vessels were used to store liquids and foodstuffs and are found in a
variety of styles: plain-surfaced (mumun), comb-patterned (jeulmun),
burnished and embellished with piercings below the rim. Amsa-dong, a
riverside settlement in modern Seoul originally dating from the fourth
millennium BC, is the best-known Neolithic site, famous for its earthenware
jars that vary hugely in size. The Three Kingdoms period in the early part of
the first millennium AD saw the introduction of higher firing temperatures
and thin-walled ceramics, made in a variety of styles and shapes associated
with the kingdoms that ruled different parts of the country. In the south,
Silla and Gaya are famous for finely modelled vessels in anthropomorphic
forms, and for ritual stands and jars, austerely decorated with geometric
patterns in bands (illus. 1). These ceramics were made between about AD
300 and 700. Iron in the clay often fired to a dark grey colour, but vessels
survive in a variety of body tones and are mostly unglazed. By this time

Korea’s ceramic technology was fairly advanced, and mass production of
vessels for placement in royal and elite tombs is doubtless only one part of
the story, since practical ceramics used by living people have mostly been
lost over time. Further north, in Goguryeo, whose capitals shifted over time
from the Yalu River area to the Taedong River (Pyongyang) and further
south, ceramics excavated in tombs include a burnished jar on three feet
that was probably excavated from a tomb near Pyongyang (illus. 2). The
kingdom of Baekje, ruling the southwestern part of Korea, had close
maritime contacts with eastern China during the early first millennium AD.
Its remarkable ceramics range from architectural tiles formed to depict
landscapes and marvellous creatures, to tall ceremonial stands decorated
with perforations and applied patterns, neatly spaced at intervals over a
vessel’s walls. Large burial jars of earthenware also survive in Baekje
tombs, evidence that clay was one of a number of materials (others were
wood and stone) used for coffin construction.

1 Bowl on high foot, 700–900, stoneware, height 20.5 cm.

     In AD 918 Wang Geon founded the kingdom of Goryeo, which would
rule much of the Korean peninsula for over 450 years. The Goryeo capital
was in the centre of the country, now known as Gaeseong. A Chinese
diplomatic mission led by Xu Jing visited in 1123 and left a precious first-
hand report. The king and courtiers were refined and observed correct
ceremony, Xu said. Goryeo green-glazed wares, known in the West as
celadons, are widely regarded as the acme of Korean ceramics. Their
refinement, unique inlaid decoration and exquisite jade-green glazes are
indeed among the world’s outstanding ceramics. Furthermore, the Goryeo

potters’ skill in moulding, carving and modelling an astonishing variety of
naturally inspired forms has captivated people for many centuries (illus. 3).
    Over the centuries of Goryeo rule, nomadic neighbours invaded from
the north on a number of occasions. Potters continued to have very low
social status and carried out their work in anonymity. The superior kilns that
supplied the capital were in the far south and organized transportation by
sea: modern maritime archaeology has revealed the perils and logistics of
supplying Gaeseong with goods from the far southwest, sailing north
through treacherous coastal waters. The royal palace in Gaeseong was
roofed with celadon tiles. Buddhist monks and lay believers sipped tea
served in delicate bowls, sometimes carved to evoke the lotus flower,
emblem of Buddhist rebirth. Wine was drunk from stemmed cups shaped to
imitate the petals of a flower head in their faceted bowls. Goryeo people
seem to have loved pattern and contrast in all their luxury goods. Like
lacquer objects inlaid with mother-of-pearl, ceramics were enlivened with
contrasting-coloured designs (illus. 4) and even decorated with copper
pigment to produce red effects, and in a very few cases with gold leaf.
Water droppers are used in preparing ink for painting or writing. The writer
would add controlled amounts of water to solid ink before mixing on an ink
stone. Water droppers are a feature of the scholar’s table in East Asia, along
with ink, inkstone, brush and paper. The two water droppers in the form of
children (illus. 5) are precious evidence for the Goryeo celebration of the
wonders of nature: monkeys, ducks, rabbits, lions, tortoises and dragons
were all contrived in clay, covered in glaze and fired for sophisticated
clients. In addition to the fabled celadons, Goryeo green ceramics were
decorated with brown pigment in numerous floral, cloud and animal motifs.
A bottle in Tokyo National Museum has a poem painted in columns of
characters around its walls: ‘Carrying a wine bottle at night to the Bright
Moon Pavilion/ I forget everything else while admiring the moonlight all
night long’, providing a glimpse of the lifestyle of the Goryeo aristocracy.1

2 Tripod jar with cover, 450–500, earthenware, height 22.4 cm.





3 Incense burner, 1100–1200, stoneware, glazed, height 15.3 cm.
4 Maebyeong (plum blossom) vase, 1200–1300, stoneware, glazed, height 42 cm.

5 Water droppers, 1100–1200, stoneware,
glazed, height 11 cm.

6 Dish, 1450–1500, porcelain, painted, diam. 22.7 cm.





7 Bottle, 1450–1550, buncheong, height 14.4 cm.

   When Yi Seong-gye established Joseon in 1392, soon moving the
capital to Seoul, the country had endured periods of turmoil and disruption,
particularly during the Mongol period (c. 1231–1350), and the new dynasty
embarked on a programme of reform and renewal. Systematic surveys of
kilns around the country were organized in 1424–5. The arrival from China
of white porcelain decorated under the glaze with blue pigment sparked a
shift in taste. Members of the court and aristocrats vied to acquire blue and
white ceramics, whether imported from China or produced locally (illus. 6).
Over time, a hierarchy of kiln sites was established, with the area of
Gyeonggi Province near the Han River, east of Seoul, emerging as the pre-
eminent ceramic centre for elite production. For hundreds of years, potters
laboured in the Official Kilns (Bunwon), making the dining and ritual
vessels needed by the court. Around the country, other centres continued to
produce varied stoneware and porcelain vessels for more general use.

Goryeo celadon was gradually overtaken by a type of stoneware
known today as buncheong, a rather rough-bodied grey ceramic that
appeared creamy or white-toned when covered with a light-coloured clay
dressing known as slip. Buncheong is a fascinating, diverse ceramic genre
that is too little known outside Korea and Japan. It exists in a plethora of
decorative styles – brushed freely, painted with brown pigment (illus. 7),
stamped with repeating flowerheads or rope patterns, carved and painted, or
simply dipped into a vat of liquid white clay to produce a thick, milky-
white coating. These remarkable, free-spirited ceramics continued in
production until the late sixteenth century, but after the catastrophic wars of
the 1590s, when Korea was invaded by the Japanese warlord Toyotomi
Hideyoshi and his followers, buncheong fell out of use. Buncheong taste
survives among the tea ceremony aficionados of Japan.
     After the Japanese invasions (Korean Imjin Waeran), ceramic
production gradually resumed along with other economic activities. The
clear failure of the court to prepare against, or to prevent, the Japanese
attacks remained a sore and present memory. Further, during the 1630s, as
China was convulsed during the dynastic transition from Ming (1368–1644)
to Qing (1644–1911), Koreans wrestled with questions of loyalty to the
Central Kingdom and of how to maintain Korea’s identity as the loyal
junior country in the Confucian world order. These issues preoccupied
kings and ministers for many decades. The reigns of Yeongjo (reg 1724–
76), Jeongjo (reg 1776–1800) and Sunjo (reg 1800–1834) saw a broadly
stable economy, with a grudging recognition that China’s era of Manchu
rule was likely to endure. In the 1750s the royal kilns settled at Bunwon,
making ceramics for court and – controversially – for private customers
whose prosperity encouraged them to consume more and more cultural
goods. Eighteenth-century porcelain is highly sought after by collectors. Its
gentle tones, interesting, solid forms and variety of amusing shapes and
decorative motifs continue to captivate. Although Joseon potters used only
cobalt blue, iron brown and copper red to decorate their vessels (always
under the glaze, as far as is known), the subtlety and elegance of their
objects is truly impressive (illus. 8).
     In the late nineteenth century, gunboat diplomacy arrived in Korea.
Isolation, for so long the preferred policy of the Joseon court, became an
impossible dream, a cherished memory. First the Japanese and later the
Western powers arrived on Korean soil to challenge China’s long-standing

position as the protector of the Koreans. The previous, nationally
recognized relationship between the Royal Household and the Official
Kilns weakened to the point where the kilns closed in 1883.
   When Japan annexed Korea in 1910 the living ceramic culture of
Korea had already declined. During the colonial period, reproduction
Goryeo celadon was made for Japanese collectors. French, German and
English imported porcelains had been used at court in the 1890s and 1900s.
Archaeological investigations in the first half of the twentieth century were
led not by Korean but by Japanese scholars. They revealed much that had
been ignored about Korea’s ceramic past. Only in the post-war period, when
North and South Korea separately began nation-building after the Armistice
of July 1953, did Korean ceramics experience rebirth and renewal. Chapter
Five describes the different paths that the South and North Korean
governments took when tackling the issue of how to train a new generation
of ceramic makers. The outcomes of these programmes – university
departments, private and state museums, a market in contemporary studio
pottery – are constantly changing, especially in South Korea, where a
number of successful, thoughtful and productive artists work in ceramics
(illus. 9, 10). In the twenty-first century the South Korean middle classes in
particular have been engaging again with their country’s remarkable
ceramic culture. School visits, new museums and tourist programmes
attracting urban residents to historic sites are introducing new generations
of Koreans and others to the unique aesthetics and physical properties of
Korea’s historic and modern ceramics.
8 Grapevine vessel, 1650–1750, porcelain, painted, height 39.7 cm.
9 Shin Sang-Ho, vase with facets, 1990, stoneware, inlaid and glazed, height 30 cm.

10 Yeesookyung, translated vase, 2014, porcelain,
gold leaf, height 47 cm.

CHAPTER ONE
         PRE-GORYEO





The Korean Neolithic peoples who lived along the coast or riverbanks most
likely discovered how to make earthenware pots by chance, leaving vessels
by the fireside and seeing them bake and go hard. It is the appearance of
pottery among a population that subsisted mainly by hunting, fishing and
gathering, using stone, bone and shell tools, that defines the beginning of

the Korean Neolithic period. Excavations have shown that there are close
links between the early Neolithic in Korea and that of the Liaodong
peninsula in northeast China.

Early Neolithic, c. 10,000–7,000 BC
The earliest pottery produced in the Korean peninsula found so far has in
fact been found on Jeju Island, to the south of the peninsula, at a site called
Gosan-ri. It was excavated in 1994 and dates to around 10,000 BC. In Korea
this kind of pottery is called Primitive Undecorated Pottery (wonsi mumun
togi). This pottery is made of clay mixed with plant material and fired at a
low temperature. It is interesting that microblades and microlithic blade
cores were found together with the pots at Gosan-ri, similar to the situation
in the early Neolithic in the Amur River basin in Russia and the early
Jōmon in the Kyushu region of Japan. Microliths were very small flints
used in making tools such as spears. Their cores were pyramidal or
cylindrical. Flint blades were struck from them. Other sites on Cheju Island
and in the North Gyeongsang Province of southeast Korea have also yielded
similar pottery mixed with plant remains.
    Other early Neolithic types of pottery in Korea are raised-design
pottery (yunggimun) and Z-shaped design pottery (jijamun). The former are
bowls with a flat base and thin clay bands attached around the mouth. They
have been found on Jeju Island and also along the south and east coast, for
example at Osan-ri. They seem to date a little later than the Gosan-ri type
and are thought to have originated from the raised-design pottery of the
Amur River basin. The Z-shaped design pots are also bowls with a flat base,
but they have continuous zig-zag patterns, a bit like the Chinese character
zhi, on them. There may be some connection between these and the Z-
shaped designed pottery of the Liao River basin in northeast China (illus.
11).
    Another type of flat-bottomed pottery found on the northeast and south
coasts in the early Neolithic has short patterns made by stamping a sharp
tool round the mouth.

Later Neolithi, c. 4000–1500 BC
Around 4000 BC the production and use of pottery spread across the
peninsula and became more common. It was at this time that the most
characteristic Korean Neolithic pottery, known as jeulmun, was widely

produced, although it had first appeared around 6000 BC. Jeulmun means
comb patterned, since the decoration was incised or stamped with a tool
similar to a comb, and it is made of sandy clay that contains quartz or mica
and sometimes also shell, asbestos, talcum or feldspar. It was formed using
the coil method, after which the surface was decorated using bones or
wooden or stone tools (illus. 12). No kilns have been found yet, but it is
thought that this pottery was fired in uncovered shallow pits acting as open
kilns, at a temperature of about 700°C.
    The patterns on jeulmun pots are geometric dots, lines and circles.
There were regional variations; for example, pointed-based pottery was
common in the north, west and south, while flat-bottomed pots were more
common in the north and east. The decoration was sometimes the same over
the entire surface of the pot, but could differ on the mouth, body and base.
Over time, decoration gradually became restricted to the rim area.
    Jeulmun pottery can be divided into three periods. During the early
period before 4000 BC, flat-bottomed pots were common and were mixed
with the earlier Neolithic pottery types as well as pottery with decoration
around the mouth (kuyonmun). In the middle period, 4000–3000 BC, the
typical pointed-based jeulmun pottery spread, although flat-based pots were
still produced in some regions. The late period, 3000–1500 BC, is when the
patterns on the pointed-based jeulmun pots became coarser, and pots
without decoration or just decorated around the mouth increased.
     ‘Lightning pattern pottery’, decorated with incised square spirals, was
another type that appeared in the northeast, and double-rim pottery emerged
along the south coast. Also, a face made of clay with features sculpted out
has been discovered at Osan-ri on the northeast coast, possibly showing the
beginnings of some sort of religious practice (illus. 13).





11 Raised-design pot, c. 5000 BC, earthenware,
height 14.5 cm.

12 Comb pattern pots, c. 4000 BC, earthenware, height 38.3 cm.

    Perhaps the best-known Korean Neolithic site is Amsa-dong, on the
Han River on the outskirts of Seoul, where thirty semi-subterranean pit-
dwellings were excavated and the site turned into a museum. The jeulmun
pots found at Amsa-dong are thought to have been used for cooking acorns.
In general, jeulmun pots of different sizes, ranging in capacity from 4 to 56
litres, are thought to have been used for preparing, cooking and storing
foods.1

Bronze Age, c. 1500–400 BC
Pottery made during the Bronze Age is largely unpatterned or plain
earthenware and called Mumun in Korean. Bronze tools, rice cultivation
and the building of dolmen – large, chambered stone tombs, often
composed of two upright rocks supporting a table-like cover – characterize
this period. The use of bronze wares did not become widespread until the
later Bronze Age. The petroglyphs at Ban’gudae near Ulsan in southeast
Korea are also intriguing evidence of the lives of Korean Bronze Age
peoples, featuring illustrations of whales, tigers, wild boar, deer and a boat
(illus. 14). The riverside rock face bearing the carvings is over 5 metres tall
and bears more than three hundred images of people, animals and tools.

Mumun pottery is much harder and less absorbent than jeulmun
pottery and there tend to be greater numbers found at one site. It is made of
fine clay with rather a rough texture due to the use of quartz sand as a
temper. It was formed using the coil method and fired in open kilns at about
870°C, considerably higher than jeulmun pottery. Many of these open kilns
have been found throughout the southern half of the Korean peninsula and
typically are round or oval shafts measuring about 4 metres by 3 metres,
with no ceiling. Closed kilns developed in the Middle Bronze Age when
straw and a layer of clay formed the ceiling, aiming to increase the firing
temperature inside the kiln.





13 Clay face, c. 5000 BC, earthenware, height 5.1 cm.

14 Ban’gudae rock carving, 400–200 BC.

   Mumun pottery was used for cooking, storing and carrying food but it
was also sometimes placed in tombs as well as used to make jar coffins. It
became well developed in the thirteenth century BC. There are regional
variations. Early mumun pottery is plain with minimal decoration around a
double rim; another type has a protruding rim around the top, impressed at
regular intervals. There is some thought that this type is connected with that
of the Liaodong peninsula region of northeast China. Then there are
earthenware bowls decorated with a row of holes around the rim, and bowls
with pedestals. The middle Bronze Age is sometimes known as the
Songguk-ri Culture due to the appearance at Songguk-ri on the central west
coast in about 900 BC of elegant jar-shaped pottery excavated from round or
square-shaped dwellings (illus. 15).
    Perhaps the most exciting development during this period is that of red
burnished pottery. It is made of very fine clay and has very thin walls,
burnished by rubbing oxidized iron on its outer surface before or after
firing. Usually the shape is that of a small pot with a short neck; these pots
have been excavated from both dwelling sites and tombs (illus. 16). Mumun
pottery is thought to have influenced the formation of Yayoi pottery, made
in Japan c. 300 BC–AD 300, particularly the Yu’usu type.2
15 Jar, 700–400 BC, earthenware, height 27.6 cm.

16 Burnished red jar, 500–300 BC, earthenware, painted, height 12.4 cm.

Iron Age (or Proto-Three Kingdoms Period), c. 300 BC–AD 300
Around 300 BC, during the Chinese Warring States period, the Chinese state
of Yan invaded the Korean peninsula and there was a mass immigration of
displaced persons. This was connected with the introduction of cast iron
technology and was accompanied by new pottery technology originating
from the Liaoning region of China.
    Earthenware appeared with clay appliqué strips around the rim
together with black burnished earthenware jars with a long neck, the latter
produced by applying lead to the surface and rubbing the vessel until it
became shiny (illus. 17).

The Proto-Three Kingdoms period, as this is known, preceded the later
emergence and establishment of the Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo, Baekje
and Silla). Also, around this time, a number of commanderies or outposts
were established by the Chinese Han dynasty in the northern area of the
Korean peninsula. The most important was Lelang (Korean Nangnang),
located near the city of Pyongyang in modern North Korea. In the southern
part of Korea there were three independent states called Mahan, Jinhan and
Byeonhan.





17 Burnished black jar, 400–200 BC,
earthenware, height 22.7 cm.

18 Jar with handles, 100 BC–AD 50, high-fired
ware, height 43 cm.





    There were three main types of pottery, known by their Korean names:
yeonjil, wajil and gyeongjil. The most common was yeonjil or soft, low-
fired earthenware. Some of the yeonjil pottery had paddled decoration on
the surface, with cord- or lattice-impressed patterns. It varied in colour from
grey to reddish-brown and was used for cooking and storage. Wajil was
finer and greyish in colour with a hardness similar to roof tiles. It has
mostly been excavated from the southeast of the peninsula. Long-necked
jars with horn-shaped handles and pouch- or bag-shaped jars were the most
characteristic types and they were intended as burial goods rather than for
everyday use. Gyeongjil was high-fired grey stoneware fired in a reducing
(low-oxygen) atmosphere and with a high level of hardness. It was
introduced in the third century AD and was made possible by the
developments in kiln technology (illus. 18).
     Tightly closed chamber kilns achieving firing temperatures higher than
1000°C were introduced, as evidenced by the excavation of kiln sites in the
middle and south of the peninsula. At first they were underground structures
but they later developed into above-ground structures. They had fuel
apertures, combustion chambers, pottery chambers and flue sections and
were climbing kilns with sloped floors. They gradually developed in
sophistication from the first century BC through to the third century AD, by
which time they featured large pottery chambers with ceilings as well as
divisions between combustion chambers and pottery chambers in order to

increase the firing temperature. The pottery was produced employing a
semi-specialized manufacturing system that involved a division of labour as
to the shaping, glazing and firing of vessels.3

Three Kingdoms Period, c. AD 300–668
Pottery has been discovered in tombs built beneath high mounds during the
Three Kingdoms period, providing evidence of the everyday wares and
burial goods of the ruling elite class of that time. Although the historical
record states that Goguryeo was founded in 37 BC, Baekje in 18 BC and Silla
in 57 BC, the period is usually taken to mean the years from about AD 300
until the unification under Silla in 668. During this period each of the three
kingdoms had a hereditary ruling class with its own laws, territory and
culture, and pottery was produced by specialized groups controlled by the
rulers.
    As far as kiln technology is concerned, climbing kilns were used that
could fire pots at 1000 to 1200°C. Bluish-grey gyeongjil stoneware was
produced that was hard and had a low absorption rate, as well as the red-
brown or grey earthenware (yeonjil) fired at a lower temperature. Kilns
have mostly been found in the south, and their structure was similar to those
in the earlier Proto-Three Kingdoms period, with a fuel aperture, a
combustion chamber, a pottery chamber and a flue section, but they were all
above ground. The gradient of the pottery chamber also increased, with
platforms inside, and there was a division block between the combustion
chamber and the pottery chamber.
       It is thought that it was during the Three Kingdoms period that the
production technology of high-fired stoneware was transmitted from the
Korean peninsula to Japan, resulting in the beginnings of Japanese sueki
ware.

Goguryeo
Goguryeo occupied a large area in the north of the peninsula, some of it
within what is now northeast China. Its origins were in the Yalu River
valley and its first capital was at present-day Ji’an, moving south to occupy
the Daedong River basin area with its later capital at Pyongyang. Goguryeo
even managed to capture the Baekje capital of Hansong (near Seoul) in AD
475 and the Baekje king was beheaded.

19 Roof tile end, 400–500, earthenware,
diam. 18.2 cm.

    More famous for its pyramid-shaped tombs with painted stone
chambers, and for the early introduction of Buddhism from China, evidence
of Goguryeo pottery is not huge, although it is recorded to have had a
government office entitled Chowaso, or Tile Production Office. Indeed,
beautiful Goguryeo roof tiles and tile-ends made of earthenware with high-
relief moulded decoration of lotus flowers and protective demon or dragon
masks have been found, evidence of how Goguryeo rulers decorated their
palaces and temples (illus. 19).
    As for vessels, low-fired earthenware jars, dishes and bowls have been
excavated from stone mound tombs in the Yalu River area and harder
stonewares from the Pyongyang area. One jar excavated in Pyongyang was
decorated with a cross-hatch or grid design. Around Seoul, cylindrical
tripods with lids and a coiled flat bottle have been excavated, dating to the
fifth century AD. Other notable Goguryeo vessels include a large jar with a
flared trumpet-shaped mouth, flat bottom and four handles (illus. 20). In
general, Goguryeo pottery used fine, sticky clay, built up with the coil
method and finished using a wheel. Sometimes the surface was burnished
or, later, a yellow glaze applied. About thirty different kinds of vessels have
been found that would have been used for storage, cooking, tableware and
transporting goods, the most elaborate being the long-necked jars and pots
with four handles. Decoration such as impressing and incising developed

into lattice, chain and diagonal abraded patterns (ammun). Grey stoneware
emerged in the later Goguryeo.4





20 Jar with flared mouth, 400–500, earthenware, height 59 cm.

Baekje
Baekje occupied the southwestern portion of the Korean peninsula and is
generally regarded as embodying the greatest artistic refinement and
sophistication of the Three Kingdoms. It had three capitals, gradually
moving south from present-day Seoul to Gongju and then to Buyeo. The
pottery technology evolved correspondingly from low-fired greyish

earthenwares to high-fired stonewares. Evidence of Baekje pottery has been
excavated from residential areas, fortresses and tombs. Pottery excavated
from a cemetery in the Seoul area includes black burnished wares that are
thought to show influence from the Yue kilns of southeast China, thus
demonstrating the cultural links between Baekje and that region at this
period, before the capital moved to Gongju in AD 475. They are decorated
with lattice patterns, grooved lines, wave patterns and spherical patterns.
    Low-fired grey earthenware vessels have been found in the fortresses
around Seoul, such as Mongchon and Pungnap, but high-fired stoneware
became more common by about the mid-fourth century, including elegant
jars and elaborate stands with three or four tiers, circular holes and
horizontal ridges (illus. 21). These stands bear comparison with cylindrical
haniwa (clay funerary objects, often figures) of the early Kofun period in
Japan.





21 Vessel stands, 400–500, stoneware, height 49.5 cm.

     Several strong kings ruled during the period when the Baekje capital
was in Gongju (AD 475–538). This was a time of much interaction and
cultural exchange with southeast China, as can be seen in the Chinese Yue
wares and white porcelains found in the tomb of Muryeong (reg 501–23),
the 25th king of Baekje, who allied with Silla to oppose Goguryeo. His
brick chamber tomb, excavated in 1971, also contained fine Korean-made

gold and silverware. Baekje also expanded relations with Japan: Takano no
Niigasa, mother of the Japanese emperor Kanmu (reg 781–806), was a
descendant of King Muryeong.





22 Incense burner, 550–600, gilt bronze, height 64 cm.

23.5 cm.





     Excavations in the Buyeo area show that by the time the capital moved
there in AD 538 many high-quality products were being made, such as the
famous Baekje gilt bronze incense burner (illus. 22). Scholarly implements
such as pottery inkstones are evidence of the lives and literary pursuits of
aristocrats and Confucian scholars (illus. 23). Elaborate pottery male
chamber pots or urinals with four legs, called hoja, have been excavated
from this area.
    Buddhist temple sites in the vicinity of Buyeo have yielded
earthenware roof tiles with elegant, moulded designs such as a bird within a
circle or a winged monster or dragon face. Some Baekje tiles decorated
with beautiful mountainous landscapes or swirling flames also show
influence from southern China and resemble landscape paintings (illus. 24).
   By this time, pottery technology had also advanced to the point where
hard, standardized grey stoneware was mass-produced under a specialized
manufacturing system. Kiln site excavations in north Chungcheong
Province have revealed semi-underground and underground kiln types. In
the underground kilns, believed to have operated from the fourth century AD,
wood for the furnace was inserted from above and the furnace mouth was
located 2 metres below the surface.

24 Tile, 600–660, earthenware, height 27.9 cm.

     In the southwest corner of the peninsula around the Yeongsan River,
pottery jar coffins have been found in residential areas and in cemeteries,
set within square or keyhole-shaped mounds similar to those of Kofun-
period Japan. Some huge jar coffins were made especially for burial of the
chiefs of the region (illus. 25).5

Gaya
Gaya was a loose confederacy of states that formed a triangle around the
centre of the south coast of the Korean peninsula and which grew out of the
twelve city-states of the former Byeonhan. It was centred on the valley of
the Naktong River, which flows out to the sea at present-day Busan. Gaya
was always caught between Baekje and Silla and was eventually conquered
by Silla in the late sixth century. The result is that it is sometimes extremely
difficult to tell the difference between the pottery of Gaya and Silla.
Considerable numbers of Gaya pots have been excavated in Japan.6
    Gaya pottery has been excavated from pit-shaped tombs and later
chamber tombs, the latter of which often contained huge numbers of tomb
pots, sometimes in separate chambers or stacked in rows at the head and
foot of the body. The pottery was sometimes accompanied by suits of iron
armour and horse trappings, evidence of the horse-riding warfare culture of
Gaya. It is thought that the large numbers of pots buried in some Gaya
tombs were used in shamanistic burial rituals, where they would have

contained offerings of food and wine, the remains of which have sometimes
been found (illus. 26).





25 Jar coffins from Naedong-ri, 450–550, earthenware.

26 Buried stem cups, 400–600, stoneware, excavation photograph.

    Both earthenware (yeonjil) and stoneware (gyeongjil) pots were
produced in Gaya. The latter were shaped using a potter’s wheel and fired
in climbing kilns at temperatures higher than 1000°C, causing a glassy
coating to be formed, a sort of proto-glaze, which enabled the pots to hold
liquids without leaking.
    The most common shapes of Gaya pots were pedestal bowls
(sometimes called stem cups) and long-necked jars, many with lids. Large
jars with round bases and tall stands with pierced decoration were also
made in fairly large numbers. Decorative techniques in Gaya consist of
incising, combing and piercing in square and triangle shapes. Some experts
maintain that one difference between Gaya and Silla decoration is that in
Gaya pedestal bowls or stands the pierced holes are in vertically aligned
rows, whereas in Silla examples the holes are aligned in alternating
positions from top to bottom (illus. 27).7
    Engaging duck-shaped vessels are characteristically Gaya. It is thought
that ducks were possibly regarded by Gaya people as intermediaries that

could guide the spirit of the dead into the afterlife. This may explain the
frequency with which duck-shaped vessels are found in Gaya tombs, no
doubt after their use in pre-burial rituals. These duck-shaped vessels usually
consist of a conical, sometimes pierced, stand, with the realistically formed
duck having a cylindrical hollow spout on its back for filling the vessel with
wine and a hole in its tail from which the contents could be drunk. The
duck’s wings are either shown as combed decoration or applied clay (illus.
28).





27 Ceremonial vessel stand, 500–600, stoneware, height 58.7 cm.

28 Duck-shaped vessel, 400–600, stoneware,
height 16.5 cm.





    The most elaborate Gaya pot, discovered in the Gimhae area, is in the
shape of a mounted soldier on horseback, the horse covered in a
representation of iron horse-armour. The pot is in fact a vessel with two
horn-shaped cups fixed on the back; these resemble rhyton vessels from
Western Asia, implying trade, possibly by sea. The production of a complex
vessel such as this suggests a highpoint of Gaya culture, and indeed its
fifth- or sixth-century date is just prior to the conquest of Gaya by Silla
(illus. 29).8

Silla
The Silla Kingdom in the southeast of the Korean peninsula adopted
Buddhism in the early sixth century and annexed Gaya towards the end of
the century. Shamanism, however, continued to be practised, and the Silla
kings probably also acted as shamans in some way, as evidenced by the
gold crowns found in Silla tombs, with their tree- and antler-shaped
decorations. Silla was known as the land of gold, as evidenced by the name
of its capital: Geumseong, or City of Gold.

30 Jar with integral pierced stand, 400–500, stoneware, height 30.3 cm.

31 Jar and tall pierced stand, 400–668, stoneware, height
34.4 cm (stand) and 30.2 cm (jar).





     Silla royal tombs were wooden chambers covered with a pile of stones
and an earthen mound. In them were buried gold crowns and vessels as well
as foreign imports such as glass, evidence of trade with China and further
west. The dangling, leaf-shaped ornaments that decorated some of the gold
crowns and vessels were also copied in Silla pottery.
     Silla pottery can be classed as stoneware. It was fired in climbing kilns
at temperatures above 1000°C, which made it extremely hard. It was thrown
on a rotating potter’s wheel and also developed a glossy surface due to the
high firing temperature. Silla kilns have been discovered and excavated in
the Gyeongju area as well as in Daegu and Gyeongsan.9
32 Jar with figurines, 400–500, stoneware, height 34 cm.

33 Sandal-shaped cup stands, 400–500, stoneware, height 16 cm (right).





34 Horse-rider shaped vessels, 500–600, stoneware, height 23.4 cm.

Many Silla pots were utilitarian stem cups and long-necked jars, which
were buried in tombs with their contents, foodstuffs for use in the afterlife
(illus. 30). Tall perforated stands were also buried. Some of these held
separate round-bottomed vessels, while in others the round bowl-shaped
vessel was integral to the stand and attached to the top of the stand. These
may have been used for pre-burial outdoor shamanistic rituals. Many of
these vessels had incised, combed and perforated decoration (illus. 31).
     Jars decorated with appliqué figures are characteristic of Silla. They
depict scenes of everyday life, including figures playing musical
instruments or engaged in sexual activity, which were presumably
connected with fertility rituals. The modelling of the figures is fairly rough
(illus. 32). There are also vessels in the shape of houses and straw sandals,
valuable evidence of architecture and clothing of the period (illus. 33).
    The most elaborate and sophisticated vessels from Silla are two ewers
in the shape of mounted horsemen of different ranks, excavated from the
Gold Bell Tomb in 1924. One depicts a servant wearing a jacket and
trousers, with a bag slung across his shoulders. The other wears pointed
shoes resting in stirrups and a high, narrow cap with broad ornamented rim.
They are both spouted drinking vessels and were found placed next to the
head of the deceased man, who was presumably a king or a prince (illus.
34).
    Another exceptional and sophisticated piece is a small vessel
excavated from the area of the King Michu Tomb. This seems to be
fashioned in the shape of a mythical beast of some sort, resembling a
tortoise-like dragon. It has a perforated integral stand, a long spout and a
pouring hole, but is far more decorative than practical (illus. 35).

35 Mythical beast with spangles, 450–550, stoneware, height 12.5 cm.

Unified Silla, AD 668–935
The period when Silla unified most of the peninsula was marked by many
cultural developments, and these were accompanied by innovations in the
pottery produced. The northern part of the peninsula was ruled by Balhae
(Parhae), refugees from Goguryeo. Since Silla had benefited from the help
of Tang China in unifying most of the peninsula, it is not surprising that
there was much Tang Chinese influence in this period. During the eighth
and ninth centuries many monks and students travelled to China to study
Buddhism or Confucianism, and Chinese goods were imported. The most
famous monk who travelled to China was Woncheuk, while Hyecho went as
far as India to visit Buddhist holy sites. Silla also had contacts with Arab
merchants and is mentioned in glowing terms in some Arab publications,
for example by the late ninth-century geographer Ibn Khordadhbeh, also
known as Ebn Khordadhbeh, a man of Iranian origin who wrote in Arabic:

What lies the other side of China is unknown land but high mountains
      rise up densely across from Kantu. These lie over in the land of Sila
    which is rich in gold. Mohammedans who visit this country are often
    persuaded by its fine qualities to settle down there. Ghorraib [ginseng],
    kino resin, aloe, camphor, nails, saddles, porcelain, atlas, cinnamon
    and galangal are exported from there.10

In fact, this was a time of openness, confidence and abundance, but also
increasing authoritarianism. Scholarship increased and technological
developments such as woodblock printing were introduced. Much effort
also went into building palaces and Buddhist temples.
    The affluence in Unified Silla, particularly in its capital Gyeongju, the
layout of which was based on Tang dynasty Chang’an, is perhaps best
illustrated, with regard to the pottery industry, by a record in the Samguk
yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms):

   When Silla reached the height of her prosperity, the capital, Gyeongju,
     consisted of 178,936 houses, 1,360 sections, fifty-five streets and
     thirty-five mansions. There was a villa and pleasure ground for each of
     the four seasons, to which the aristocrats resorted . . . During the reign
     of the forty-ninth King Heongang (874–885), houses with tiled roofs
     stood in rows in the capital and not a thatched roof was to be seen.11

36 Floor tile, 668–800, earthenware, height 35.4 cm.

    Examples of the pottery roof tiles used extensively in the villas,
palaces and temples around Gyeongju have been excavated from the Anapji
pond site along the shore of an artificial lake built in the late seventh
century under King Munmu. This, together with four palace buildings, was
excavated in 1975–6, revealing many architectural tiles, pottery, lacquer and
Buddhist images as well as a pine boat. Some of the floor tiles excavated
are decorated with the posang or ‘precious visage’ flower, and others with
lotus flowers, both showing the prevailing influence of Buddhism, which
had become the official religion (illus. 36). Their decoration also resembles
patterns on textiles found at Silk Road sites. Other pottery tiles, particularly
those placed at the ridge end of the roof, were decorated with a fearsome
face, which has been interpreted variously as a monster mask or a dragon
face; in both cases the function of these tiles would have been protective
(illus. 37).12
    The adoption of Buddhist practices led to the production of Buddhist
reliquary containers (often using metal or glass) and cinerary jars for
cremated ashes, instead of the large quantities of tomb pottery found from
earlier periods (illus. 38). These jars were often decorated with small
stamped or impressed designs rather than the incised and pierced decoration
of earlier periods. Stamped motifs include Buddhist clouds and lotus
flowers: the knobs on the lids were often in the shape of a lotus flower. This

decoration has been compared to that of ring-punched and chased silver and
gold vessels of the sort that were popular in Tang China. Some of the jars
can be dated from inscriptions and one has signs of the zodiac around the
neck.
    Chinese pottery excavated from sites around Gyeongju is evidence of
international trade. This includes a Tang sancai or three-colour ware
cinerary urn, as well as a Chinese Yue ware celadon found placed inside a
Unified Silla earthenware outer vessel. These rare and exotic pieces were no
doubt regarded as extremely precious and high status at the time (illus.
39).13
    Some of the pottery excavated from Anapji pond also provides
evidence of the lifestyle of the time. For example, a bowl decorated with
painted clouds and an inscription including the word ‘tea’ suggests that it
was used for tea drinking in a Buddhist context. Pottery water droppers and
inkstones excavated from the Gyeongju area are evidence of the scholarly
pursuits of the owners, while a charcoal stove decorated with birds presents
a picture of the sort of utensils used in daily life.14
    Small numbers of unglazed free-standing tomb figures, representing
people and animals, are extant that may date to the Unified Silla period.
These were no doubt influenced by the more sophisticated tomb figures of
the Tang (illus. 40).

    As far as kilns are concerned, the tradition of climbing kilns was
maintained, although those around Gyeongju tended to be clustered
together, whereas those in the regions were fewer and more individually
situated. The types of pottery produced in them differed as well. The pottery
produced in the Unified Silla period was harder and less absorbent than
earlier wares. Shapes of vessels produced included bowls with short
pedestals, long-necked pedestal pots, flattened round bottles and lidded jars.
    Some Unified Silla vessels were covered with a rudimentary ash glaze.
This technical step, combined with influence from celadons and white
wares imported from China, was to develop into the beginning of the
production of celadons in the ninth and tenth centuries and white porcelain
during the Goryeo period. There was no problem of attaining the high
temperatures needed to produce celadon and white porcelain as these could
already be achieved.
     In the Balhae area in the north of the peninsula, Goguryeo traditions of
pottery making continued, particularly grey pottery and the use of coarse
clay; glazing was also introduced, perhaps influenced by Tang three-colour
wares.15

CHAPTER TWO
       GORYEO
         PERIOD





It is fortunate that ceramics are rather hardier than paper, silk or wood and
cannot be melted down, unlike wares made of precious metals. This means
that more survive than works in those other materials. It is also fortunate

that a particular sort of ceramic – high-fired green stonewares of the Goryeo
period, now called celadons in the West – became so popular in Japan and
later when exported to Europe (illus. 41, 42). This led to them being prized
and collected, and thus preserved. In fact, the term ‘celadon’ was coined in
the seventeenth century in France, referring to the shepherd Céladon in
Honoré d’Urfé’s pastoral novel L’Astrée, whose clothes are described as
being trimmed with pale green ribbons of the same colour as the newly
arrived and prized ceramics (see illus. 198).

History
Goryeo (918–1392) was a high point in Korean history, marked by its
admiration of China and the extent of its cultural and economic exchange
with Song China, expressed in the words of Taejo (reg 918–43), the first
Goryeo king and founder of the dynasty: ‘We in the East have long admired
Tang ways. In culture, ritual and music we are entirely following its
model.’1 Goryeo literati participated in civil service examinations modelled
on the Chinese ones and spent their days writing poems and reading
literature. It is therefore not surprising that the elegant ceramics produced in
the early Goryeo for the educated upper classes who read and wrote
Chinese were greatly influenced by China.
    During this period, however, there were also three invasions of the
Goryeo by the nomadic Khitan people of the Liao dynasty on their
northwestern borders, which the Goryeo managed to repel. This led to
interchange with Liao refugees and craftsmen, and cultural influence from
the Liao sometimes manifested itself in the ceramics produced in Goryeo.
The Chinese envoy Xu Jing (1091–1153) refers to them in his account: ‘I
heard that among the several tens of thousands of Khitan prisoners who
submitted to Goryeo, one out of ten were craftsmen or artisans. The most
talented among them were chosen to reside in the royal palace.’ Some Liao
earthenware ceramics in the shape of leather bottles were imported and used
in the Goryeo, while Goryeo celadons sometimes reflect Liao influence in
their shape, such as vases with a ‘dished mouth’ (illus. 43). Floral scrolls
and openwork are shared characteristics, and Goryeo celadons sometimes
resemble Liao green-glazed earthenware figures. Some Goryeo celadons are
decorated with motifs that it has been suggested are derived from Liao wall
paintings. These include ducks, reeds and willow trees.2

The later Goryeo was a time of Mongol influence. Due to invasion by
the Mongols, who had also invaded China, the Goryeo kings intermarried
with Mongol princesses, and their sons were sent to Beijing, now ruled by
the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Mongol dress and language were used at court in
the Goryeo, and falconry became popular. One Goryeo king, Chungnyeol
(reg 1274–1308), even married a daughter of Kublai Khan. Again, this
influenced the ceramics produced in the later Goryeo period of the
thirteenth and fourteenth centuries (illus. 44). They became more densely
and elaborately decorated, usually with inlay, and human figures were
introduced, but the quality also declined as they became more widely
produced and available to more people. Another factor was the intermittent
raids along the south coast of Korea by Japanese pirates. This was the area
where most of the celadon kilns were located, so the coastal attacks led to
the potters dispersing and producing wares of varying quality at more
inland sites. Ultimately this led to the emergence of inlaid buncheong wares
in the fourteenth century.

Evidence
There is a great deal of evidence to take into account when studying
ceramics of the Goryeo period. There are references in literature, historical
records, poetry and travellers’ journals and some rare representations in
paintings of the period. Many of the actual surviving examples of Goryeo
ceramics seen in museums today were discovered as a result of building
railways towards the end of the nineteenth century and beginning of the
twentieth. Others were excavated from tombs, many in the period of the
Japanese occupation from 1910 to 1945. Excavations are continually

producing new evidence, particularly from kiln sites and, more recently,
shipwrecks.
     Literature shows that Goryeo celadons were highly prized in China.
The Song dynasty writer Taiping Laoren (dates unknown), for example, is
often cited as evidence that they were held in high esteem. He compared
them with the highest quality and most treasured products of China when he
wrote: ‘The books of the Academy, the wines of the Palace, the inkstones of
Duan, the peonies of Luoyang, the tea of Jianzhou, the brocade of Shu, the
porcelains of Dingzhou . . . the secret colour wares of Gaoli [Goryeo] . . .
are all first under heaven.’ Also, the Chinese envoy Xu Jing, who visited
Korea in 1123 and wrote a long account of his travels, commenting on all
aspects of Goryeo society, was likewise very impressed by the celadons
being produced there:





45 Tea bowls, 1100–1150, glazed stoneware, height 8.3 cm (max).

46 Roof tile, celadon, 1100–1200, glazed stoneware, height 27.2.

    The pottery wares are green in colour and are called kingfisher-
     coloured by the people of Gaoli. In recent years they have been made
    more skilfully and their colour and lustre have become finer. There are
    wine pots of gourd shape with small covers in the form of a duck amid
     lotus flowers. They also make bowls and dishes, cups and tea-bowls,
     flower vases and hot water bowls, all copied from the forms of Ding
    ware . . . but the wine pots are . . . different.3

    The historical records tell us that celadons became so popular that by
the mid-twelfth century they were even used for roof tiles on the summer
palace built by the eighteenth king, Uijong (reg 1146–70) (illus. 46). Roof
tiles had usually been made out of cheaper earthenware. The official history,
Goryeo-sa, records:

    More than fifty sections of people’s houses were destroyed and the
    Taepyong-jong building constructed. The Crown Prince was ordered to
     inscribe a tablet; famous plants and flowers were installed; rare and
     precious articles were displayed on all sides. To the south of this
     building a lake was made and the Kwallan-jong pavilion built. To the
     north, the Yang-i-jong pavilion was constructed and roofed with
     celadon tiles.4

47 Kundika, 1250–1350, inlaid stoneware, height 44.5 cm.

    Poems were written about Goryeo celadons at the time. For example,
the poet Yi Gyubo (1168–1241) referred to celadons, writing:

    Aglow in jade green
    Tempered through many a searing flame
    Unblemished as crystal
    Enduring as rock
      I see now the crafter’s skill
      Is touched with the heavenly gift.

Yi Saek (1328–1396) wrote: ‘The shining jade green is lit like the heavens/
A single glance can clear my eyes.’5
    There are also some examples of vessels portrayed in paintings of the
period, mostly Buddhist paintings, which were of extremely high quality
and precious due to the prevalence of Buddhism among the elite. The
vessels included are those made especially for Buddhist use, such the
kundika (spouted water sprinkler, illus. 47) or alms bowl.

Evidence from tombs and temples
Goryeo tombs varied in type from stone chambers to earthen pits. The
practice of cremation was widespread among Buddhists, and some ceramic
funerary urns have been discovered; however, interment, secondary burials,
exposure of bodies to the elements and the preservation or scattering of
bones were also practised. Limited use of slate coffins for bodily remains
seems to have been practised by the elite. Some of these coffins have been
found but unfortunately none were excavated in situ, making it difficult to
be certain about how they were employed: they do not seem large enough
for a recumbent adult corpse (illus. 48).
   Many celadons have been found in Goryeo tombs. Rather than being
buried for the deceased to use in the afterlife, it is thought that they were
placed in the tombs more as a sign of the status of the deceased and the
respect accorded to them by their descendants.6

48 Cinerary chest, 1150–1250, carved slate length 74.5 cm.

    The celadons found in the tombs of the Goryeo royal family include
the tombs of kings Injong, Myeongjong and Huijong, as well as queens
Wondeok and Sungyeong. These were all produced in the twelfth and
thirteenth centuries and were made in the kilns in Gangjin and Buan. They
have high-quality glaze and decoration and were made using spurs and
saggars. (Spurs, triangles of quartz or silica, are put between each vessel to
stop them sticking to the base of the kiln or to each other; saggars are
containers, covers or upturned boxes made of clay that can resist firing.)
Three of these royal tombs were located on Ganghwa Island and date from
the period of exile from the capital when the court fled from Mongol
invaders in 1231, but even those contain high-quality celadons. King
Injong’s tomb contained four very beautiful early celadons that can be
dated, as an epitaph in the tomb was dated 1146. There were also a silver
spoon and chopsticks set, a bronze box inside a stone box, both in the shape
of an elongated flower, and a bronze seal (illus. 49).

49 Artefacts from a royal tomb (attributed to King Injong), c. 1146, various materials.

    As well as royal tombs, celadons have also been excavated from the
Goryeo royal palace site at Manwoldae in the capital Gaeseong (now in
North Korea). The most well-known one is an inlaid vase decorated with an
image of a monkey, together with rare gold painting. The joint Northern and
Southern Korean excavations of 2007 at Manwoldae unearthed celadons
from a variety of periods all through the Goryeo dynasty.7
    Celadons have also been found at the site of a royal lodgings used by
Goryeo kings in Paju, as they travelled between Gaeseong and Seoul. A
variety of vessels, incense burners, pillows and plaques were all of high
quality and also made in the Gangjin and Buan kilns.8
    Non-royal Goryeo tombs, such as those of local officials, have also
been excavated. Over the years there have also been many unofficial
excavations or tomb robberies, particularly in the early twentieth century as
Goryeo celadons became traded and collected. A variety of wares have been
unearthed in this way, including both high- and low-quality celadons.9
    Most Buddhist temple sites have yielded celadons, showing the large
quantities used by Buddhist monks. Although bowls are the largest in
number, other items such as pillows, incense burners, cups and kundikas
have also been retrieved. Among the well-known Buddhist temple sites are
Mireuksa in Iksan, Godalsa in Yeoju and Seonwonsa in Ganghwa.10

Evidence from shipwrecks
The numbers of celadons excavated from shipwrecks have increased
dramatically in the last forty years, starting in 1976 when a fisherman
fishing off southwest Korea discovered some ceramics in his net; this initial
find led to the discovery and nine-year excavation of the Sinan shipwreck.
Since then, maritime archaeology has regularly revealed shipwrecks all
along the south, southwest and west coasts of Korea, plotting the route by
which the ceramics were shipped up to the capital at Gaeseong and to other
regions. Maritime transport was safer than carrying fragile ceramics
overland and it also allowed for larger shipments. Although the Sinan ship,
which went down around 1323, during the Mongol Yuan dynastic rule of
China, contained predominantly Chinese ceramics en route from Ningbo in
southeast China to Japan, its excavation led to the discovery in Korean
coastal waters of many more ships that carried celadons made in local kilns.
Moreover, some of the celadons were found to have wooden tags with
inscriptions on them, showing where and when they were made and even
what they contained and for whom they were made. Many of them were
offered as tax or tribute to the government and court. So far, tens of
thousands of such ceramics have been discovered in the sea. Bowls, dishes
or cups of the same size and shape were packed together in rows within
wooden frames, secured with string and then stacked vertically in crates
(illus. 50). The ships used to transport ceramics were traditional Korean
flat-bottomed freight ships designed for transporting heavy cargo such as
grain.
    Although items have been discovered underwater in about two
hundred coastal locations, perhaps the most well-known underwater
excavations are those off the islands of Wando, Biando, Daeseom and
Mado, the last between 2008 and 2010. More than 30,000 ceramics were
excavated off Wando island, most likely produced in the Haenam kilns of
South Jeolla Province. In excess of 3,000 ceramic objects were recovered
off Biando island, and these appear to have been produced in the Yucheon-ri
kilns at Buan, Chungcheong Province, judging from their shapes and
decorative techniques, such as inlay and moulding. The more than 20,000
ceramics excavated off Daeseom and Mado islands were probably made at
Sadang-ri in Gangjin, South Jeolla Province. In all cases the types of
vessels were predominantly bowls, dishes and cups, but sometimes bottles
such as maebyeong and ewers were found.

In the Wando excavations, part of the ship’s hull was recovered,
enabling a reconstruction of the original ship. The Biando shipwreck was
discovered when a sea wall was built and the water was re-channelled. Off
Daeseom island a small octopus was discovered in a celadon bowl, as well
as part of the hull of a ship and some more unusual pieces, such as a lion-
shaped incense burner, a toad-shaped inkstone and a lobed ewer. The
inscribed wooden tags are proof that this ship was going from Gangjin to
Gaeseong. As for the excavations around Mado island, there have been
three ships discovered so far, and the wooden tags provided proof that the
first ship set off in 1207–8 and was transporting tax goods. In the second
ship, two celadon maebyeong bottles had tags showing that one, with
incised lotus decoration, contained honey, while the other, with inlaid
decoration of peonies, willows and bamboo, contained sesame oil. This is
very interesting, given it had previously been thought that maebyeong
bottles were used just for wine (illus. 51).11

Technology
The best-known type of ceramic ware made in the Goryeo was celadon. Its
Korean name is cheongja, meaning ‘green ware’. In fact, the ware is a high-
fired stoneware made of a greyish hard-paste clay found in southwest Korea
as well as southern China. The raw material for Goryeo celadon ceramics is
low-clay, rich in quartz and with a high proportion of potassium oxide.12
The main development needed to produce the stoneware body was the
ability to reach high firing temperatures so that the clay vitrified (turned
into a glass-like material) and the texture became hard. The stoneware body
would then be covered with a translucent glaze coloured with iron oxide. In
some cases the wares were biscuit-fired (given a first firing prior to
glazing), the glaze was applied and then they were fired a second time at a
higher temperature. In others there was just one firing.
    As far as the glaze is concerned, the level of iron oxide is fairly low
(around 1.5–2.5 per cent by weight) and the green colour is produced when
the ferric oxide (Fe2O3) turns into ferrous oxide (FeO) as a result of losing
oxygen. This chemical reaction takes place during reduction firing.
Reduction firing is achieved by limiting the supply of oxygen by using wet
wood to fire the kilns, which creates a smoky atmosphere, and by tightly
closing any kiln openings. In cases where oxidation occurs during the
firing, the green colour is not the beautiful bluish-green but instead a
yellowish-brown. Oxidation occurs when a larger amount of oxygen is
present, the wood is dry, and it burns well. If there is too much iron oxide in
the glaze (about 5 per cent) then it can turn brownish-black. The other vital
element in producing celadons is titanium. The grey clay body of celadon is
due to the presence of about 1 per cent titanium dioxide (TiO2) combined
with 2–3 per cent iron oxide. If the celadon glaze also contains titanium
dioxide, it tends to turn a more olive-green colour.13
    The firing temperatures achieved in Goryeo period kilns are difficult to
determine exactly. However, it is generally agreed that the first biscuit-
firing temperature was about 800–900°C, and the second firing about 1225–
1250°C.14 At temperatures higher than 1250°C the body would tend to
collapse. There is also the question of how long the wares were held at the
peak temperature.
    The colour of the glaze on Goryeo celadons differs from that on
Chinese celadons. This is because the small manganese content is slightly

higher than the small titanium content. The glaze also contains about 3 per
cent iron.15 Much scientific research has been carried out in recent years
both in Korea and in the West on the chemistry of clays and glazes, giving
rise to new discoveries about the material qualities of Goryeo ceramics.16
     Nigel Wood is a scholar who has analysed and compared clays and
glazes used in early China and in Korea during the Goryeo. Notably,
Goryeo glazes are high in titanium dioxide and iron oxide in comparison to
Chinese Longquan, Ru and Yaozhou wares. Scientific analysis of
significant numbers of sherds has also allowed researchers to explain the
comparatively opaque appearance of Korean green-glazed ceramics, since
titanium dioxide affects the translucency of glazes that contain other oxides
such as iron and manganese.17 Wood has also highlighted the debate about
transmission of taste and style in East Asia in the twelfth century. Ru wares,
made in north China for the Song imperial palace, have always enjoyed
high prestige, not least because of their rarity. This has led to speculation
that Korean potters wanted to emulate Ru ceramics when they made high-
quality jade-green wares at the Gangjin kilns in the eleventh century.18
Wood argues that since it seems unlikely that court officials or potters in
Goryeo Korea could have seen or handled Ru wares, the suggestion that
Korean potters were strongly influenced by a Chinese Ru prototype is not
convincing. It is more likely, in his view, that Yue ceramics, from the kilns
in Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces of China, reached western Korea and
shaped preferences for colour and lustre in the early Goryeo period. Wood
has also noted that Ding wares, with their elegant, moulded decoration, can
also be considered a source of design transfer from Song China to Goryeo
Korea.
    Regina Krahl has researched collections in the UK and Germany and
has only recently re-examined brushwashers in the Dresden and Percival
David Foundation collections, persuasively proposing a Ru attribution for
two pieces previously identified as Goryeo celadon.19 The subtle
differences between celadon stonewares made in Song China and Goryeo
Korea can lead to differences of opinion among expert curators and
collectors, who are naturally familiar with the current state of the art market
and the prices achieved at auction for Song Chinese and Goryeo Korean
pieces. Ru ware is distinguished by a fine ‘cracked ice’ crackle in the glaze,
not found in the Korean production. The spurs on Ru vessels are famous for

their neat ‘sesame seed’ shape and precise placement, while the Goryeo
firing supports are somewhat rougher in general (see illus. 78, 79).
   A distinctive kind of foot-ring found on tea bowls in the early period of
celadon production has been closely studied, since it too indicates
connections with Yue wares. The ‘sun halo’ or haemurigup foot-ring, also
referred to as a ‘sun disc’ foot or a ‘ring’ foot, is common to Yue bowls and
Goryeo green-glazed bowls. Already in the 1960s the British collector and
scholar Godfrey Gompertz noted that ‘there are two kinds of foot in Yueh
ware, the first rather tall and splayed outward towards the base and the
second low and flat, with a wide foot-rim and a round recessed zone in the
centre. The second type is quite common in early Koryŏ celadons.’20
Gompertz concluded that a relationship certainly existed between Yue and
Goryeo potters, and his view has been supported by excavations undertaken
in Korea in the 1990s.21

Kilns
The evidence for the kilns used in the Goryeo comes from excavations,
which show that the ninth- and tenth-century kilns were located in the area
around the Goryeo capital of Gaeseong and also in Hwanghae Province.
These early Goryeo kilns were built with bricks and often very large, about
40 metres long. It is thought that these kilns were most likely built either by
or with the help of Chinese potters from the Yue kilns in Zhejiang, southeast
China, since they are very similar to those found in the Yue area. The exact
nature of the communication between the potters of Yue and those of the
Goryeo is uncertain, but it probably resulted in some way from the
government and trade links between China and Korea at this time. Well-
known excavations of brick kilns include Seo-ri and Bangsan-dong. When
Korea’s major ceramic areas moved south and west to Jeolla Province,
between about 1050 and about 1200, mud and rock kilns became
prevalent.22 The mud kilns around Gangjin were smaller than the northern
brick kilns, being about 10 metres long; they had a slope of 13–15 degrees
and so can be regarded as climbing kilns, also known as dragon kilns. It is
thought that pre-existing mud kilns, used earlier for making earthenware,
were most likely converted to produce stoneware. The smaller kilns had
some advantages in that they were simpler to build and use, particularly
with regard to controlling the firing temperature, they could be moved
easily, and were generally more flexible. The use of mud kilns spread all

over the southwest, particularly to Haenam, and gradually all kilns used
during the rest of the Goryeo period came to be mud ones of varying sizes
up to 20 metres long (illus. 52, 53).23

   An important step in producing beautiful, unblemished celadons was
using protective saggars inside the kilns. These are containers, covers or
upturned boxes made of clay that could resist the firing. They protected the
piece being fired from any ash or other debris falling from the roof of the
kiln. The pieces to be fired were each placed inside such a cover or saggar.
Some saggars had holes in their sides to allow gas to escape. Saggar-
protected ceramics were of a high quality and usually placed individually
inside the saggar.

Some local regional kilns would make lower-quality celadons without
the use of saggars, simply stacking the pieces to be fired in a sort of
pyramid with the largest at the bottom and the smallest at the top. The
potters would place some, usually three, very small spurs made of pointed
triangles of quartz or silica between each vessel in the stack, to stop them
sticking to the base of the kiln or to each other. The small marks made by
these spurs are characteristic of high-quality Goryeo celadons, and the use
of the spurs is another example of influence coming from China, where they
were also used, particularly in Ru and Yue kilns.24 Firing ceramics in stacks
and without saggars could lead to impurities from the kiln attaching
themselves to vessels, or to the vessels at the bottom being pressed down
and marked, or distorted or damaged on the base. Waste heaps at excavated
sites have numerous examples.
    The distribution of the celadon kiln sites known so far shows that the
area near Gaeseong, the Goryeo capital, had the greatest number. The
largest production sites, however, were in the southwest, in Chungcheong
and Jeolla provinces, in the areas around Buan, Gangjin and Haenam. The
Gangjin and Buan areas produced more high-quality pieces, whereas the
Haenam area had more mass production of everyday wares. So far 188 kiln
sites have been identified in Gangjin, 85 in the Buan area and 170 in the
Haenam area. Since no early celadons have been excavated from the Buan
kilns, it is thought that they started being used after the Gangjin kilns,
although there are many similarities in operation methods. In the early to
mid-Goryeo the production at Haenam and Gangjin was roughly the same
in terms of quantity, but of course not quality.25

Vessel Shapes
There is a link between ceramic vessel shapes and those made of
metalwork, such as silver and bronze. Often the same shapes occur in both
materials, with ceramics mostly copying metalwork shapes, such as in the
case of three- or four-legged incense burners copying ancient bronze shapes
(illus. 54). While some Goryeo celadon vessel shapes show influence from
China, such as cup stands, maebyeong jars and tea bowls, there are some
shapes that are uniquely and characteristically Korean. The Korean love of
the natural world manifests itself in the shapes chosen as well as in
decorative motifs. For example, vegetable and fruit shapes are the model for
vessels such as melon-shaped wine ewers, gourd-shaped bottles or peach-

shaped water droppers (illus. 55). Flowers are replicated in the shapes of
small cosmetic boxes, cup stands, saucers and bowls, and some items are
fashioned in the shape of animals, such as monkeys or ducks, and
sometimes even children (illus. 56). Xu Jing describes one such example:
‘The wine jar is shaped like a gourd. At the top is a small cover and the jar’s
surface is decorated with lotus flowers and prostrate ducks.’26

    There are examples of potters fashioning parts of vessels such as
handles or spouts in the shape of bamboo, or adding flowers in the form of
lids or knobs (illus. 57). Animals such as rabbits sometimes form the base
or legs of vessels, while lions are used on the lids of incense burners with
their mouths open to emit the smoke of the burning incense. This is also
referred to by Xu Jing: ‘The lion emits incense smoke and is also made in
kingfisher-coloured ware. The top consists of the crouching animal, which
is supported from below by raised lotus leaves. Of all the pieces, this one is
the most sublime’ (illus. 58). Xu Jing describes many vessel shapes in his
account, but it is not always clear whether the items are in metalwork or
ceramic, unless he specifically states which material he is referring to. He
does say that ‘as for other drinking and eating vessels, many are in the
shape of zun or yi wine vessels or the pu or kui food vessels.’27 These
presumably refer to Chinese bronze shapes. Among the other shapes of
Goryeo vessels listed by Xu Jing are water bottles, a stem cup with saucer, a
mountain of the immortals incense burner, wine crocks, basins with black
flower decoration, facial ointment flasks, a blooming lotus ewer, portable

bottles, oil bottles, kundikas, flower vases, water cauldrons, water pitchers,
hot water bottles, brass basins, tripod incense burners, ceramic wine jars
and ceramic incense burners. Vessel shapes of course differed according to
use, whether at court, at table, in Buddhist rituals, on architecture or
furniture or by ladies for cosmetics. There is even one celadon ewer in the
form of a Daoist Immortal holding a basket of peaches. The celadon roof
tiles commissioned by King Uijong are usually seen as an example of
conspicuous consumption.

Decoration
At first the celadons produced in the Goryeo period were either plain and
undecorated or had incised designs. The emphasis was on the shape of the
vessel rather than the decoration, although there are beautiful examples of
very simple and very complex incised designs. In this respect, early Goryeo
celadons were similar to Chinese celadons. The incised designs would have
been made when the clay body was leather-hard and before glazing and
firing. Later in the Goryeo, carved designs were incorporated, especially on
the outside of tea bowls (illus. 59), where lotus leaves were popular, as in
Chinese Yue wares. Another decorative technique was the use of moulds to
impress designs, particularly on bowls. This enabled more complex designs
to be mass produced with less effort, as the moulds could be reused.





58 Lion incense burner, 1100–1200, glazed
stoneware, height 21.2 cm.

    The most well-known technique of decoration in the Goryeo, however,
was that of inlay, called sanggam in Korean (illus. 60). Although inlaid
wares and slip-painted wares were made in Tang China, inlaid celadon is an
innovation of which Koreans are very proud. It is a development of the
incising technique mixed with the slip-painting technique: the incised
design is filled in with special materials that produce either bright white or
dark black colours. One infill material, consisting of quartz, glass and clay,
produces a mineral called mullite when fired. The other material contains

iron oxide, along with oxides of calcium, phosphorus and manganese, and
becomes very dark-coloured when fired. The two contrasting colours
accentuate the designs on the vessels. Glaze was always applied just before
firing, when the vessel’s body and inlaid design had dried out in the potters’
workshop for some days. Inlay was also popularly used in Korea on lacquer
(inlaid with mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell) and metalwork (such as
bronze inlaid with silver), and there was an overlap between the decorative
motifs employed in the different media. One decorative motif particularly
common in both inlaid celadons and lacquer was that of a stylized
chrysanthemum (illus. 61). The use of inlay to decorate celadons developed
during the Goryeo and into the Joseon, where it evolved into buncheong
wares. The beginnings of inlay on celadons and its chronological
development is the subject of some debate at present, but it is generally
thought to have been introduced in the twelfth century and developed
rapidly in the early thirteenth.

One way in which inlay further developed was with the creation of the
reverse inlay technique, in which the background of the design is inlaid
rather than the design itself, leaving the design in the original colour of the
body and celadon glaze, while the background is inlaid with white or black
clay (illus. 62). It is sometimes combined with the normal inlay technique
in one object, where the inside might have a reverse inlay scroll design and
the outside a normal inlay design.
    Another decorative technique that is thought to have originated in the
Goryeo is that of underglaze copper-red painted celadons. Again, Tang
China saw the first use of copper red (on the glaze of ninth- and tenth-
century Changsha wares), but it was not used under the glaze in China to
decorate celadons. It is a notoriously difficult technique to use as copper red
is not easy to control during firing, when it can turn green instead of red. It
was used initially to decorate details of inlaid motifs, such as the tips or
centres of flowers, but there exist a few pieces where it was used to
decorate the entire vessel. The British Museum’s lavishly painted tea bowl
is evidence of the high quality achieved (illus. 63), and there are also
several very famous ewers of thirteenth-century date, such as the one in the
Leeum Museum in Seoul, where the outline of the carved lotus petals is
beautifully painted in underglaze copper red. Some celadons were painted
in underglaze iron brown, while in some the iron brown decoration covered
the entire body of the vessel (illus. 64).
   On very rare occasions gold was used, painted over the glaze. The gold
paint is made from gold powder mixed with gelatin. After the gold
decoration was painted over the glaze, the vessel would be fired again at a
relatively low 800°C. Sometimes there would already be an inlaid pattern,
which would be outlined, highlighted or enhanced in gold overglaze, such
as in the vase inlaid with a monkey and tree design found at the site of the
Goryeo royal palace at Manwoldae, near Gaeseong. Very few examples
exist – currently only ten are known – and often there are only traces of
gold remaining on the surface. A thirteenth-century gold-painted stand in
the Victoria and Albert Museum collection has inlaid decoration of
phoenixes, cranes and dragons, with gilding on the rim and base (illus. 65).
It would most likely have held a lidded bowl and spoon such as the similar
one in the Leeum Museum in Seoul. Most of the remaining seven known
gilded celadons are small incense boxes.

It is thought that gold-painted celadons would have been made for
royal use, and indeed there is evidence in the Goryeo historical records that
gold-painted celadons were twice sent as royal gifts to the Chinese Yuan
court in the late thirteenth century. The style of decoration on the gold-
painted celadons is more detailed and complex and of a type that may have
appealed to Yuan Mongol taste. It could also be that the development of
gold-painted celadons is linked to or influenced by Chinese Ding wares,
which sometimes had gold leaf decoration, or possibly by Chinese Jian
black wares, which had powdered gold decoration. The gilded decoration
also reflects the well-developed Goryeo technique of painting illuminated
sutras in gold and silver powder, which was prevalent in the late thirteenth
century when the gilded celadons were produced.28
