    Some celadons have been found with inscriptions in Chinese
characters. Chinese script was of course used during the Goryeo rather than
the native Korean phonetic Hangeul script, which was not introduced until
the fifteenth century. Some of the inscriptions on vessels are lines of poetry
or simply instructions as to placement of multiple parts, such as celadon
tiles. Inscriptions such as ‘palace’, ‘royal palace’ or even ‘long live the
emperor’ clearly refer to the place where the vessel would be used, in these
cases the royal palaces. Others have the names of government offices, such
as ‘royal pharmacy’, ‘royal alcohol distillery’ or ‘royal treasury’. There is

one inscribed with the name of the tomb of a queen, Noguk, who died in
1365. All these inscriptions are evidence of the use of celadons by the court
and aristocracy.
   A majority of inscriptions are of dates in the Chinese sixty-year
calendar cycle used during the Goryeo. They provide very useful
information about when pieces were produced, when certain kilns were
active or about dating tombs or sites in which they were found. The
challenge is that each cyclical date could be in one of several cycles; for
example, the inscription gisa could refer to 1269, 1329 or 1389. Most
inscriptions date to the thirteenth or fourteenth centuries (illus. 66).29

Decorative motifs
As with the vessel shapes, the Korean love of nature also manifests itself in
the way in which celadons are decorated. Very often the decorative motifs
refer to plants, flowers, trees, birds and animals. Natural phenomena
abound, such as waves and clouds. Particularly popular flowers are the
chrysanthemum, lotus, peony, hibiscus and the bosanghwa, an imaginary
Buddhist flower sometimes called the ‘precious visage flower’. The
chrysanthemum signified nobility, being one of the ‘Four Gentlemen’ in
China. It is also associated with autumn. The lotus has Buddhist
associations, symbolizing purity, since it rises out of the mud of the pond as
the Buddha rises out of the dirty world; while the peony carries a meaning
of wealth, prosperity and peace. The significance of the hibiscus, also
known as the rose of Sharon, stems from its Korean name, mugung, which
means ‘eternity’ or ‘inexhaustible abundance’. It has in more recent times
become the national flower of Korea.

    Leaf scrolls feature on many celadons, particularly tea bowls, whether
inlaid or painted. It is not always clear what type of leaf is being depicted,
but there are examples of ginseng leaves as well as vine leaves. Bowls
decorated with carved upright lotus leaves in regular rows around the
outside are also common and show links with Chinese wares (illus. 68).
    Bamboo, willows, reeds and water birds are a favourite motif on inlaid
celadons in particular. Willows were associated with Buddhism and are
often seen in Buddhist paintings of the period, held by the bodhisattva
Gwaneum. The willow and water bird motif is often used to decorate
Buddhist water sprinklers. Bamboo is a symbol of scholarly integrity due to
its ability to bend in the wind but not be broken (see illus. 57).

Many-seeded fruit, such as melons, grapes and pomegranates, have
auspicious meanings and are associated with abundance (illus. 67). Groups
of babies and small children are also depicted, showing a desire for many
offspring. Peaches signify wishes for immortality and lychees mean love.
     Turtles, monkeys, rabbits, fish, frogs, lions, dragons and cranes all
appear on celadons, either as decoration or making up part of, or the entire,
body of the vessel. They all have symbolism that would have been
immediately recognized by Koreans at the time: turtles and cranes for
longevity, fish for abundance and so on. Many of these symbolic meanings
had links with Daoism or Buddhism. Monkeys were thought to be clever
and cunning and therefore carried wishes for success as well as long life.
They also represent a pun on the Chinese characters for monkey and for
feudal lord, which were both pronounced the same, thus expressing a wish
for a high-level government post. Many decorative motifs represented such
puns, which ultimately derive from China.
    The crane and cloud motif is often used on inlaid celadons, particularly
maebyeong bottles. Sometimes the cranes are enclosed in roundels. Cranes
symbolize long life as well as transcendence and a means of getting to the
heavens. Because they are thought to mate for life, they also express a wish
for a long marriage. Repetition of this motif all over the vessel would
reinforce the message, especially when paired with clouds (illus. 69).

    As producers of rain, clouds sustain long life. In their swirling forms
they contain the Daoist breath of life (Korean gi, Chinese qi). When their
vapours gather around the mountaintops, they represent the uniting of yin
and yang (Korean eum and yang), soft and hard, changeability and
permanence. The shape of the clouds in some cases resembles the form of
the mushroom of immortality, reinforcing their connection to longevity. In
Daoist philosophy, water is one of the five eternal elements – together with
earth, fire, metal and wood – that make up the cosmos, so both clouds and
waves contain this symbolism when used as decorative motifs.

In fact, Daoism and the belief in Daoist Immortals is often present in
celadon decoration, but especially in the crane-and-cloud design. Goryeo
literature abounds in Daoist Immortals riding on cranes, and evidence of
Daoist practice can also be seen on some celadons that have inscriptions
linking them to use in Daoist rites and to constellations important in
Daoism, such as the Seven Stars and the Big Dipper.
   On relatively rare occasions in the later Goryeo (fourteenth century),
celadons were decorated with human figures, usually representing well-
known stories from history or literature. One such example is a jar inlaid
with a scene of the story of the Chinese calligrapher Wang Xizhi watching
geese, after a famous Yuan dynasty painting.30
       It is appropriate that some celadon vessels made to copy the shapes of
ancient and archaistic Chinese bronzes should also have moulded
decorations of monster masks, dragons and square-spiral thunder patterns,
just as the bronzes they are copying did.

How Were Celadons Used?
Celadons were used by the court and the aristocracy, as well as in Buddhist
monasteries and Daoist rituals. They were not used by ordinary people as
they would have been much too expensive. They were made by closely
controlled communities of potters under local government supervision and
transported to the capital area for use by the elite. We know that, unusually,
they were used in architecture as roof tiles by Uijong, the eighteenth
Goryeo king, who ruled from 1146 to 1170, and they were also most
probably used to decorate furniture; rectangular decorative plaques or tiles
exist that are thought to have been inserts for furniture such as tabletops;
and celadon garden seats were also made (illus. 70). Most of the celadons,
however, would have been used at table: bowls, cups, cup stands, ewers and
dishes attest to this use (illus. 71). They were also used by aristocratic ladies
as containers for items of toiletry and cosmetics, such as bottles for hair oil
or covered small boxes for rouge and face powder (illus. 72). Sometimes
these bottles and covered boxes are found in sets – the boxes are round or
form parts of a flower. They have been found in tombs together with bronze
mirrors, hairpins, earpicks and sewing equipment such as needle holders,
evidence of the lifestyle of aristocratic ladies.
    Gentlemen used celadon water droppers and inkstones on their desks,
as befitted Confucian scholar-gentlemen. Water droppers have been found

in the shapes of ducks and other animals (see illus. 56). Brush stands and
brush rests were also made in celadon as well as seals, spittoons and
buttons.
    The monks in Buddhist monasteries were often sons of the aristocracy
and very well educated, copying out sutras in beautiful calligraphy in gold
and silver ink. Celadon incense burners, pure water holders or sprinklers
(Korean jeongbyeong, Sanskrit kundika), spouted bowls, ewer and bowl
sets, Buddhist figures such as Luohan, and tea bowls all show that celadons
were in use in Buddhist monasteries in the Goryeo (illus. 73). Kundikas are
described by Xu Jing thus, although he is most likely referring to metal
ones, the shape of which was copied in celadon:

    The kundika has a long neck and a stout body; on the side there is a
     spout. The spout is divided into two sections that are connected with a
     hinge. In the middle of the neck there is a rim and above the rim there
      is another small neck that looks as thin as a hairpin or brush. They are
    used by aristocrats and state officials and in Buddhist and Daoist
     temples and people’s homes. They can only store water. They are one
     foot two inches high and four inches in diameter at the belly and
     contain three pecks.31

    Tea drinking played an important part in Goryeo society, both secular
and Buddhist, as it did in China and Japan. It is said that tea plants were
introduced to Korea from China during the eighth century. A tea ceremony
called Jindarye was held at various royal Goryeo ceremonies, and the court
started to bestow tea as rewards to people. The Goryeo histories also
mention different venues used for tea drinking.32 It is sometimes said that
tea drinking was a good way for Buddhist monks to keep themselves alert
during endless hours of meditation and chanting. At this time, tea was made
and drunk in bowls and there was no use of teapots. The bowls were quite
large. Large numbers of celadon tea bowls remain, some plain and others
with incised, carved, inlaid or painted decoration (see illus. 45). One
common type has the outside decorated with vertical carved lotus petals,

making the shape of the bowl itself resemble a lotus flower, an appropriate
shape for Buddhist use (see illus. 68).
   Xu Jing describes the importance of tea drinking:

     Recently the Koreans have become fond of drinking tea. They are also
     adept at making tea utensils, such as the black cups decorated with

    The question of what the beautiful maebyeong or ‘plum blossom’
bottles or vases were used for has often been debated (illus. 74). The term
maebyeong is a later one, showing that they were sometimes used as flower
vases to hold a single branch of plum blossom in their narrow neck.
However, it is likely that originally they were used to contain liquids such
as wine, honey or oil (as is evidenced by those found in shipwrecks). They
had conical lids with a flat top, which could be turned upside down and
used as a cup. Many of these lids have been lost. Xu Jing describes flower
vases thus: ‘The flower vases are narrow and pointed above and round
below, like a suspended gall-bladder . . . they are at all times filled with
water and contain flowers. In former times they were not very well made
but recently the Koreans have become quite proficient in making them.’
Which existing vessels fit this description is difficult to say. He also talks of

Links with Other Materials
There is no doubt that many celadon vessel shapes mimic those of
metalwork such as silver and bronze. Ewers, bowls, cups and cup stands,
dishes, pillows and incense burners are all examples of vessel shapes that
occur in both.
    Of course, some of these vessel shapes derived from Chinese bronzes,
such as three- and four-legged tripods. These were copied in Chinese Song
dynasty celadons as well as in the Goryeo, although not often put to the
same use: sometimes they were used as planters, for example. Some were
derived from Liao metalwork, such as a silver ewer excavated from the
tomb of the Liao princess Chenguo, dated to 1018.35 Some metalwork
vessel shapes were particularly difficult to reproduce in ceramic, such as the
kundika (see illus. 47).
    There are also many examples of decorative techniques that can be
seen in both ceramic and metalwork, such as incising or chasing, moulding,
inlaying and piercing or openwork. Bronzes inlaid with silver are
sometimes copied in inlaid celadon and the decoration is similar in subject-
matter, such as that of ducks among willows.
    Some ceramics of the Goryeo also show influence from lacquer or
wood in their shapes and particularly in the inlay technique. For example,
the popular inlaid decoration of stylized chrysanthemums on some lacquer
pieces is reflected on celadons (see illus. 60).
     Decorative motifs seen on celadons, such as roundels of stylized
flowers, also reflect patterns decorating the silk robes worn by deities in
Goryeo Buddhist paintings (illus. 75).

75 Roundels on a silk robe, detail from Buddhist scroll
painting, 1300–1400, ink and colour on silk.





Links with China
In his travel account the Chinese envoy Xu Jing several times refers to the
similarity between Goryeo celadons and Chinese Song dynasty wares. For
example, when describing lion-shaped incense burners, he writes: ‘Of all
pieces this one is the most sublime. The rest are very similar to the old
secret colour ware of Yuezhou or the new ceramic wares from Ruzhou.’ He
also says: ‘The Koreans can also make bowls, plates, wine cups, small cups,
vases, vessels for hot liquids and refined cups. Because all are modeled on
the established system of vessels from China, I have omitted to draw
them.’36 These references show that Goryeo wares were similar in shape
and glazes to Yue wares and Ru wares. This is interesting because Yue
wares were produced in southeast China and Ru wares in north China,
showing that the routes by which Chinese ceramics were transmitted to
Korea must have come both through the north, most likely overland, and
the south, most likely by sea.
       It is generally accepted that celadon technology was first brought to
southwest Korea by sea from the Yuezhou area. During the ninth century
the Koreans had a reputation as skilled sailors and navigators, especially
around the coast of southwest Korea and in the East Sea between Korea and
China. They were led by Jang Bo-go (d. 846), a military officer in eastern
China who became established as an influential maritime figure in that
region, leading Korean communities who enjoyed a semi-autonomous
status on the Shandong peninsula. He later returned to Korea and built a

garrison on his native Wando Island off the southwest coast, during the
latter years of the Unified Silla period, in order to fight the slave trade. It is
thought that Koreans under Jang Bo-go were instrumental in bringing
celadons and celadon technology to Korea.37
    As mentioned earlier when looking at technology, one of the obvious
similarities between Chinese and Korean celadons is the style of foot on tea
bowls, which were produced in large numbers both in China and Korea.
The foot was wide at the base and very low, resembling a circular jade ring
with a hole in the middle, known as bi or huan in Chinese. In Korean this
kind of foot was called a haemurigup, as it resembled the sun’s halo.
Excavations at Seo-ri, Bangsan-dong and Jungam-ri have established that in
the ninth century, kilns in central Korea were already producing large
numbers of celadon bowls that closely resemble Chinese Yue ware bowls.38

    Other similarities to Yue wares are in the carved vertical lotus petals
decorating the outside of many early Goryeo tea bowls; it is sometimes
difficult to differentiate them from Yue bowls. There are also various types
of bottles and jars, such as those with the ‘dished’ type of mouth (see illus.
43), those with vertical ribs and a trumpet mouth, and of course the
maebyeong bottle, which all resemble Chinese Yue wares.
    The similarity of some early Goryeo wares to Ru ware lies in the
bluish colour of the glaze, due to small amounts of titanium oxide (less than
half that found in Chinese Yue or Yaozhou wares), and to the simple, plain
but classically beautiful forms with minimal decoration. It is sometimes
difficult to differentiate early Goryeo from Ru wares (illus. 76, 77). The use
of three small spur marks on the base of the vessels is also testament to the
influence of Ru ware (illus. 78, 79). The ceramic scientist Carolyn
Kyongshin Koh Choo comments that this similarity is puzzling as the two
wares are made of very different kinds of body and glaze material: the
northern Ru ware used highly kaolinitic clay, whereas Goryeo wares used
porcelain stone low in aluminium oxides. As mentioned earlier, Wood
suggests that Ding wares may have been the link.39
    The influence of white Ding wares from northern China on Goryeo
celadons can be seen in vessel shapes and decorative techniques and motifs,
as can that of southern Qingbai wares, both of which ultimately copy silver
vessels (illus. 80).

80 Ewer and basin, 1100–1200, parcel gilt silver,
height 34.3 cm (ewer).





    There are some similarities between Chinese Yaozhou wares and
Goryeo wares, particularly those with a more olive-green glaze. The use of
moulds for decoration inside tea bowls is common to both, as is the
introduction of painted slip decoration, which of course was a precursor in
Korea of the development of sanggam inlay. The question of exactly how
Chinese wares influenced Goryeo wares and vice versa is a complicated one
that needs more research.
     In general, the shapes of Goryeo wares often mimicked those of
Chinese Song dynasty pieces, but there was a gradual transformation as
well as an introduction of new shapes. The maebyeong vase is a well-
known example, the earlier Goryeo versions having straight sides more like
Chinese wares, while the later ones developed a more curvaceous profile.
    The fact that Goryeo celadons have been excavated from sites in China
is proof that they were valued and exported there as part of the close trading
relationship between China and the Goryeo. In the Hangzhou area, capital
of the Southern Song, high-quality celadon vessels have been excavated
from Huangcheng and from the tomb of Empress Gongshengrenlie (reg
1202–24). A gourd-shaped ewer dated 1184 was also found at a tomb in
Babaoshan, Beijing. In the late thirteenth and the fourteenth centuries there
was also trade in ceramics between Goryeo and the Yuan, possibly
facilitated by Muslim merchants. The Goryeo ceramics were mostly
excavated from tombs in the Liaoning area of northeast China, although
some small numbers have been discovered in Inner Mongolia, Hebei
Province (in the tomb of a Yuan prime minister, Shi Tianze), Jiangsu and
Zhejiang provinces.40

Links with Japan
Goryeo celadons have also been found in Japan. Although there is no
historical record of exchanges of ceramics between Japan and Korea during
the Goryeo, there is of course evidence from the fourteenth-century Sinan
shipwreck that such exchange and trade happened. In the ship, which was
en route to Japan from Ningbo in China, there were seven Goryeo ceramics
among the huge numbers of Chinese ones. This suggests that there was
some measure of trade or exchange of Goryeo ceramics between Korea and
Japan via China during the Yuan dynasty.
    There is also archaeological evidence of such trade and exchange
links. Fairly large numbers of Goryeo ceramics have been excavated from
sites in Kyushu, southwestern Japan. For example, in Hakata, a port that
was one of the main points of interaction between Japan and mainland Asia,
many Goryeo celadon vessels dating from the eleventh to the thirteenth
centuries have been found at the important Dazaifu administrative centre
and diplomatic guest house site. It is estimated that these were products
from the Gangjin, Buan and Haenam kilns, and they were mostly bowls and
dishes for everyday use.
    Celadons have also been excavated in the Nagasaki area and on
Tsushima Island (a phoenix-shaped ewer), at the Kaijinjinja shrine in Saga
prefecture and on Okinawa. The last date to the fourteenth century.
     Furthermore, a variety of Goryeo celadons have been found in sites in
Tokyo, Kyoto, Kanagawa and Kamakura, some being high-quality inlaid
celadons. The bottles and jars excavated in Kyoto and Kamakura are of
noticeably higher quality than those found in Hakata and are in different
shapes.41

Other Ceramic Wares Made in the Goryeo
White porcelain wares were produced throughout the Goryeo period in
limited numbers. It is probably the case that white porcelain was made in an
attempt to reproduce Chinese Ding wares. The porcelain body is described
as ‘soft-textured’ by Choo, but there were some pieces that were made with
a hard-textured white body. Several of the kiln sites where white porcelain
was produced at this time were among those that produced celadon, such as
Bangsan-dong (a particularly early site in Gyeonggi Province), Yucheon-ri
in the Buan area and Seo-ri and Sadang-ri in the Gangjin area, as evidenced

by the excavation of quantities of sherds. Yucheon-ri is known for
producing higher-quality white porcelain. One site, Wonsan-ri, is located in
modern North Korea. Researchers believe that the shift in production of
court ceramics from central to southwestern Korea followed the destruction
of the kilns at Wonsan-ri. White porcelain of this time mostly had a creamy
or ivory colour with a finely crackled glaze. It was decorated with some of
the same techniques used on celadons, such as incising, moulding, carving
and inlay. It was also made in some of the same shapes, such as cup stands,
bowls and maebyeong jars (illus. 81). A particularly beautiful and high-
quality example of Goryeo white porcelain is the melon-shaped wine ewer
and warming bowl in the Museum of Oriental Ceramics in Osaka, which
has a bluish tinge resembling Chinese Qingbai wares (illus. 82). Although it
is clear that Goryeo potters knew how to make white porcelain and there
was plenty of suitable clay, it seems that the overwhelming preference
among users in the Goryeo was for celadons.42
    Black tea bowls are referred to by Xu Jing: ‘They are also adept at
making tea utensils, such as the black cups decorated with golden
flowers.’43 Black wares were the result of using large amounts of iron oxide
and are sometimes called iron brown wares. Iron oxide was used for
underglaze decoration on celadons and many of the designs used show
influence from Chinese Cizhou wares. However, it was also used to paint
over the entire surface of the vessel, apart from the base, and then covered
with a celadon glaze. In such cases a completely black ware is produced.
Bottles, ewers and bowls were all produced entirely in black. Some were
left this way, but there were also several ways in which others might be
decorated, perhaps with an incised design, inlaid in white or painted with
white slip. Many of the entirely black wares were made at Haenam in South
Jeolla Province (illus. 83).

CHAPTER THREE
THE JOSEON
DYNASTY AND
THE COLONIAL
  PERIOD

The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea from 1392 to 1910, an exceptionally long
reign. In looking at the ceramics made during these five centuries, it is
helpful to consider the historical, political and aesthetic movements that
changed Joseon society over time. For this reason, this chapter will divide
the subject into two large chronological periods, before and after the wars
of the 1590s, known as the Imjin Waeran, or Japanese Disturbance of the
Imjin Year (1592 in the Gregorian calendar, conventionally known by its
cyclical year name in East Asia). The last period of the Bunwon kilns and
the ceramics of the Japanese colonial period are briefly discussed. After a
review of Joseon ceramic technology and kiln operation, the chapter
considers some special wares (onggi vessels, and ceramics from the far
northeast of the peninsula), concluding with discussion of Koreans’ ceramic
contacts with their East Asian neighbours.
    The fourteenth century was a time of tumultuous change across East
Asia. In Korea the Goryeo court had already abandoned resistance to the
Mongols in 1270. Economic conditions and government control of the land
were disrupted and unpredictable. Potters and their kilns were affected by
the military unrest and lack of security that spread across the country. The
fine, green-glazed ceramics that had been manufactured in such great
quantity between 1100 and 1250 had ceased production, and in their place
emerged a rougher type of stoneware. By about 1350 Mongol control of
China weakened, allowing brigands from China to swoop down into Korea
from the land border in the north and forcing the court to abandon the
capital, Gaeseong, to take refuge on Ganghwa Island. At the same time,
security along Korea’s coastline was threatened by Japanese attacks. During
the golden era of the mid-Goryeo, huge ships loaded with cargoes of
thousands of celadons from Jeolla Province had navigated the treacherous
route northwards to the capital, bringing cups and bowls, bottles, water
droppers and even ceramic drums and green-glazed roof tiles to customers
there.1 By the fourteenth century, life in settlements along the shoreline had
become precarious as Japanese raiding parties attacked at will, causing
whole communities, including potters, to move inland in search of safety.
Since many Goryeo kilns had operated near the sea, ceramic artisans
relocated to places such as the Chunghyo-dong kiln site in Jeolla Province
that previously had been minor centres. The once monumental coastal kilns
of Gangjin and Buan fell into decline.

Against this background of protracted disorder and national weakness,
a military commander, Yi Seong-gye, took matters in hand and ousted the
last Goryeo rulers, establishing a new dynasty with the title of Joseon and
ruling as King Taejo from 1392 to 1398. To emphasize the break with the
past, the capital was moved from Gaeseong to Seoul. It was during the reign
of the fourth Joseon king, Sejong (reg 1418–50), that the wide-ranging
changes in government, and the benefits of comparative stability and order,
became particularly apparent. The production and use of ceramics were
reviewed and reorganized as part of the ambitious projects of the new
dynasty. Surveys of kilns across the country were carried out in 1424–5,
recording manufacture of both stoneware and high-fired porcelain. The new
dynastic rulers were profoundly influenced by the philosophy of Confucius,
and in particular by the version of his doctrines known as neo-
Confucianism that held sway in China after about AD 1000. Neo-Confucian
philosophy lays stress on ritual, etiquette and correct behaviour. Above all it
stresses the role of the virtuous ruler. It proposes a model of government
where correct moral principles and actions begin with the monarch and then
reach down into other classes through a strict, hierarchical social system.
Respect for ancestors was demonstrated through carefully choreographed
ceremonies involving ritually appropriate utensils, including ceramics.
Regulations and instructions about Confucian rituals were published by the
Korean court, with the 1474 ‘Illustrated Explanation of the Five Rites of
Government’ providing a template for the archaistic, Chinese-designed
vessels that were required in Confucian ceremonies.
   An all-encompassing code of behaviour laid out the rules to encourage
correct relationships between king and courtier, father and son, elder and
younger brother, and husband and wife. Neo-Confucians taught that
austerity was a virtue, and so for ceramics this meant that the sumptuous,
green-glazed wares of the Goryeo fell out of favour, because they were
broadly associated with extravagance and with Buddhist culture. The
Joseon period saw a remarkable and unmistakable turn towards plain white
vessels. The scholar Seong Hyeon (1439–1504) wrote that ‘during the reign
of King Sejong royal ceramics consisted exclusively of white porcelain
wares.’2 White porcelain was highly sought after but initially could not be
produced in sufficient quantity to meet demand. For the first two centuries
of Joseon rule, a second type of ceramics, known nowadays as buncheong,
was also produced in kilns located around the country. A high-fired

stoneware with an ash glaze, buncheong ware is the direct material
successor to Goryeo celadon.
    This shift to preferring white ceramics coincided with the rise of
Jingdezhen in Jiangxi Province as China’s pre-eminent porcelain production
centre. Pure white vessels, painted under the glaze with blue pigment,
offered a startling and dramatic change from the green wares that had
dominated Song and Yuan China, in the same way that green ceramics
prevailed in Korea during the Goryeo. When imperial gifts of white Chinese
porcelain were presented at court in Korea early in the fifteenth century, a
new fashion in ceramics gripped the country. The court soon ordered local
potters to make white cups, bowls, vases and dishes for use in the royal
household. Since cobalt (the mineral pigment used to create blue designs)
was rare, expensive and imported through China, the proportion of painted
wares to plain white ceramics in Korea remained low. The following
discussion first considers porcelain production before looking at buncheong
ceramics.

Purity and Austerity: Porcelain, 1392–1600
With an active, reforming court in Seoul that emphasized the need for ritual
and proper behaviour, there was a need for a regular supply of high-quality
ceramics to use in the royal household. Appropriate vessels for dining and
for national ceremonies, such as weddings, birthdays and funerals for the
royal household, were accorded huge importance by the neo-Confucian
elite of scholars and officials, who saw their mission as one of reshaping
Korea’s social and family life according to Confucius’s teachings. An area
in Gwangju county, in Gyeonggi Province3 (not to be confused with the city
of the same name in Jeolla Province, which also features prominently in
Korea’s ceramic history), was chosen in 1467–8, some seventy years after
the founding of the dynasty, as the site for directly managed official
government kilns, whose task was to produce white porcelain vessels for
court and government use. These official kilns are often referred to as
Bunwon, or Branch Department, because the court administered them as a
subsection of the Saongwon, or Bureau for Royal Cuisine.
    From the fifteenth century until the seventeenth, the Bunwon kilns
moved around various locations in the Gwangju area, shifting to a new site
each time the local supplies of kiln fuel were exhausted. In 1752, during the
reign of King Yeongjo (reg 1724–76), the kilns settled in one place,

Bunwon-ri, until they finally ceased operations in the late nineteenth
century. The Bunwon kilns focused on producing high-quality, pure white
porcelain that was more prestigious than other types of ceramic. The
essential features of a ceramic-producing centre were all present in the area:
plentiful wood to fire the kilns, a good supply of clay for forming the
vessels, and convenient transport to carry the finished ceramics to the
capital along the Han River.
    The royal porcelain-producing kilns made many of the most famous
and beloved porcelains of the Joseon period, but there were also many
regional kilns in other parts of the country making ceramics for clients at
various levels of society. Differences in quality control were marked. Court-
commissioned porcelains made in the royal kilns would be fired in
protective containers to avoid contamination from atmospheric dust and
grit. Other, lower-quality pieces would be placed uncovered in stacks inside
the kiln, with only small spurs of clay separating the layers of bowls or
plates from each other. Joseon white-bodied wares were high-fired and
glazed with a lime glaze that gave a milky-white colour. They differ from
the white wares, small in number, made in southwestern kilns in the Goryeo
dynasty (see illus. 82). No direct connection between the two wares has
been established. Rather, the vogue for white porcelain in the early Joseon
was sparked by encounters with Chinese ceramics, which took place in the
context of diplomatic exchanges between the two courts.
    The colours and shapes of ceramic vessels went through profound
changes in the fifteenth century. For ancestor worship and court
ceremonies, plain white vessels were made. Ceremonial ceramics were
produced with white clay, and also using stoneware, in the type of ceramic
known as buncheong.4 Examples are a stand in the shape of an elephant
(illus. 86) and a high-footed white porcelain bowl with cover (illus. 87). No
similar pieces were ever produced in the Goryeo. Ceramics were also
produced to enable the realization of neo-Confucian ideas about preserving
the physical body. Within the neo-Confucian tradition there was a deep-
seated reverence for the physical body of the royal person, since the
principles of Confucian teaching emphasized the bond between parent and
child, and the need for the young to respect and protect the old. A new
practice was introduced of preserving the placentas of royal and aristocratic
babies in specially made jars, often in pairs with one nested inside the other
(illus. 88). This was because the placenta was treated with the same

reverence as other parts of the royal person. Placenta jars would be ritually
buried in a tomb, a custom unique to Korea. The placenta, carefully stored
inside its double-layered jar and packed with straw and interred, would in
turn be protected by the auspicious geomantic features of the royal tomb
complex. Joseon rulers and officials accorded great importance to
geomancy, which was understood as a system of tapping into the natural
forces of the landscape to protect the ruler and his people. Palaces, cities
and residences were built in places that enjoyed good geomantic powers,
ideally with mountains to the north and water to the south. The royal
household, in the form of the physical bodies of its members, could be
cherished and protected from harm by placing the placenta in a jar for
posterity, and carrying out appropriate ceremonies there.

    At the end of a life, ceramics were part of remembrance. Ceramic
epitaph tablets recording the life and good deeds of exemplary Confucian
men and women, sometimes running to a dozen or more rectangular slabs
of porcelain bearing painted texts written in cobalt or iron-rich pigment,
were made to be buried with the deceased (illus. 89). These epitaph tablets
were permanent and unlike paper did not decay, so they preserved the
account of the person’s family and activities for later generations. The
practice of burying epitaph tablets with the deceased began in the Three
Kingdoms period, with examples surviving from Goguryeo, Baekje and
Silla. During the Goryeo, epitaph tablets were made of stone and consisted

of one substantial slab incised with a fairly short text. In the Joseon dynasty
some tablets continued to be made of stone, but ceramic epitaph tablets
were more widely produced.5 The two porcelain epitaph sets in the British
Museum commemorate the achievements of two scholar-officials. The set
of fourteen pure white porcelain tablets, inscribed with neat columns of text
in regular script, gives an account of the life and family achievements of a
certain Kim Jun-geun (1783–1814), a scion of the Kim family of Andong,
one of Korea’s powerful lineages, which produced many high-ranking
scholar-officials. The text records the achievements of Kim himself, his
wife Madame Jo and his nephew Kim Byeong-hak (1821–1879), who
served as prime minister. Since Kim Jun-geun died in 1814 and his wife in
1860, it seems that these epitaph tablets were made some decades after
Kim’s death and interred in the couple’s joint tomb. The lidded bowl with
an epitaph bears a cyclical date that may be equivalent to 1877 (illus. 90).
The text records the achievements of Kim Ju-gwang, a member of a
different clan, the Gwangsan Kim, and was composed by the great-
grandson of the deceased, Kim Gi-ryeon. In both cases, cobalt blue pigment
on bright white porcelain clay produced a prestigious and enduring epitaph
text, one intended to remain in the tomb of the deceased for all time. It is
striking that the calligraphic style and pigment density are more consistent
on the tablet than on the bowl. The calligraphy on the epitaph of Kim Ju-
gwang is of varied density and ranges from dark inky-black through to pale
greyish-blue.

     In addition to such biographical tablets, Joseon tombs also contained
funerary vessels that were provided for the deceased to use in the afterlife.
These were usually made, according to neo-Confucian teaching, on a
miniature scale, because it was thought that the spirits did not require
normal utensils and that smaller-sized versions were appropriate.6 In this,
the Joseon burial practices differed from those of the Goryeo, where life-
size pieces were interred. Sets of bowls, bottles, cups and stands (illus. 91,
92, 93) were made in white porcelain and despite their plain appearance
convey a sombre sense of reverence for the dead, in keeping with their
purpose. Other sets of funerary vessels have been excavated in various
royal and elite tombs, including an intriguing group from the tomb of
Wonbin, first concubine of King Jeongjo, who died in 1779. Among the
bowls, cups and other ceramics in her tomb are vessels that may have been
produced in Arita, Japan, where Korean potters captured during the
invasions of the 1590s had been instrumental in building Japan’s porcelain
industry.7
    Beyond the court palaces, porcelain was produced in large quantities,
and the majority of pieces were used for tableware and food storage in
upper-class households, rather than for court ceremonies. Poorer families
used rougher ceramics, made in local kilns. Regional porcelain kilns mostly
made plain white bowls, jars and cups for everyday use. The high-quality
jars, bottles and bowls that are familiar from their display in prestigious
museum and private collections constitute the luxury, top-rank segment of
porcelain production. They were almost all produced at the various
locations of the royal kilns in Gwangju. Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century
blue-and-white porcelain is particularly rare and sought after. A few
outstanding pieces reflect the refined, literary tastes of the neo-Confucian
scholar-officials of the time. One distinguished, Chinese-influenced vessel
is the jar with plum blossom and bamboo motifs (illus. 94). Other early
vessels depict dragons, emblems of royal power, and elegant scrolling
patterns incorporating flowers and birds. Most decorated porcelains were
painted by trained artists; some rare examples of inlaid decoration on
porcelain survive, including a bowl in the National Museum in Seoul,
National Treasure 175 (illus. 95).

   Two famous and striking tall jars, both in university museum
collections in Seoul, illustrate the fascination the natural world exercised on
early Joseon artists. The jars are close to 50 centimetres in height and have
generous curving shoulders tapering down to a narrow base. Both were
made by trained artists who confidently introduced uplifting Confucian
themes when painting on the brilliant white bodies of the vases. On the jar
in the collection of Ewha Womans University, a gnarled pine tree meanders
diagonally upwards, sheltering a wistful scholar who sits with his tea
utensils and incense burner (illus. 96).8 Based on evidence from
excavations, this jar is believed to have been formed, painted and fired at
Beoncheon-ri No. 9, part of the official kiln complex. The Dongguk
University Museum jar, previously held at Hwaeom Temple, Chirisan, is the
earliest dated piece of Korean blue-and-white to survive (illus. 97). Since it
was preserved for many years in a Buddhist temple, it may have been used
as a container for lotus blossoms during religious ceremonies. The interior
of its neck was originally inscribed with the characters Hongzhi er nian (弘治二
年), a Chinese reign date equivalent to 1489. The jar is painted with a
darkish-blue pigment and was covered in a blue-tinged glaze before firing.

Its decoration depicts contorted vine branches alongside star-like bamboo
plants, in a tour de force of the painter’s skill.9

Complaints about excessive use of blue-and-white porcelain recur in the
court Annals from time to time, suggesting that demand remained strong
despite royal disapproval. Efforts to locate a local supply of cobalt (Korean
hoehoecheong) are also noted from time to time in the official records.

Creativity and Diversity: Buncheong Ceramics, 1392–1600
If the early Joseon was a time of innovation and new ceramic practice, the
period was also one of continuity and adaptation. Along with the newly
popular white porcelain vessels, kilns in different parts of the country

continued to turn out high-fired stoneware covered with a pale grey-green
glaze. Familiar shapes such as maebyeong, pear-shaped bottles and large
jars were made, and new styles of vessel were added to the repertoire,
influenced by the ritual requirements of the Confucianizing state. The
surface decoration techniques used on Goryeo celadons, such as inlay and
underglaze painting with iron-rich pigment, were still practised but
produced a different effect. Considering the enormous scale of the kilns that
had produced green-glazed stoneware in the Goryeo dynasty, it is not
surprising that when potters eventually returned to their accustomed work
patterns, stoneware production resumed at kilns across the land. Joseon
period stoneware looks quite unlike Goryeo celadon in colour, decoration
and form, but it is the child of the previous dynasty’s ceramics, continuing
the practice of creating contrasting designs on the stoneware ceramic body
(illus. 98). Joseon stoneware exhibits a wide range of aesthetic effects, both
formal and informal. Different regions of the country produced buncheong
ceramics in different decorative styles, such as inlaid, stamped and carved
designs. Joseon stoneware is today admired in Korea and abroad for its
originality and expressive qualities. For many enthusiasts of ceramics,
buncheong ware is the pinnacle of the Korean potter’s art. The technical
achievements of buncheong potters include powerful carved designs like
the V&A lotus bottle (illus. 99), with its sublime flowerhead reaching up
from the lower body in a way that merges the carved surface decoration
with the volume of the vessel’s belly.
    The Korean art historian Ko Yu-seop (1905–1944) coined the term
buncheong to describe these Joseon-period stoneware vessels (illus. 100).11
His terminology conveys the qualities of this pale, decorated ‘stoneware
whose surface is partially or entirely covered with white slip and has a gray-
green colour’.12 Buncheong is today the accepted academic term when
discussing the slip-decorated stonewares of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century
Korea. Western collectors, however, first learned about buncheong ware
around the turn of the twentieth century. This was a period when Korea was
opening up to international contacts and when Japanese art dealers in
particular were actively mediating between Korea and the outside world.
The American entrepreneur Charles Freer (1854–1919) devoted his later life
to collecting art. He learned to use Japanese terms such as hakeme (brushed
slip), kohiki (dipped slip), mishima (inlaid with slip) and unkaku (white and
black inlays) to describe the Korean ceramics he bought from Japanese

dealers.13 Today the language of Japanese connoisseurship has been
displaced by a standard terminology generated by Korean art historians.
Nonetheless, the Japanese terms are remembered as a reflection of the
colonialist aesthetics of the period when the international market first took
an interest in Korean stonewares of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
They also remind us that the Japanese were the first outside Korea to
appreciate and collect buncheong ceramics.

    King Sejong (reg 1418–50) is remembered as the great reforming and
stabilizing monarch of the early Joseon. During his reign, in 1424, a survey
of kiln sites was conducted, recording 139 porcelain-producing and 185
stoneware-producing kilns. During the first decades of the new dynasty the
court had obtained the ceramics it required from different locations across
the country, but when the royal kilns were set up in the Kwangju area in
1467–8, clear differences became evident in the quality of pieces made for
court use and those made for other clients. While official and high-quality
porcelain vessels, including majestic, Chinese-influenced blue-and-white
wares, were produced in the royal kilns, other centres also continued to
operate, supplying different ceramics to the royal household on contract.
The fifteenth century was a time of great originality and variety in Korea’s
ceramic history. As late twentieth-century excavations and scientific
analyses have revealed, numerous kilns in Gyeonggi, Chungcheong, Jeolla
and Gyeongsang provinces were active in the fifteenth and early sixteenth
centuries, often producing buncheong wares in the first decades, followed
over the years by porcelain as the demand for white ceramics increased.

The attractiveness of pure white porcelain influenced the types of
buncheong ceramics being produced. To disguise the dark, iron-containing
clay of the buncheong vessels, a coating of white slip (clay diluted with
water) would be applied across the surface of the vessel before firing, to
impart the overall impression of whiteness. Buncheong wares, made at sites
across the centre, southeast and southwest of the country, demonstrate a
playful spirit, a direct engagement with observed nature.

    One well-known kiln that manufactured buncheong ware is Chunghyo-
dong in Jeolla Province, excavated in 1963 and 1991. Vessels decorated
with incised and carved designs of flowers, fish and animals were produced
there (illus. 101).14 By contrast, buncheong produced in kilns in Hakbong-
ri, Chungcheong Province, included free-spirited pieces painted with
striking abstract and pictorial designs (illus. 102). Ceramics made in these
Chungcheong Province kilns, first excavated in the 1920s by Japanese
archaeologists, were initially known outside Korea as ‘Keryongsan wares’,
named after the mountain, also spelled Gyeryong, or Chicken Dragon
Mountain, which lies near Gongju City.15 More recently they have often
been named by scholars and at exhibitions as Hakbong-ri wares, referring to
one of the major kilns in the Mount Gyeryong district. It is thanks to the
acute powers of observation of local makers in the Mount Gyeryong area,
who may well have been uneducated, that the beauty of country life in
fifteenth-century Korea could be recorded for posterity. The potters
produced a light-hearted range of bottles and jars that carry painted scenes
executed in earthy iron tones. These decorated vessels with their pictorial
and abstract designs evoke timeless scenes of bird, fish and plant life in the
countryside (illus. 103). Black-painted buncheong ceramics from kilns near

Mount Gyeryong have been discovered in many different situations,
including government offices, temples, residential areas and tombs.
Memorial tablets were also made at Hakbong-ri, a site from which ceramics
have been found all across southern Korea. Mount Gyeryong, with its
abundant clay and firewood, was a good ceramic area even before the
Joseon. With established transport links as a staging post between the grain-
producing areas of Jeolla Province and the capital, it clearly offered an
advantageous distribution hub for the products of local kilns. Little is
known, however, about the management of the Mount Gyeryong kilns or
their trading mechanisms.16

   Many different kilns in Gyeongsang Province also produced
buncheong ceramics, often with dense stamped patterns of chrysanthemum
heads, rope twists, stars or dots that covered the entire surface of the vessel,
with the exception of the base (illus. 104). Buncheong bowls, dishes and
jars bearing inscriptions were also produced in considerable numbers in
kilns in Gyeongsang Province and beyond. It has been suggested that the
practice of adding ownership names to vessels was an attempt to reduce
pilfering, or to ensure that ceramics ordered for use in government offices
did not fall into unauthorized hands.17 The inscribed characters were

variously placed, either on the exterior walls of a vessel or in the well of a
bowl. Some examples of ownership and administrative inscriptions on
buncheong wares give a sense of the royal household’s numerous offices
and bureaux. They include ‘Yebinsi’ (Office for Guests and Banquets),
‘Gyeongseungbu’ (Office for the Education of the Crown Prince),
‘Naeseom’ (Office for Palace Kitchens), ‘Seongju Jangheunggo’ (Seongju
Warehouse) and ‘Gyeongju Jangheunggo’ (Gyeongju Warehouse).18 Some
inscriptions denote cyclical years, which have been used to date objects.
Most inscriptions are in Chinese script, which continued in use throughout
the Joseon period for official names of court offices. Interestingly, a stem
cup that was excavated at the Chunghyo-dong kiln site in Jeolla Province
bears a Hangeul inscription with the letters ‘Eojon’. Since the Hangeul
writing system was promulgated in 1446, this cup must postdate that year.
Other vessels excavated at Chunghyo-dong have potters’ names inscribed
on them.19
    Buncheong vessels were also made in a delightfully diverse range of
shapes, including flat-sided bottles like the Jeolla Province bottle in the V&A
(illus. 105) and the slip-brushed ‘drum type’ bottle in the British Museum
(illus. 106). As the ceramic historian Kang Kyu-sook has noted, it was the
skills of the displaced potters from the Goryeo kilns at Gangjin that lay
behind the originality and wide-ranging forms of buncheong. She notes that
the fourteenth century was a time of change in both China and Korea. The
Gangjin kilns, where the best Goryeo pieces had been made, were closed
and the potters moved to different parts of Korea, eventually making new
types of ceramics that grew into buncheong in the fifteenth century. She
attributes the pale colour of buncheong wares to the desire of these potters
to emulate white porcelain.20 Free from close court control, potters
produced fresh designs and styles. Around 1466 the porcelain-producing
kilns in the Gwangju area of Gyeonggi Province were chosen to supply
ceramics for palace use. Before that time, a variety of locations supplied
high-quality stamped buncheong wares to the court, with firing done inside
saggars rather than in stacks in the open kiln oven. Royal-command
ceramics were requisitioned as a kind of tax-tribute payment and as such
were subject to rigorous quality control. Firing inside the saggar would
ensure that the ceramics were free from accidental contamination with kiln
ash. For this reason, among the pre-1466 stamped buncheong wares one

sees a number of meticulously decorated stamped pieces, sometimes
inscribed with the name of the commissioning court department.

Recovery, Prosperity and Decline: Ceramics of the Later Joseon, 1600–
1910
The first two centuries of Joseon rule had transformed Korean society root
and branch. Ideology was the driving force of this change. Korean society
in Goryeo times had operated as an inclusive descent group, with female
and male links having equal social and economic importance. The neo-
Confucian world order of the Joseon was one of exclusively male
inheritance. The dynasty’s tenacious belief in an idealized vision of rule by
sage-kings, basing their policies and actions on those of China’s rulers of
antiquity as interpreted by the philosophers of the Song dynasty, produced a
set of rules and customs that put decorum and hierarchy centre stage.
Primogeniture became the law, and in practice this meant a strong
preference for the first-born male offspring. Ancestor worship and ritual
status were of central importance, at court for the royal family and in every
household of the upper class. An important duty of the senior male

descendant was to perform the correct rituals to honour and reassure the
ancestors. Confucian philosophy also stressed the absolute duty of the
living to care for the elderly while alive, and to ensure that ancestors’ spirits
could rest in peace eternally.21 The ceramic industry operated inside this
world order, supplying vessels that could be used in solemn ritual practices
as well as the more everyday, utilitarian wares of the common people.
Commerce was not encouraged by the Joseon state, and nor was the pursuit
of fresh ideas and novel designs. All these philosophical and political ideas
had a significant effect on the way potters worked. The potters themselves
were of a low social status, just as their predecessors in earlier times had
been. They worked with their hands, unlike the scholar-officials of the
yangban class, who devoted their time to reading Chinese historical and
philosophical texts and to elegant pursuits such as calligraphy and painting.
Manual work was off limits for the elite. Men who passed the state
examinations could move towards positions in the government ranks,
whether at court in the ministries that administered national affairs or as
governors or magistrates in the provinces. Power and policy resided inside
the palaces in the capital: local enterprises were not permitted to develop
fresh products. Ceramics were made solely for use inside Korea. Export and
sales were considered unnecessary and undesirable.
   When the Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1536–1598) attacked
Korea in 1592 and again in 1597 as part of an ill-judged attempt to invade
China, the peninsula was ravaged by the invaders, who swept northwards
from the south coast, encountering little resistance. Although the Japanese
were ultimately defeated in December 1598, the buncheong-producing
kilns, already in decline, never recovered. The Imjin Waeran or wars of the
1590s ended in defeat for Japan following a tremendous naval battle off the
south coast at Noryang, Gyeongsang Province, with the Korean and
Chinese side led by the heroic admiral Yi Sun-sin (1545–1598), who lost
his life at the moment of victory. Hideyoshi had died three months earlier,
and the defeat at Noryang marked the end of the Japanese onslaught. The
consequences of Hideyoshi’s ambition to rule beyond the Japanese
archipelago reverberated across Asia throughout the following decades. In
Korea, to compound the brutal shock of the Japanese invaders’ attacks from
the sea, a further onslaught followed in the mid-seventeenth century.
Manchu forces invaded Korea from the north in 1627 and again in 1636. In
China this was the time of transition from the Ming to the Qing dynasties, a

time when Korea’s ‘older brother’ as a Confucian state was defeated and
supplanted. The Korean court had long been a loyal admirer of the Ming
and was reluctant to acknowledge the legitimacy of the Manchu as rulers of
China when the Ming finally fell in 1644.

From Turmoil to Stability, 1600–1752
A striking feature of seventeenth-century Korea’s ceramic history is the
disappearance of both the buncheong kilns and of cobalt-blue decoration on
porcelain. We have seen that buncheong kilns were already declining during
the sixteenth century and that their wares by then used ever more white clay
to produce a paler colour. Some sixteenth-century buncheong pieces were
even submerged or painted in liquid clay to cover their dark bodies and
produce the effect of white porcelain. Porcelain’s bright clay (unlike
buncheong stoneware, porcelain clay fires to a white colour and contains
few impurities) and luminous effects when glazed and fired eventually
displaced stonewares and became the sole ceramic type accepted by the
Korean court and elite. Naturally, the porcelain-producing kilns suffered
along with the rest of the country during the Japanese invasions, and potters
were among the 60,000 captives forcibly ‘led away in chains and bamboo
collars by Japanese slave traders’ and taken to Japan, according to the diary
of the Japanese Buddhist priest Keinen, who accompanied one of the
daimyo in the invasion force.22 The seventeenth century therefore was a
time of low production and relaxed control from the capital. Cobalt
pigment, an expensive import, was out of reach since there were neither
funds to buy it nor goods to trade for it. Potters turned to a different, locally
available pigment, iron brown, to paint decoration on porcelain.
     Despite the dire economic circumstances that gave rise to the use of
iron brown decoration on porcelain vessels, these glorious ceramics of
seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Korea are widely considered to be
among the greatest artistic works the country ever produced. Constrained by
austerity and shortages of material, artists painted exquisite, spare
compositions on the plain white jars and bottles available to them. Using
pigments derived from iron oxide, coloration ranging from warm chocolate
through silvery charcoal to deep inky black was achieved, with exquisite
painted designs of vines, bamboo and dragons predominating. Brown
decoration painted under the glaze had been known in Korea for hundreds
of years, from Goryeo times, and in the Hakbong-ri painted type of

buncheong. The elegant, flattened bottle in the Fitzwilliam Museum in
Cambridge, with its painted decoration of bamboo stems and leaves, is an
example of a seventeenth-century picnic flask, probably made at Seondong-
ni, a kiln in the Gwangju area (illus. 107). The bamboo stems on both sides
are painted in a calligraphic style exhibiting strong, fluid brushstrokes. The
leaves have an asymmetric design, ending in dark tips. Many shards
excavated at Seondong-ni have similar bamboo-painted decoration,
reflecting the practice of having high-class ceramics painted by trained
court artists, whose style followed prescribed rules. Bamboo leaves in this
manner are associated with the painter Yi Su-mun (fl. fifteenth century).
Bamboo was of course an important subject for Korean artists. The
examinations for court artists required aspiring painters to depict four
subjects: in descending order of importance, these were bamboo, landscape,
humans and animals, and flowers and plants.23
   A very different use of brown pigment is seen on a massive jar
depicting a meandering branch bearing grapes and vine leaves (illus. 108).
Its bold design was executed in iron pigment and has yielded blue, brown
and green tones of great subtlety to depict the grapes that droop vertically
away from the spreading vine. A globular jar from a regional kiln in
Gyeonggi Province in the British Museum collection is a free-spirited,
almost abstract work, with a tumbling leaf and branch design sweeping over
the curves of the jar (illus. 109). The dragon jars of the seventeenth and
eighteenth centuries that were painted in iron brown are known for their
lively, humorous qualities. Painters decorating large globular and baluster
jars often left large areas of white porcelain untouched, using the vessel
walls as the background to the composition of dragons, coiled and
powerful, in pursuit of the flaming pearl and bestriding the clouds. These
jars are found both with bands of lotus leaves and clouds, as in the V&A
example (illus. 110), and without any framing of the main design. The V&A
dragon has a remarkable narrow head with protruding eyes and a humorous
expression.

     In the eighteenth century, regional porcelain kilns also produced jars
painted with copper pigment, giving a rich red colour to their designs. The
graceful lotus jar in the V&A (illus. 111) was one such, and it has been
suggested that these red-painted local wares were used in Buddhist settings
since some, such as this piece, have Buddhist-inspired designs. Bought in
London in 1913, the lotus jar quickly attracted approving comments from
early twentieth-century British potters and art historians. Its powerful lines
and relaxed use of space were admired perhaps more in Europe than in
Korea, where copper-red decorated porcelain was certainly produced and
used but, for reasons that remain obscure, was held in lower esteem than
underglaze-blue decorated wares. The Joseon period’s lack of enthusiasm
for red-and-white ware is intriguing since Korean potters of the Goryeo
dynasty had been early to incorporate copper-red pigments in their designs
(see illus. 63, 64).24 Other eighteenth-century regional vessels with red
designs include faceted jars and bottles that were probably used as
containers for liquids and foodstuffs (illus. 112). Some have distinctive
overlapping disc designs evenly spaced at half-height on the facets. Later
red-decorated porcelains were made at the royal kilns and included large
jars with red and blue designs (illus. 113). On the evidence of the Bunwon
pots that have survived, copper-red pigment was used more often as a
complement to blue designs rather than a substitute for them, although a

small number of red monochrome pieces are known, notably the long-
necked bottle with repaired mouth in the Fitzwilliam Museum. Unique
among Joseon-era bottles, it is entirely covered in copper-red pigment and
has a subtle honeycomb pattern (illus. 114).

    The reigns of kings Sukjong (reg 1674–1720) and Yeongjo (reg 1724–
76) witnessed steady social and economic recovery after the Japanese and
Manchu invasions. The neo-Confucian scholars at court grudgingly came to
terms with the new rulers of China, slowly accepting the authority of the

Qing dynasty. Korea’s political class continued to study Confucian texts in
pursuit of a correct understanding of Confucian morality.25 Despite keen
interest in observing and understanding Chinese artistic trends, the court
made no attempt to follow the Chinese fashion for overglaze enamel
decoration on porcelain. This conservative approach to ceramic decoration
stemmed from the deep-seated attachment of Korea’s rulers to the
Confucian virtues of plainness and frugality.





114 Long-necked bottle, 1800–1880, painted porcelain, height 28.5 cm.

While many writers criticized Chinese ceramics decorated with
overglaze enamels as vulgar and brash, the scholar-official Bak Chega
(1750–1805) took a different view. Bak joined four diplomatic missions
from the court of King Jeongjo (reg 1776–1800) to Beijing, in 1778, 1780,
1790–91 and 1801. He was a member of the Practical Learning school
(Silhak), which criticized his country’s obsession with ritual and orthodox
philosophical studies as sterile and wasteful, proposing instead that court
and society should pay attention to real-life subjects like agriculture and
engineering in order to improve life for the people of Korea. In his
Discourse on Northern Learning, written immediately after his first visit to
Beijing, Bak argued in favour of adopting Chinese customs and recognizing
the superior achievements of China in most spheres of activity. He even
criticized Korean porcelain, comparing it unfavourably to the Chinese
wares he had seen while travelling, as the following passage shows:

    With Chinese porcelain, none exist that are not exquisite. Even
    ramshackle houses in a remote village have wares painted in splendid
     blue and gold colors, including bottles, cups, kettles, and rice bowls.
    This is not because the people are fond of luxuries. A potter’s work
    simply ought to be of such quality. The pottery of our country is very
     crude. Because it is baked with sand still stuck to the bottom, it comes
     out rough, as if dried grains of cooked rice were embedded in it. If you
     pull it toward you on the table, it scratches the surface; when you wash
       it, bits of leftover food still remain behind. If you put a piece of pottery
    on the floor, it is wobbly and liable to tip over. The lip is also warped,
    and the overall color is ugly beyond description. Indeed, you need only
    look at our pottery to see how extreme the lack of technique in this
     country has become.26

The Practical Learning school, however, was ultimately unable to change
the court’s determination to avoid ostentatious and extravagant styles.
   Few descriptions of the potters’ lives survive, but one poet and painter,
Yi Ha-gon (1677–1724), wrote vividly about the Bunwon kilns:

    Clouds over the river become rain in the night
    Strong winds pass through the trees of the valley
     Potters living together at the corner of the mountain

Endure hardship of forced labour
    They say they went to Yeongnam
    For fine clay to ship by sea
    Clay white as snow
      Is best for firing royal vessels
    Although potters did their best
   Many vessels were rejected
    Clay as soft as cotton
    Wheel moving when touched by foot
   A thousand vessels shaped on the wheel
    Bowls, plates, bottles, jars, smooth and gentle
    As many as 30 names for bowls
    As many as 400 vessels from a royal kiln
    Cannot express the beauty of shape, colour and quality
     All are precious beyond measure.27

Yi Ha-gon was a friend of the great artist Jeong Seon and of the painter Yun
Duseo. Having failed the civil service examinations, he wrote under the
studio name Damheon (Luminous Residence). His paintings survive in
collections including the Gansong Art Museum and the National Museum
of Korea.
    During the eighteenth century the royal kilns in the Gwangju area
resumed production. Geumsa-ri, near the Han River, was the last temporary

centre for the royal kilns before the king decreed that they should be settled
permanently. Geumsa-ri porcelains were made from about the 1720s to the
1750s and are prized for their warm tone and delicate decoration. A faceted
jar in the Museum of Oriental Ceramics, Osaka, is a much-loved example
of the restrained, lyrical style of the best Geumsa-ri pieces (illus. 115). First
thrown on the wheel to create a globe, the jar was skilfully cut back to
produce eight flattened sides. Orchids, asters, bell-flowers and pinks were
painted on the jar in pale blue, within panels that each straddle two facets,
rather like a melody with a syncopated rhythm. This style of decoration,
also found on round and faceted bottles and brush-holders, with generous
expanses of white space complementing the plants, is known in Japan as
‘autumn grasses’. Geumsa-ri porcelains command affection and devotion
among connoisseurs, who appreciate their poetic spirit, emotional warmth
and quiet confidence.

Bunwon-ri and Porcelain, 1752–1945
King Yeongjo settled the royal kilns near the confluence of the South and
North Han rivers, at Bunwon-ri, Namjong-myeon, Gyeonggi Province,
which then became the established hub of official porcelain manufacture.
Its products multiplied in type and in decorative style. Many of the
surviving masterpieces of Joseon porcelain were made at the Bunwon-ri
kilns in the eighteenth century. These include majestic jars bearing coiled
dragons and other auspicious designs that were produced for court use
(illus. 116). Dragons, powerful and vigorous creatures associated with
imperial authority, were once again painted in shades of blue. Their densely
grouped scales could encircle the broad shoulder of a jar or bottle. Dragons
were depicted in pursuit of a flaming pearl, which became a conventional
motif. Dragons on Joseon-era ceramics have four feet and either four or five
claws. Confucian ritual decreed that five-clawed dragons were the
prerogative of the ruler. Dragons on Joseon jars are depicted in movement
among clouds. Their features include protruding eyes, a beard, whiskers, a
mane and horns. Many dragon jars are designed with a band of yeo ui
lappets at the neck and a stylized lotus petal design near the foot, although
variations are numerous. These framing devices focus attention on the
dragon form as it dominates the available pictorial space. Although dragon
jars were produced in significant numbers and display a conventional,
repetitive illustrative repertoire, close examination reveals a wide variety of

subtle variations, reflecting the ingenuity and imagination of the court
artists who decorated these ceremonial vessels at the royal kilns. The
distinctive Korean practice of leaving the borders of the decoration
undefined appears in a number of dragon jars and bottles (illus. 117). As
well as the dragon, auspicious animals painted on jars and bottles by
porcelain artists included the phoenix, the tortoise and the crane.
Additionally, tigers, magpies, kirin (a type of magical beast) and birds, fish
and insects were all depicted on Joseon porcelain as well as being modelled
to form ingenious water droppers and cup stands. Tableware and scholars’
implements such as water droppers and brush pots were made in eye-
catching shapes and with carved, openwork and multi-coloured designs
incorporating blue and red pigments. Korean potters’ love of natural
subjects and shapes found full expression in the ceramics of the eighteenth
century.

porcelain, height 48.5 cm.

    The reigns of Yeongjo and Jeongjo were also the era when large plain
white jars were made, vessels that for many collectors and ceramic
enthusiasts in Korea and internationally have come to define the special
qualities of Korean porcelain, known today as dal hangari or moon jars.
Dozens of these remarkable, heavy vessels made of plain white porcelain
survive, with about thirty in public collections in Asia, Europe and North
America. The fine jar in the British Museum (illus. 118) has a powerful,
quiet presence. Formed of two wheel-thrown, bowl-like halves, the jar was
joined at the centre before glazing and firing. Its shoulder carries traces of
ash, and the clear, pale glaze is scratched in places, evidence of its hundreds
of years of pre-museum life. The eminent British potter Bernard Leach
(1887–1979) bought this jar in Seoul in the course of his travels in Korea in

the 1930s,28 valuing it at just 10 yen when shipping it back to the UK.29
Leach was (both literally and figuratively) a towering figure in twentieth-
century ceramic circles in the UK and internationally. In lectures and
teaching, he praised the qualities – form, glaze, quiet beauty – of vessels
made in the court-sponsored kilns of medieval China and Korea. Born and
raised in colonial Hong Kong and in Japan, Leach appropriated East Asian
ceramics in his own ceramic practice, having studied in Japan, and enjoyed
a lifelong relationship with Yanagi Sōetsu (1889–1961). He aspired to
produce work that was ‘both good to use and to look at’ and saw in Chinese
and Korean ceramics an ‘eclectic modernism’ well fitted to the
internationalist ethos of the twentieth century.30 As that century’s pre-
eminent potter and enthusiast for the vital spirit and useful qualities of
Chinese and Korean ceramics, Leach was by far the most significant voice
in introducing both Goryeo and Joseon ceramics to the Western public. His
hostility to mechanized, mass-produced domestic objects led him to a
practice, and a study, of ceramics that accorded a special position to the
Korean wares.31 Remarkably, the Leach jar, made in Korea by an unknown
craftsman, has become ‘the most iconic object in the history of British
studio pottery’, according to the curator Glenn Adamson,32 partly as a result
of a well-known photograph by Lord Snowdon of the jar in Lucie Rie’s
studio (illus. 119).

   Moon jars are unique to Korea, and perhaps because their plain,
imposing presence delights and affects everyone who sees them, they have
enjoyed a resurgence in the late twentieth and the twenty-first centuries,
attracting living ceramic artists to the challenge of producing such vessels
and thus continuing the tradition of the eighteenth century potters’ art.
Leach wrote in Beyond East and West (1978) of his love for Korean
celadons of the Goryeo dynasty, but, he continued, ‘the pots I came to love
still more were white or blue-and-white porcelain . . . in all things these pots
are of a different ethos . . . the porcelain itself and the form spoke of that
beautiful countryside, not of China.’33

    King Jeongjo, the grandson of Yeongjo, was a strict and exacting
Confucian monarch who set store by virtuous behaviour and adherence to
rules about plainness and modesty. Neither in ceramics nor in other areas of
life did Jeongjo tolerate novelty or experimentation. During his reign,
merchants and urban dwellers became more affluent and eager to buy
beautiful porcelain, influenced by increasing knowledge about ceramics in
Qing China, where many styles were available to purchase, including
polychrome overglaze enamels. Jeongjo commanded in 1791, some forty
years after the royal kilns had settled at Bunwon-ri, that no high-quality
pieces except for plain dining wares should be made:

      If anyone is found producing vessels aside from tableware, bottles and
    cups in violation of the law, the senior official in charge will be
     dismissed and the lower official shall be removed from his post. From
      this day forward even among ceramic goods usually fired, those not
     absolutely necessary or urgently needed are strictly prohibited . . . If
     caught, the working level officials of the palace hall involved and the
    eunuchs will be given 100 lashings and the kiln official shall be exiled

for an indefinite number of years. This order shall be hung on a board
    and referred to and acted upon at all times by the officials of the
    Saongwon and Bunwon.34

Jeongjo’s instruction is evidence both of his adherence to neo-Confucian
moral precepts and of the tensions in the increasingly prosperous society of
the late eighteenth century.
    One result of the king’s attempt to stop the kilns making fancy and
unusual painted ceramics was the introduction of a range of plain white
ceramics with raised designs, such as the rectangular bottle in the V&A with
a design of crane, deer, bamboo and bats across its walls and at the
shoulders (illus. 120). Other white monochromes that combined obedience
to the law with attractive surface decoration would incorporate raised
Chinese characters such as bok (富), meaning wealth, and su (壽), meaning
long life, on the walls of bowls and bottles. There are also numerous
openwork designs, particularly for brush holders. These were made with
integrated designs carved out of the vessel wall, including trailing vines
with squirrels and a phoenix moving among clouds (illus. 121).
     Despite Jeongjo’s strictures against high-quality painted ceramics, the
Bunwon-ri kilns did in fact produce a cheerful range of ceramic forms
during the 130 years of their operation. Jeongjo’s heir, King Sunjo (reg
1800–1834), did not continue his predecessor’s campaign against
ostentatious designs in ceramics. Pieces for use in the studio of a gentleman
were made in a variety of attractive styles such as the brush-washer in the
shape of mountains in the British Museum (illus. 122). This intricately

modelled bowl, painted under the glaze with cobalt and iron pigment,
evokes one of Korea’s best-known mountain ranges, the Diamond
Mountains (Geumgangsan), by forming the walls in craggy, mountainous
forms. At intervals around these walls are monks, pagodas, pine trees, a
tiger and a stone lantern. On the base are three fish swimming in line among
waves. In addition to his basin for washing brushes, the scholar in his studio
also required other vessels as he worked. Water droppers held the water that
would be mixed with solid soot-based ink to mix up the correct amount for
the task at hand. They too could be modelled with scenes from the Diamond
Mountains, or, as in this case, made in a peach shape (illus. 123). Little
water droppers were made in ingenious shapes, including fish, peach and
house, reflecting the modelling skills of the potters and the owners’ need for
portable objects that gave visual and tactile pleasure. These small-scale,
personal ceramic objects could be given as gifts, carrying wishes for
examination success, long life or good fortune through puns and
calligraphic inscriptions. Their decoration was painted, incised or carved
(illus. 124).

     Bottles of various shapes and decorative styles were produced in
quantity at the Bunwon-ri kilns during the eighteenth and nineteenth
centuries. Many were round-bodied with long necks, but a few faceted
pieces were also made, such as the plain ritual flask with characters je
hyeon ju byeong (祭玄酒瓶), meaning ‘bottle for presenting dark wine’, painted
in four simple roundels (illus. 125). Such bottles, like other implements
bearing the character je for offering, were designated for use in solemn
ritual settings. A few monochrome flasks were made, no doubt appealing to
the prosperous merchant class that flourished from the late eighteenth
century onwards. An example is the fine bottle with an incised design of a

mountainous landscape beneath generously applied cobalt pigment (illus.
126).
    Aside from these few examples made in exceptional shapes and
colours, most late Joseon bottles from the Bunwon-ri kilns were formed of
white porcelain painted under the glaze with lively designs in cobalt blue.
Readily available for purchase in the late nineteenth century, when
Europeans and North Americans first took up residence in Seoul, blue-and-
white bottles made their way into several Western museum collections.
While lacking the elegant refinement of earlier Joseon wares, late-period
Bunwon ceramics have many attractive qualities. Geometric forms, models
of landscapes, creatures and plants and punning decorations bearing
messages of goodwill distinguish these porcelains, reflecting the taste and
interests of the upper class as five centuries of the Joseon dynasty’s rule
drew to a conclusion. A tall bottle with butterflies and peonies encircling its
bulbous body is typical of the type (illus. 127). Flower patterns including
chrysanthemums, as on the graceful bottle with flower-heads and leaves
across the body, were another favoured decoration (illus. 128). As well as
long-necked bottles with squat bodies, the Bunwon-ri potters made smaller
bottles with globular or tubular shapes and graceful plant decoration under a
blue-tinted glaze. They also made Western-style tableware (illus. 129).

     After almost half a millennium of consistently Confucian, isolated
national life, Korea was forced in the 1880s to open its borders to the
outside world. The challenges to political and economic life were acute, as
the court and the government struggled to adapt to a world of warships,
missionaries, diplomats and international trade, while resisting attempts by
aggressive neighbours to gain a foothold inside the country. Japan’s ever
more transparent intention to take over the Korean peninsula created an
impossible context for the well-intentioned efforts of the court of King
Kojong (reg 1864–97, emperor 1897–1907) to transform his country into a
modern nation and member of the international world order. The basis of

society was changing rapidly, and the ceramic kilns at Bunwon-ri could no
longer function as providers of ritual ceramics for use at a court where life
revolved around Confucian ceremonial occasions. The National Palace
Museum of Korea holds nineteenth-century French, German and English
porcelain imported for use at court. As part of its attempt to modernize
government, the royal household imported contemporary European
ceramics in the 1880s, 1890s and 1900s and used them during formal
meals.35
