The Bunwon kilns were privatized in 1883: state support and
management were withdrawn, and the potters subsequently operated for a
short time as a separate business, supplying stores directly with their
ceramics. This was a period of rapid change, as international trade began to
alter the supply of goods in Korea. Foreign, industrially made ceramics
were reaching the market, and the expansionist ambitions of Japan would
soon bring an end to the remnants of the Bunwon-ri trade. Potters dispersed
around the country to work on a small scale, while the Japanese colonial
government, which ruled after the annexation of Korea in 1910, pursued its
aim of turning Korea into a source of raw materials for Japanese industry
and a market for Japanese manufactured goods. The 1910s and ’20s saw
little activity in the Korean ceramic industry, but the 1930s were a time
when a few Korean entrepreneurs were able to establish factories, such as
Milyang, Haengnam and Chungbuk. The main trend in this period was the
introduction of utilitarian ceramics from Japan into the Korean market.36
    The Japanese Government General did, however, support the
restoration of a number of traditional ceramic-producing areas, including
Gwangju. Another interesting feature of colonial Japan’s interaction with
Korean ceramic history was the creation of factories making reproduction
Goryeo celadon. Tomita Gisaku (1858–1930) was a merchant who was
particularly active in building up the celadon industry, establishing Samhwa
Goryeoso, a celadon factory, in Jinnampo, Pyeongan Province, in 1908 and
subsequently establishing more celadon factories. ‘Sin Goryeoso’, as these
kilns were known, made reproduction celadon following a mainly
traditional style but introducing some fresh design schemes. Later, in the
1920s, a number of Korean potters also founded celadon businesses.37
    The Japanese colonial government also organized exhibitions,
including craft exhibitions, under the auspices of the ‘Joseon Art
Exhibition’ (illus. 130). These endeavours, however, had little effect on the
stagnant state of the Korean ceramic industry. Japanese ceramics collectors
and potters, including Kitaōji Rosanjin (1883–1959), visited Korea and
were inspired by the ceramics they saw and the kiln sites they visited (illus.
131). Writing about the overall condition of the Korean ceramic industry
during the Japanese colonial period, however, the scholar Eom Seung-hui
noted that ‘modern Korean ceramics underwent difficulties that mirrored
the upheavals taking place within the national governance structure. In the
end, its fate was intertwined with that of a Joseon which could not

appropriately cope with the rapidly changing situations.’38 In Chapter Five
we shall consider the rebirth of ceramics as a national enterprise in later
twentieth-century Korea.

Technology of Porcelain and Buncheong Production
It is important to be aware of the terminology used by ceramic researchers
in East Asia and in the West. In the latter, potters differentiate between
earthenware, stoneware and porcelain. Earthenware bodies, which are
porous, are fired at temperatures below 1000°C, often contain high
proportions of iron, and fire to a red or dark grey colour. Stoneware is fired
at around 1200°C, resulting in a hard, impermeable body. The clay colour
varies but is usually pale grey. Porcelain bodies, fired at temperatures up to
1350°C, are particularly hard and pure and white. In East Asian scholarship,
by contrast, the same word describes earthenware and stoneware.39 Both are
called ‘low-fired ceramics’ (Korean to, Chinese tao). Since Korean
celadons have a firing temperature close to that of porcelain, East Asian
authors describe them as ‘high-fired ceramics’ (Korean ja, Chinese ci), the
same word used for porcelain. In Europe and North America most writers
follow the convention of reserving the term ‘porcelain’ for white-bodied,
high-fired wares with a high degree of purity. In this book we have
followed the Western convention of distinguishing between celadon, a high-
fired stoneware, and high-fired white ware with a body free from
impurities, known as porcelain.





131 Kitaōji Rosanjin, pair of bowls, c. 1930–50, Korean
clay, made in Japan, height 8.6 cm each.

Porcelain
After 1469, when the Joseon court chose Gwangju county, Gyeonggi
Province, as the area for producing the most prestigious vessels, porcelain
production developed rapidly. Both local and regional clays were used.40
The whiteness of porcelain is caused by the clay the potters used. Compared

to celadon, which has a greyish-coloured body after firing, porcelain clay is
low in iron and other impurities. Porcelain had been made in Korea as early
as the tenth century, in the same kilns that produced celadon ware, and thus
Goryeo porcelain stands after only Chinese porcelain in the ranks of the
world’s earliest porcelains. Unlike Goryeo porcelain, which fires to a
creamy hue, Joseon porcelain is brilliant or milky white. At Seori, a ceramic
centre in Gyeonggi Province that was excavated in the 1980s, huge Goryeo
period kilns produced whitewares and celadons together.41 What is still not
entirely clear, however, is the relationship of Goryeo porcelain to Joseon
porcelain, in terms of technology transfer.
   When the Joseon court surveyed hundreds of kilns around the country
in 1424–5, sources of clay as well as functioning kilns were identified.
Once established in Gwangju, the royal kilns requisitioned clay from a
number of sources, including nearby Seo-ri, site of the Goryeo porcelain
kilns mentioned above. In the eighteenth century the poet Yi Ha-gon wrote
about clay and its preparation, mentioning shipping Jinju clay up from the
south and commenting on the quality and purity of different clays.42 Since
potters’ clay was sourced and transported to the official kilns from different
regions, and since regional kilns often used local materials, the composition
of Joseon porcelain clays is varied. In general, however, they consisted of
three parts silica and one part aluminium oxide, sometimes described as
‘quartz-mica’ type porcelain. (One much-admired clay includes a small
amount of potassium oxide in its composition, producing an attractive
snow-white colour when fired.43) Geologically, the southern part of the
Korean peninsula, where the majority of significant kilns are located, forms
part of the same tectonic region as south China, with a rock formation that
produces ‘quartz-mica’ type porcelain material.44 The porcelains of the
Joseon kilns contained very little kaolin.
    Most porcelains were thrown on the potter’s wheel, with the potter
seated and turning the wheel by foot. The ceramic historian Bang Byung-
sun notes that Yi Ha-gon, in the above-mentioned poem about a private
firing of an epitaph at a government kiln in 1709, described a ‘kicking
wheel which turns by itself’ (illus. 132).45 Bang also draws attention to the
techniques for making flat-walled bottles and boxes, in which potters
worked with slabs of prepared clay rather than with moulds. Some

outstanding pieces combined wheel throwing with slicing to produce
faceted vessels.
    Although there are a few inlaid pieces from the fifteenth century,
underglaze painting is by far the most prevalent decoration on Joseon
porcelains. Carved pieces and applied decoration are also found in
eighteenth- and nineteenth-century production. Out of all the decorated
pieces of Joseon porcelain, those with underglaze blue designs painted with
cobalt are the great majority. The blue colour produced when ground cobalt
is painted on the walls of a porcelain vessel captivated Koreans throughout
the five centuries of Joseon rule. At various times the court made vigorous
efforts to restrict the use of cobalt strictly to the royal household. Cobalt
was sought out and mined in Korea itself, in an attempt to find a cheaper
source of the pigment, but there is no consensus among senior scholars who
have excavated and analysed blue-and-white painted porcelains that locally
sourced cobalt ore was ever made into a pigment that was applied on
porcelain. Kim Jae-yeol suggests that an elegant lidded jar painted with
dark blue birds on a plum tree branch (illus. 133) may be evidence of the
use of local cobalt, which produced a deeper, blacker colour than imported
cobalt,46 and Hwang Hyun Sung states that domestic cobalt can be
distinguished from imported cobalt by its higher iron and manganese
content,47 but other Korean scholars, including Choo48 and Bang, state that
only imported cobalt was used on Joseon blue-and-white wares.49 Whatever
the case about native and imported cobalt, the high price of cobalt was a
constant concern, up until the time when cheaper cobalt mined in China
became available as an alternative to the Middle Eastern cobalt. By the
nineteenth century the price of cobalt was lower, and many more lavishly
decorated blue-and-white vessels were produced.50

blue painted, height 16.5 cm.





    The high point of iron oxide pigment use in Joseon Korea was the
seventeenth century, after the Japanese invasions of the 1590s. The famous
jar with trailing grapevine, National Treasure 107 in Ewha Womans
University Museum (see illus. 108), is a masterpiece of painterly decoration

on generously proportioned porcelain,51 done entirely in brown pigment
and achieving remarkable gradations of colour, from intense blue-black in
the grapes to light grey-green in the leaves that tumble across the broad
shoulders of the jar.
    The third colouring agent in the Joseon potter’s cupboard was an
underglaze red, produced from copper oxide or copper carbonate.
Notoriously volatile and challenging to apply and to fire, copper-red
pigment was in widespread use from the eighteenth century onwards and
has been noted and admired by many international studio potters in modern
times. Red-decorated bottles, jars and knick-knacks were made both in the
official kilns and at regional centres. A few particularly fine pieces, with
painted scenes and decorative motifs combining red and blue colouring
effects, were produced at the royal kilns. Korean potters applied copper in
innovative and technically impressive ways both in the Goryeo and in the
Joseon, but the taste for red decoration on ceramics never dominated.52
    Joseon porcelains, whether plain or painted, were always glazed before
firing. The purpose of glazing ceramics is, of course, to seal them, making
them watertight. Joseon porcelains were covered in a watery glaze just
before going into the kiln. Made of a mixture of wood ash (the flux) and
clay, the glaze mixture vitrified (became glassy) during firing and bonded
with the clay body of the vessel, thus making an attractive, shiny,
impervious outer surface. The glaze used on Joseon porcelain is known as
lime or ash glaze. Because the porcelain body and the glaze applied to it are
similar in chemical composition, the ‘fit’ of the glaze to the vessel is good
(heating and cooling, expansion and contraction during firing take place at a
similar rate). Bang Byung-sun notes that in the eighteenth century a change
occurred in the glaze applied to Joseon porcelains. Instead of lime glaze, a
lime-alkali glaze was used in the final centuries of the dynasty.53 (Lime-
alkali glazes differ from lime glazes because, in addition to ash, they also
contain an alkaline fluxing agent. They give a particularly smooth, lustrous
appearance to the surface of the vessel.) Coloration in the glaze is produced
by the presence of metallic elements. Korean porcelains of the Joseon have
traces of iron oxide in their glaze, with smaller quantities of other elements
such as titanium or magnesium altering the colour produced during firing.
The atmosphere in the kiln also determined the colour of the glazed vessel,
since an oxygen-rich atmosphere produced more yellowish colours, while a
‘reducing’ (oxygen-starved) atmosphere yielded blue or green glaze tones.

In addition to the numerous official kilns in the Gwangju area, there
were kilns producing porcelain wares all around the country, and since the
1980s a good number of them have been excavated, allowing us to refine
and expand our understanding of the processes used by the potters.54 Kilns
in the Joseon were ‘tilting and stepped’, meaning that they were built on a
hillside and consisted of a series of chambers at rising levels. The fuel was
wood, and the main firing temperature for porcelain was around 1250°C,
about 50°C higher than the celadon kilns’ temperature. Biscuit firing (first
firing, prior to decorating and glazing) at about 900°C was widely but not
universally practised, followed after cooling by glazing and a second firing
at the higher temperature. The structures adopted for kilns altered over time,
as recorded by Kang Kyung-sook.55 Features including the presence of an
extra chamber for biscuit firing, the use of a fire cylinder in the middle of
the chamber, the area of the kiln and the incline of the hillside (natural or
man-made) are all relevant to research in the development of ceramic
technology in Joseon Korea.
   Much of the evidence has been challenging to investigate, whether
because of economic development or because of amateur excavations
during the Japanese colonial period. Two highly important porcelain kilns
that have proved difficult to explore are Geumsa-ri,56 which came into its
own during the long reign of King Sukjong (reg 1674–1720) and which is
known for the making of large moon jars and for numerous shards of
faceted vessels; and Bunwon-ri, the last centre of the official kilns, active
between about 1752 and 1883.57 The site at Bunwon-ri was disturbed in the
early twentieth century when a school was built where once dozens of kiln
sites and waste heaps had stood (illus. 134). Despite the losses, however,
the story of porcelain production in the Joseon dynasty has become clear,
and many details have emerged to explain the differences in quality that
exist between particular types of vessel. In the top-rank kilns there was
widespread use of saggars (protective containers) to shield the ceramics
from kiln grit and ash, suggesting that saggar-firing was preferred when
producing vessels for the court. In other kilns, vessels were simply stacked
on top of each other for firing. The supports that separated each vessel from
its upper neighbour sometimes stuck to the finished piece or left a small
mark. Such marks are useful when ceramic archaeologists attempt to
determine the type and status of a kiln or a waste heap. Many waste heaps

were of considerable size, since the potters would discard warped, misfired
or otherwise unsatisfactory vessels.





134 View of Bunwon-ri, 2022.

    The special qualities of Korean porcelain of the Joseon period reflect
the originality and sensibilities of potters and their patrons. With its rather
heavy body, Korea’s porcelain clay led to robust forms with a strong
geometrical quality, including monumental globular jars, flat-sided bottles
and boxes, as well as cylindrical containers pierced and reserved to produce
light-hearted openwork forms. The moon jars, formed on the potter’s wheel
in two parts, would have been too heavy if made in one single vessel. Their
appeal, and quiet charm, is partly attributed to the unpredictable nature of
the making process.58 The two halves of the globe are ‘luted’ together,
producing a seam that is discreet or prominent. The firing might cause the
upper or lower half to expand more than the other, producing an
asymmetrical profile. Tiny amounts of grit or metal in the clay might

produce flecking or dusting effects under the glaze when the jar is lifted out
of the kiln. These unpredictable outcomes of the making process are at the
heart of the moon jar’s appeal.
    The spacious, gracious charms of Korean porcelains – both plain and
underglaze-painted – are widely admired. The background to their making,
including their clays, pigments and glazes, allows a rounded understanding
of the close relationship between the natural world in which they originated
and the finished, fired pot. Joseon porcelains are the product of a society
where natural forms, materials and subjects were universally enjoyed. There
are more inquiries to make about the materials and the manufacture of
Joseon porcelains from various regions and periods.

Buncheong
Our knowledge of the circumstances that produced buncheong ceramics has
increased enormously thanks to twentieth- and twenty-first century
excavations and publications by Korean archaeologists and art historians.
Excavations at one of the largest buncheong sites, Chunghyo-dong, near
Mount Mudeung in South Jeolla Province, have revealed the scale of
production. Seven kilns and a 3-metre-high refuse layer were investigated,
with kiln number two, more than 20 metres long, and the refuse layer later
opened for visits as a site museum.59 A range of decorative surface effects –
impressed floral and other repetitive patterns, sgraffito and incised
decoration – was found (see illus. 101). Dated and inscribed pieces have
allowed researchers to trace the beginnings of porcelain production in the
1450s to 1470s, alongside buncheong ware. Some vessel forms were
common to the buncheong and the porcelain potters, such as large jars. All
buncheong ceramics are stonewares, and an important feature that
distinguishes them from late Goryeo celadons is that their clay bodies are
coarser, retaining impurities and not carefully worked to a fine consistency.
Buncheong bodies are generally rather high in iron. Their glazes generally
resemble the glazes on Goryeo celadons, with the caveat that the level of
titanium and iron oxides is lower,60 attributable to multo or water clay being
used in the preparation of the buncheong glaze.
    Compared to porcelains, the buncheong ceramics delivered a much
wider range of surface decorative effects. The potters who had once made
inlaid Goryeo celadons were able to innovate, trying out different shapes
and surface effects. In some cases more than one decorative technique

would be used, as in the case of an inlaid and stamped dragon bottle in the
V&A collection.61 The densely packed stamped decorations found on many
buncheong wares made in Gyeongsang Province kilns exemplify the long-
standing Korean flair for contrasting inlaid designs upon ceramics,
metalwork and lacquerware.
     Elsewhere, a very different buncheong artistry flowered. A rougher,
more spontaneous effect was obtained in those buncheong ceramics that
were first partly or wholly covered in white slip and then carved. Many of
these sgraffito technique pieces have flower-head decorations that create an
impression of bursting outwards from the darker shade of the background.
Made in kilns in Jeolla Province, these are exceptionally fine ceramics that
integrate form and surface decoration with confidence and élan.
    Hakbong-ri in Chungcheong Province (located near Gongju, capital of
the Baekje kingdom, which ruled southwest Korea from 18 BC to AD 660) is
another major production centre for many different types of buncheong and
various other ceramics.62 It is best known in Korea and internationally for
vessels in shapes that are not often found in other production centres,
bearing vibrant iron-painted decoration over a covering of brushed white
slip. Part of a large complex of ceramic kilns in the scenic area around
Mount Gyeryong, the Hakbong-ri kilns were on an impressive scale, some
numbering seventeen firing chambers and extending 30 metres or more in
length. Their period of activity was about a hundred years during the
fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Two kilns in the area were fully excavated
in the 1990s and found to have a column placed in the centre of the firing
chamber.63 The kilns at Hakbong-ri must have produced very large
quantities of buncheong ceramics, judging by the huge piles of wasters
excavated at the site. Hakbong-ri iron-painted buncheong ware looks
remarkably similar, on first acquaintance, to Chinese Cizhou ceramics, but
no evidence of a direct connection between the two types has so far been
established.64 Humorous, lively and closely observed motifs were the
hallmark of the Hakbong-ri potters’ art. Produced contemporaneously with
the literati-style blue-and-white porcelains at the official kilns in Gyeonggi
Province, Hakbong-ri buncheong was decorated by local artists whose
training had not exposed them to the conventions of Chinese aesthetics.
    As love of white ceramics became ever more deeply embedded in
Joseon society, buncheong ceramics in the latter part of the fifteenth century
became ever lighter and whiter. One method of achieving a monochrome

pale effect was to brush the vessel with slip, allowing the strands of the
brush, of a type known in Korea as a guiyal, to create a pleasing lined
pattern on the surface. Applied horizontally or vertically, the sweeping
brushstrokes are further evidence of the spontaneous, free-spirited approach
adopted by buncheong potters. As the vogue for pure white ceramics gained
ground, rather than brushing the slip on to the vessel before firing,
buncheong potters made their cups, bowls and bottles appear white by
dipping the whole piece in a thick coating of cream-coloured slip. The
Korean name for dipped ware is deombeong. Many of the plain white tea
bowls admired by Japanese chanoyu (tea ceremony) aficionados are
covered in plain white slip. This style of buncheong is associated with the
philosophical notion of ‘expansiveness’ whereby the potter’s close personal
association with the materials of his profession produces pieces that are
simultaneously modest and magnificent, at once transcendent and earthy.

Popular and Regional Wares: Onggi Ceramics and Hoeryeong
Stoneware
No account of ceramics in Korean society during the Joseon dynasty would
be complete without reference to the popular food and household ware
known as onggi. Onggi, literally ‘earthenware vessel’, is a kind of large,
glazed jar used for different types of food storage. It is formed from coils of
coarse, dark-coloured clay and dipped in wood-ash glaze before firing over
many days in a kiln at a temperature of 1000–1200°C. As well as large
storage jars, there are numerous onggi basins, spouted jars, chamber pots,
chimney pipes and cooking pots. Until the mid-twentieth century Korean
towns and villages were dotted with groups of onggi jars, laid out on
terraces and balconies and containing each household’s supplies of pickles
and preserved foodstuffs. Dark-bodied, these jars would fire to a rich brown
colour, embellished in many cases with free-flowing finger strokes done by
the potter before firing (illus. 135).
    Modern urban Koreans live in apartments with refrigerated storage and
no longer turn to onggi to hold their condiments, but the jars themselves
have seen a renaissance since the late twentieth century as collectors and
makers have stubbornly persisted in celebrating the large egg-shaped
vessels whose place in the Korean kitchen is of long standing. Studio
potters including Lee Kang-hyo (b. 1961) have turned onggi production into
a performance art, drawing viewers into the physical drama of creating a

tall, heavy-walled vessel out of coils of worked clay (see illus. 158). In a
few villages around the country, onggi are made in traditional workshops to
supply affluent urban Korean customers who admire and collect their
country’s heritage ceramic vessels. The potter forms the vessel on a wheel
sunk into a pit in the ground. After a bottom disc is placed on the wheel, the
potter feeds coils of clay slowly until the required height is achieved. The
walls of the pot are then patted and slapped to smoothness, and any lines or
handles are added. The pot is air-dried before being fired in a closely
packed kiln at a temperature of around 800°C.





135 Onggi jar with cover, 1875–1925, high-fired earthenware, height 113.8 cm.

Although onggi were a ubiquitous feature of pre-modern Korean life
and are a distinctive, handsome type of vessel requiring skill and
discrimination on the part of the maker, they were previously viewed by art
historians as low-status wares, ‘of no esthetic or cultural value to
Koreans’.65 Changes in modern lifestyles, including interest in well-being
and healthy eating, have however sparked a fresh interest in onggi, because
their thick, long-fired walls are ideal for encouraging fermentation, when
foodstuffs require cool, slightly porous containers to promote slow chemical
reactions between ingredients and preservatives. Certain modern Korean
food brands feature onggi vessels in their marketing materials, thereby
expressing authenticity in their commitment to promoting Korea’s food
culture.
    The government of South Korea supports a scheme to assign the title
of ‘intangible cultural asset’ to individuals and enterprises practising
designated crafts and art forms. Onggi making is intangible cultural asset
number 96, taking its place alongside skills such as paper making, lacquer
art and embroidery.66 The current holder of the title is Kim Il-Maan, who
with his family runs the Ohbuja Onggi Studio.67 The Kim family members
create their wares with little help from modern machinery, hand-processing
the raw clay, forming the large vessels with thick coils of prepared clay that
are pressed upwards by the wheel-man, the potter, to form a robust jar. The
jars are air-dried, then dipped in a wood-ash glaze before firing in a wood-
fired kiln.68
    Because onggi were considered a popular ware, their manufacture and
distribution were not court-controlled, and few textual records survive of
the longevity and circumstances of onggi manufacture in pre-modern
times.69 Many depictions of onggi jars in genre paintings have survived,
however, enabling ceramic historians to demonstrate that these jars were
common-place around the country. The court artist Kim Hong-do (1745–c.
1806) depicted a group of onggi jars on a terrace in his painting Life in
Retreat Is Better than High Ranks, extolling the superiority of a life in
nature compared to holding official office and showing that the custom of
storing foods and pickles outdoors in large jars was common during the
Joseon (illus. 136).

136 Kim Hong-do, Life in Retreat Is Better than High Ranks (detail), 1801, eight-fold screen, ink and
colour on paper.

137 Bowl from northeastern kilns, 1700–1800, glazed stoneware, height 13 cm.

     In the far northeast of the Korean peninsula, close to the Chinese
border and the Tumen River, and along the coast nearby, ceramics were
made at Heoryeong, Puryeong, Gyeongseong and Jueuronjang, especially in
the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (illus. 137). Known also by their
Japanese name, Kainei ware,70 these are rugged vessels with a variety of
different glaze effects including creamy white, light green and ‘flambé’
blue. Northeastern stoneware ceramics resemble Chinese Jun ware in
having dark bodies and streaky feldspathic glazes.71 The ash glaze known
in Japan as namako is an opaque dark brown colour with bands of blue and
white. The kilns are believed to have been founded by Buddhist monks
from nearby monasteries in the twelfth century.

The International Dimension of Joseon Ceramics

In the later nineteenth century Joseon Korea was introduced to the
international community as a ‘hermit kingdom’, an epithet that has
obscured the substantial and ongoing contacts that linked the Korean
peninsula to its two most important neighbours, China and Japan. These
interactions in the East Asian sphere included ceramics both as material
manifestations of cultural relationships and, to a lesser extent, as traded
commodities. As we have seen, the formative decades of Joseon rule, in the
early fifteenth century, were dominated by the shift to a neo-Confucian
world view that Korea wished to share with the Ming dynasty of China. The
royal kilns’ efforts to produce blue-and-white porcelain were a direct result
of encounters with Chinese white porcelain from the Jingdezhen kilns. The
decoration that adorned Joseon ceramics depicted subjects that Korea
shared with China: auspicious and powerful creatures, scrolling flower-
heads and plants, poetic scenes, graceful calligraphic phrases and couplets.
    Documentary records of Chinese porcelains reaching Korea survive
from the reign of King Sejong (reg 1418–50), and it is clear that white
porcelain was first made in Korea in the fifteenth century as an attempt to
emulate the Chinese product. Also in King Sejong’s reign, the Chinese
emperor requested 210 pieces of fine white Korean porcelain to be made
and set as a tribute. Thus official exchange of porcelain between Korea and
China took place in the fifteenth century. Diplomatic exchanges and low-
level, surreptitious trade across the land border and by sea all played a part
in introducing each country’s ceramics to the other, but the general
antipathy to commerce that dominated Korean life meant that purchasing or
selling ceramics was an activity that could attract punishment. In 1448 King
Sejong commanded the Ministry of Rites to prohibit all ceramic trade on
the route to and from Beijing and Liaoning Province,72 while in 1467 King
Sejo (reg 1455–68) banned commoners from using wine vessels made of
gold, silver or blue-and-white porcelain, on penalty of receiving eighty
floggings, thus demonstrating that blue-and-white porcelain was regarded
as a rare and elite ware. We noted earlier that in 1475 the Annals of King
Seongjong criticized the yangban class for their extravagance in using ‘only
blue-and-white porcelain vessels imported from China . . . Despite the
difficulty of transporting the porcelain from China, every house possesses
them’ – showing once more that a supply of blue-and-white wares from
China was available, despite the court’s passionate pleas for restraint.

Chinese ceramics were prestigious, well-made and plentiful. They clearly
reached Korean customers in some quantity.73
     In the late eighteenth century, during the reign of King Jeongjo, some
writers made disparaging comments about Korean ceramics seen in
comparison with Chinese wares. Reformist scholar-officials such as Pak
Che-ga (1750–1815), Yi Hui-gyeong (1745–1805) and Jeong Yak-yong
(1762–1836) all commented unfavourably on Korean technology, and in
Pak’s case criticized Korean porcelains for their heaviness and careless
finish. Despite this, no change in Korea’s official policy of frugality and
plain design was permitted at the time.74
     In sharp contrast to the relationship with China, Joseon’s ceramic
dealings with Japan were diverse and fraught with tension. The nexus was
one of persistent demand from Japan, which before the mid-seventeenth
century had no domestic ability to produce porcelain, and reluctance
bordering on irritation from the Korean side. Ostensibly taking the form of
diplomatic exchanges of gifts, purchases of goods by Japanese visitors to
the Korean peninsula took place regularly. It is easy to imagine that white-
bodied ceramics were extremely attractive to Japanese who interacted with
Joseon. In the sixteenth century, kilns in the southern provinces of
Gyeongsang and Jeolla traded unofficially with Japanese merchants and
seafarers, leaving scant records of their activities, since by law Koreans
were forbidden from dealing with foreigners.
    During the sixteenth century a fashion for plain, unaffected Korean
bowls gained currency in tea gatherings in Japan. Plain Korean bowls, both
buncheong and porcelain, were highly sought after by tea ceremony
masters.75 In the seventeenth century the Waegwan or Japan House, a
settlement on the south coast of Korea, was authorized to operate a kiln that
produced ceramics for the Japanese market. Traders from Tsushima, the
barren island that lies between Korea and the Japanese island of Kyushu,
also played an active role in supplying Korean ceramics to Japan.
Additionally, and better known, are the vessels made in Japan by Korean
potters who were kidnapped and taken to Japan during the military
invasions of the 1590s. These potters settled in areas of the islands of
Kyushu and Honshu and later played an important part in the development
of Japan’s porcelain manufacturing from the seventeenth century
onwards.76

The place of Korean buncheong and porcelain bowls in Japan’s tea
culture is highly significant. Tea gatherings in the wabicha style were
fashionable in Japan between about 1550 and 1770.77 Tea bowls from
Korea, known in Japan as Kōrai chawan, were part of the accoutrements
used during tea gatherings, which were intimate affairs held in austere,
plain surroundings. Tea bowls carried with them associations with the
samurai class and with the Zen Buddhist practice of taking tea in a quiet
thatched hut, in a modest room floored with tatami mats. Some tea bowls
were given names by their owners; they were carefully protected in special
containers, to be brought into service for special moments when invited
guests of the bowl’s owner could examine and admire them. Famous tea
bowls changed hands for large sums of money. Tea aficionados would treat
famous bowls as if they had souls: ‘By imbuing material objects with life
and spiritual power, tea masters were able to turn the tea ceremony into an
assembly of souls, in which human beings and tea utensils communed with
each other through the aesthetics of tea.’78 It is estimated that today more
than 600 Korean-produced tea bowls of the sixteenth and seventeenth
centuries are held in Japanese collections. In many cases the potters who
made them were unaware that these modest vessels would be treasured and
culturally assimilated as part of Japan’s ritualized tea culture (illus. 138).

138 Tea bowl, lacquer repairs, 1500–1600, buncheong, height 8.1 cm.

     Further Japanese encounters with Joseon ceramics took place before
and during the period of colonial rule. The writer and collector Yanagi
Sōetsu (1889–1961), founder of the Mingei folk craft movement, loved
Joseon ceramics and introduced other influential makers and writers to their
beauty. It was primarily thanks to Yanagi that Bernard Leach engaged with
Korean ceramics and purchased the luminous moon jar now in the
collection of the British Museum (see illus. 118).79 Yanagi visited Korea
frequently between 1916 and about 1928. Even after 1930, when his work
in Japan prevented him from travelling so frequently, he continued to visit
Korea and to write about Korean ceramics and other crafts. Yanagi’s ideas
on Joseon ceramics were to influence many twentieth-century scholars.
They remain controversial in Japan and Korea until now, despite
recognition that Yanagi was critical of the politics of the Japanese colonial
regime.80 Like other Japanese and Western collectors and curators of the

time, Yanagi saw Korea as a child-like innocent, passive and melancholy in
nature. As Kim Brandt has argued, ‘[during the 1920s] . . . by using
opportunities created in Korea by Japanese rule and by adopting selected
aspects of Western-style colonial knowledge, Yanagi and others gained
potent forms of cultural and social authority in Japan, Korea and even the
West.’81

CHAPTER FOUR
MODERN AND
CONTEMPORARY:

 NEW BEGINNINGS
 IN A DIVIDED
 COUNTRY

The late twentieth century was an eventful period in Korean ceramic
history. Following liberation from Japanese colonial rule in 1945 came the
tragedy of war between 1950 and 1953, leading to the division of the
country. Over the succeeding decades, with the country divided into a
socialist north and a capitalist south, the economy began to recover. In
North Korea, as we shall discuss below, artists worked in a system where
government values and cultural programmes determined the scope of their
practice and the circumstances of their working life. The conflict and
destruction that led to division meant that contacts between colleagues,
families and enterprises were cut off. Ceramics were hardly a priority at that
time of poverty and hardship, but the Cold War years of the 1950s to ’80s
laid the foundations for ceramics as an art form in both modern Koreas.
    South of the 38th parallel, the government of the Republic of Korea
had its capital at Seoul. Traditionally, ceramics had been produced
principally in Korea’s southern provinces. When tentative steps were taken
in the 1950s to reanimate ceramics as an artistic manufacture, the kiln areas
of Gyeonggi Province, where the official kilns of the Joseon era had
operated, were a site of investigation. In the decades that followed, South
Korea actively promoted ceramics as a studio practice, with artisans
carrying forward family traditions and investigating the clays, decorative
styles, glazes and firing practices that their forebears had known. At the
same time, some university departments trained potters to make work in
local and international styles. The recovery of the ceramics heritage of
Korea was slow and painful, since the Japanese colonial period had been a
time when most Koreans ceased using and thinking about ceramics in their
everyday lives. Furthermore, the post-war years were characterized by
poverty and economic reconstruction. The public had scant interest in the
nascent ceramic profession in the universities, especially because tableware
and everyday ceramics had been replaced by stainless steel and nickel
utensils.1 Nevertheless, the pioneering efforts of the post-war years paved
the way for growth. Before and after the millennium, Korean potters built
strong reputations working in vernacular and modernist idioms. In the
twenty-first century, Korean art schools and universities have trained large
numbers of ceramic specialists, while admittedly also being affected by the
international trend in practice-based arts education away from the physical
and towards the digital, a movement that can be detrimental to developing
clay-based working. The modern period in South Korea is a rich subject for

research, since the careers and philosophies of individual artists have been
recorded and presented in group and individual exhibitions and can
therefore be traced and interrogated in a way that is impossible for the
ceramics of earlier times. By contrast, access to artists based in North Korea
has been difficult for researchers in the West. The diverse and creative
works of ceramic artists working in Pyongyang and other North Korean
centres are under-recognized and deserve to be better understood.

Ceramics in South Korea: Post-war Artists
The first three universities to provide ceramic education were Seoul
National University, Ewha Womans University and Hongik University, all
in Seoul. Many of their faculty and graduates have built careers in ceramics
and in teaching. Korea’s pre-modern achievements in ceramic production
have been reinvigorated, particularly since the 1980s, by artists reclaiming
their national origins and traditions. At the same time, Korean potters have
travelled and interacted with colleagues in North America, Japan and, to a
lesser extent, Europe. Although a fine art college was established at Seoul
National University in 1945, including an applied arts department, the
university began training ceramic artists only in 1962, when the artist Kwon
Soon-Hyung (b. 1929) returned to Korea from Cleveland, Ohio, and set up
the department in which he would serve as professor (illus. 139).2 He was
an influential figure in the creation of modern ceramics as an artistic
discipline in Korea, one whose earlier training as a painter infused his later
work as a potter, as seen in his focus on colours and patterns (illus.
140).Kwon’s two-dimensional work is well known, with a high-profile
example in a tile mural installation for the 1963 Sheraton Walker Hill Hotel,
Seoul, one of the earliest luxury international hotels (and named for the
American commander of the U.S. Eighth Army, Walton H. Walker, who died
in Seoul in 1950).

139 Kwon Soon-Hyung, bulbous vase, 1990–92,
glazed porcelain, height 24 cm.





140 Kwon Soon-Hyung, Land of Beautiful Scenery, 1978, porcelain tiles, 3.6 × 4.5 m.

    Another pioneer of ceramics in new Korea is Kim Yik-Yung (b. 1935),
Professor of Ceramics at Kookmin University from 1975 to 2000. Kim’s
faceted porcelain vessels refer directly to the austere ritual forms of the

Joseon period (illus. 141). A dynamic personality who has run a successful
studio while teaching, Kim came to studio ceramics after a degree in
chemical engineering and postgraduate work at Alfred University, New
York state, and further research in Tokyo. Her international outlook
complements her thoughtful exploration of monochrome Joseon forms,
achieved with grainy, kaolin-rich clay, which produces minuscule brown
dots in the glaze. Over the decades of her life as a potter in Korea, she has
maintained relationships with international artists that have enriched and
enlivened her practice. Indeed, her starting point as a maker was the
encouragement of an Englishman, Bernard Leach, to explore her country’s
ceramic history. Their meeting in the United States during the 1970s took
place at a time when Korean society was uninterested in ceramics and few
Korean students chose to pursue a life working with clay. Over the years,
architectural and large-scale ensembles have enriched Kim’s repertoire,
reflecting a sustained interest in sculptural form and the infinite potential of
clay in modern life.3





141 Kim Yik-Yung, offering vessel, 1991,
porcelain, height 17.5 cm.

stoneware, height 16 cm.

A very different professional and family background brought Hwang
Jong-ku (1919–2003) (illus. 142) to the professorship in Ewha Womans
University, where a well-equipped teaching facility was established in 1958.
As the children of Hwang In-Choon (1894–1950), a well-established
celadon artist during the period of the Japanese occupation, Hwang Jong-
Gu and his sister, who spells her name differently, Whang Chong-nye (b.
1927), grew up in the historic city of Gaeseong, where their father ran a
celadon factory. Brother and sister both dedicated their careers to making
green-glazed stoneware, celadon, and to training a new generation of
ceramic artists. At Ewha, Hwang passed on his mastery of the art of
forming and decorating celadon. His tenure lasted from 1958 to 1984,
during which time he established the university’s influential Ceramic
Research Center. Experimenting with kiln management, he produced high-
quality celadon in an oil-fired kiln, with a lower wastage rate than when
using a wood-fired kiln.4 His meticulously formed and glazed jade-coloured
celadons with inlaid decoration are testament to his perfectionist quest to
engage with his country’s most refined pre-modern ceramics, the exquisite
celadons of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries (illus. 143). His sister,
initially trained as a painter, has chosen to work in the buncheong idiom,
although decorating her vessels in unusual colours. The brush she uses to
paint abstract linear patterns on her vessels is similar to the simple kwiyal
brush that Joseon potters used to produce brushed slip buncheong. Professor
Whang Chong-nye taught at Kookmin University and continued working
and exhibiting into her nineties (illus. 144).5

    Hongik University is a post-Second World War foundation in Seoul
with a strong reputation in art, design and architecture. Won Dae-jeong
(1920–2007) was appointed professor of ceramics in 1967 (illus. 145),
having first trained in painting and later studied ceramics in the United
States and at Tokyo National College of Arts. Won’s practice began with a
strong, painterly focus on surface decoration. Later, however, he turned
towards pure white porcelain. Acclaimed and feted in Korea during his
lifetime, Won is known for achieving perfect harmony of glaze and body,
and for his subtly shifting forms that combine serenity with severity.6
Earlier at Hongik, Stanley Fistick, an instructor in ceramics at Ohio State
University who served as an adviser on design and education under the
auspices of the U.S. State Department, had taught ceramics in the early years
of the department’s work (illus. 146).7
    The 1950s and ’60s were thus a time of new beginnings for the
intellectual and practice-based study of Korean ceramics. After decades of
decline and public indifference to Korea’s ceramic past, the new university
departments were training interested students and exploring the technical
and aesthetic qualities of celadon and porcelain. Contacts with American

and Japanese potters enlivened the scene and brought a spirit of inquiry and
professional support to the field.
    While the academic framework for ceramic studies was being
constructed, with substantial investment in university departments, artisan
potters continued their work in producing celadon and porcelain,
particularly around Icheon, in the traditional ceramic area of Gyeonggi
Province. Famous among these is the Yoo family. Yu Geun-Hyeong (1894–
1993) was a potter who combined rigorous investigation of celadon
materials and techniques with a determination to produce fresh and
authentic pieces. With his eldest son Kwangul, he established a museum
dedicated to Korean ceramics in 1990, the Haegang Museum in Icheon. Yoo
Kwangul (b. 1942) is today the holder of the studio name Haegang (illus.
147) and continues to work with the next generation, his son Jaehyoung.8
Yoo Kwangul’s celadon work displays a range of forms and colours,
including rectangular bottles and lidded boxes. Outside the university
world, the Yoo family’s sustained research into clays, firing atmospheres
and surface decoration have been recognized in Korea as an important
continuation of the celadon potter’s craft in modern times.

147 Yu Geun-Hyeong, maebyeong, 20th century, glazed stoneware, height 38 cm.

   A towering, if controversial, figure in modern Korean ceramics is Shin
Sang-Ho (b. 1947), one of the most prolific and multi-talented artists in
clay. Shin’s eclectic practice in the earlier part of his career spanned
porcelain, celadon and buncheong ceramics (illus. 148). A graduate of
Hongik University, he was Dean there from 1998 to 2004. In the course of
extensive travels, Shin has also worked on a larger scale, initially producing
sculptural, animal forms that seemed to connect, however tenuously, to the
buncheong creatures he had made in the 1990s. A move to make dazzling
pictorial and sculptural works took place in the 1990s and 2000s, with a

vibrant, densely packed exhibition at the Clayarch Gimhae Museum
presenting sculptural, installation and architectural pieces.9 Brightly
coloured ‘fired painting’ installations and numerous ground-breaking
presentations overwhelm the viewer with their sheer chaotic, furious
energy. Shin’s practice has been described as ‘the most fiercely ambitious
body of work of any Korean ceramic artist’, one whose sense of scale, of
relationship to other cultures and personal relationship to his own culture
have ‘redefined the territory in which those around him can operate’.10 Shin
himself has written frankly of his frustrations as a Korean artist, and his
single-minded pursuit of freedom of expression:

    They say that honoring our own cultural tradition is the key to keeping
     oneself in touch with one’s own identity. How ludicrous! The world
    always changes . . . identity exists only inside of my own universe
    anyway. So how dare anyone exploit something so personal . . . many
     times the crude stubbornness of human nature to fear and despise the
     unfamiliar and the unknown drives me insane.11

cm.

Shin Sang-Ho’s passionate pursuit of artistic truth, and his eclectic practice,
have unfolded in a period when Korean artists have travelled widely,
encountering countless possibilities as a result of exposure to new visual
sources. He expands the boundaries of ceramics as an expressive medium,
anticipating the work of younger artists who move away from the vessel
and work in ceramics as part of a diverse practice. An interesting early
example of his collaborative practice is the 1985 plate painted by Song Soo
Nam (illus. 149).
    Yun Kwang-cho (b. 1946) is a fellow graduate of Hongik University,
one whose life in ceramics could not be more different from that of Shin.
After graduating, Yun studied in Japan in 1974–5 with a descendant of the
Korean potters who had settled in Karatsu (Kyushu) after the Hideyoshi
invasions of the 1590s. Yun’s teacher there was Nakazato Tarouemon, a
thirteenth-generation potter. In the studio he later founded, deep in the
countryside near the ancient Silla capital, Gyeongju, Yun has produced
monumental and daily use ceramics. Two forces have shaped Yun Kwang-
cho’s ceramics: his Buddhist faith and the buncheong technique. The rough,
impure clay of buncheong and the rustic designs he applies to the vessels
reflect a philosophy of communion with nature,12 reminding us that

historically Korean artists frequently took comfort and found refuge in the
mountains and valleys of the countryside. Reclusion, the love of tranquil
places far from the ties and burdens of the city, is a long-standing theme in
East Asian art and literature.
    To create his solid, heavy vessels, Yun generally builds with slabs or
coils of clay, producing massive, straight-walled jars and vases whose upper
edges seem to undulate like the ridge of a mountaintop (illus. 150). He uses
a simple brush to apply cream-coloured slip to the iron-rich clay, producing
a two-tone palette where the clay colour is partially obscured by the
covering. Many of his pieces have simple geometric decoration incised into
the white slip; others bear the texts of Buddhist sutras. The Heart Sutra, a
short text much favoured by artists and calligraphers in China, Japan and
Korea on account of its manageable length, can be scratched into the white
slip covering a tall vessel, in blocky Chinese characters. As a practising
Buddhist, Yun values the meditative, repetitive nature of the solitary
potter’s working life, considering himself a creative rebel against the
globalizing influences on the modern art scene.13 He forms his work alone,
without assistance, treasuring his place in Gyeongsang Namdo, far from
city life, and naming his ceramics ‘Meditation’, ‘Windy Valley’, ‘Mountain
Dream’ and the like.

painted stoneware, height 40 cm.





    Another ceramic artist who has lived and worked in the countryside
throughout his career is Min Young-ki (b. 1947). Trained in Korea and
again with Nakazato Tarouemon, whose family had been forcibly moved to
Japan during the Hideyoshi invasions of the 1590s, Min seeks a life in

harmony with nature. His spacious studio is located at the foot of Mount
Chiri, in Sancheong, South Gyeongsang Province, an area of natural beauty
in the south of Korea. Min Young-ki makes buncheong ceramics of various
styles, but he is known above all for fine, modest tea bowls, which enjoy a
strong reputation in Korean and in Japan, where he holds exhibitions of his
work.14 The rough clay of the Sancheong region is used exclusively,
requiring lengthy and arduous preparation before it can be thrown on the
wheel or coiled. Min makes brushed and inlaid buncheong bowls and
bottles that incorporate rustic designs of houses, plants and birds. Wood
firing in a traditional kiln is practised, and the wastage rate is considerable.
Min’s tea bowls, which sell for high prices to Korean and Japanese
customers, range in colour from pale cream to pink and russet brown (illus.
151). When drinking whipped, powdered green tea, one can see and smell
the frothy lightness of the tea while holding the bowl and enjoying its shape
and surface qualities.
    The artist and Kookmin University professor Roe Kyung Jo (b. 1951)
has made ceramics in various styles and is known also as a modernist
painter. Above all, however, his reputation has been built around the
production of marbled ceramics, a unique style of mixed-clay ware in
which he excels (illus. 152). Growing up in a cultured, well-connected
family in Seongbuk-dong district, Seoul, Roe showed an early talent for
painting: his teacher, Kim Young-ki (1911–2003), was the son of the royal
painting tutor Kim Gyu-jin (1868–1933) (illus. 153). Roe studied at Kyung
Hee University College of Fine Arts before spending two years in Japan at
Kanazawa College of Art and Crafts, where he deepened his knowledge of
decorative glazing effects. During his student years, he had been inspired by
lectures from Choi Sun-u (1916–1984), director of the National Museum of
Korea, to engage with Goryeo and Joseon ceramics, experimenting with
producing various styles including white porcelain. Impressed by the young
Roe’s talent and dedication to studying Korea’s traditional ceramics, Choi
Sun-u became a mentor, one who supported Roe’s work at the university
and in the gallery. Roe’s marbled-technique vessels (yeollimun) have
contrasting surfaces and straight-walled shapes with a quietly confident
presence. A connection between Roe’s paintings and pots becomes
apparent, as both simplify contours and use colour with restraint. Although
the marbled ware that inspired Roe’s trademark style flourished and
disappeared during the Goryeo dynasty, his forms have a strong flavour of

the Joseon period, being cube-like, flat-profiled, square or rectangular.
Many monumental pieces have a weighty stillness, reflecting Roe’s
meticulous, precise working style that has clay at its core.





151 Min Young-ki, bottle, 1991, Buncheong, stamped, painted, height 21 cm.
152 Roe Kyung Jo, rectangular vase, 2000–2005, marbled clay, unglazed, height 32 cm.

153 Kim Gyu-jin, calligraphic scroll, 1900, ink on paper, scroll 220 × 65 cm, panel 132 × 51 cm.

    The principal source of his clay is the Icheon region.15 Stencils are
used to mark patterns on the leather-hard clay, removing a layer a few
millimetres deep. A piece of contrasting clay with the same design is rolled
into the cavity in the clay. After further drying, excess infill clay is scraped
off, leaving the motif clearly visible. The technique is similar to that used
by Goryeo potters inlaying designs in stoneware. Another decorative
method is to mix different coloured clays together, mosaic style. Naturally,
the different clays must dry and shrink at a similar rate. Roe roughens the
walls of his vessels, thus accentuating the granular quality of the clays,
which are mainly red or cream in colour. The contrasting colours of Roe’s

marbled vessels are earthy, with transparent or semi-transparent glazes
gently veiling the surfaces. Firing is at the rather high temperature of
around 1280°C. Roe has stated that ‘the monochrome period of white
porcelain ware, that is representative of the Choson [Joseon] period,
corresponds with the Minimalism in modern art. The source of inspiration
for my work is partly in Minimalism as well as Korean crafts.’16 Roe
combines a demanding professional life as a senior university leader with a
studio practice at Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province, where he has assembled
a huge set of sherds and kiln wasters, brought together over a lifetime of
collecting and studying. It is unsurprising that this energetic, erudite potter’s
studio has been the destination for numerous international museum and
ceramic visitors, since there is so much to learn about modern Korean
ceramics there.
    Another maker familiar to overseas visitors to Korea is Park Young-
sook (b. 1947). A charismatic personality, Park grew up in Gyeongju, in an
area close to one of Korea’s most famous temples, the Bulguk or Buddha
Land Temple. The daughter of a shop owner, she collected antiquities in the
archaeologically rich area around her home. In later life, she threw herself
into making ceramics as a serious undertaking, despite having little artistic
education. She has collaborated over several decades with the distinguished
artist Lee Ufan, who was born in 1936 in Korea and has lived in Japan
(illus. 154). Park’s remarkable vocation to produce both buncheong and
white porcelain has brought her fame and success, with work held in many
of the world’s museums. She has poured passion and creative determination
into her enterprise of perfecting and reimagining the Joseon globular jars
known as moon jars, producing luminous pale vessels on a gigantic scale,
some as tall as 64 centimetres high (illus. 155). Meticulous attention to clay
quality, glaze materials and firing atmosphere have characterized her pure
porcelain, produced in an airy studio outside Seoul. In a foreword to an
exhibition of moon jars, the artist wrote:

   When I would try to make a single, finished form, I would put it in the
     kiln and then, when I took it out, I found that one side had slipped,
    warped. This was because while the upper and lowers sections were
     firing in the intense flames, they accepted each other, letting go of their
   own individual shape in order to fuse into a single shape . . . The
     creation of the single complete shape of a Moon Jar is surprisingly just

like human life . . . two different people meet and find mutual
     understanding . . . Moon Jars are human life itself.17

    The potter Kim Sok-Hwan (1932–2012) exhibited widely in her native
country and internationally. In addition to white porcelain works like the
tilted, grey-glazed jar formed of two parts joined at the middle (illus. 156),
she also produced stoneware, in the form of long-necked jars and crocks,
reminiscent of the onggi storage vessels used in pre-modern Korean
households. These red-bodied pieces are formed of iron-rich clay and can
also be considered as referring to the monumental ceremonial ceramics of
the Three Kingdoms period (see illus. 30). Kim Seok-hwan taught ceramics
at Dangook University in Seoul from 1971 to 1999. In 2008, towards the
end of her life, Kim founded the Dolsuk Ceramic Art Museum in Anyang
City, near Seoul, which takes its name from her sobriquet. Her engagement
with the vernacular ceramic tradition was sustained throughout her long
career.18

154 Park Young Sook, Lee Ufan plate, 1994,
porcelain, diam. 30 cm.





    Also responding to the ceramics of the Three Kingdoms period is the
influential university professor and curator Cho Chung-hyun (b. 1940), who
trained at Ewha Womans University and Southern Illinois University in the
1960s and ’70s. Cho works with traditional coarse clays, thrown and
assembled before firing. Many of her pieces are tall vessels that stand on a
raised foot, recalling the ceremonial earthenwares of the Silla dynasty.

Cho’s long career as a teacher and maker positioned her to shape the
development of ceramics in late twentieth-century Korea. She encouraged
her students to draw out connections to Korea’s long ceramic history.19 She
was a founding member, in 1978, of the Korea Contemporary Ceramic
Artists Association, which organized exhibitions and debated issues
connected with the field of ceramics in modern Korea.20 In her work, often
introducing contrasting blue inlaid decoration into the rich red clay of her
pierced pedestal vessels, she has innovated boldly by introducing non-
functional onggi shapes (illus. 157). With their shiny salt glazes and their
haunting sculptural forms, Cho’s high-fired onggi are an imaginative re-
engagement with the ceramics of the first millennium AD, deftly joining
ancient in modern, East and West.

    Lee Kang-hyo (b. 1961) has worked for over thirty years making
onggi-derived pots, but his search for what he has described as a ‘beautiful
life’ led him to work far away from the university campus. His
‘postgraduate’ years were spent as an apprentice in an onggi studio in South
Gyeongsang Province. He was drawn to the tall, generous forms of storage
vessels and the warm, earthy tones of onggi clay. A charming and
passionate potter, Lee Kang-hyo has written that ‘the everlasting theme of
my work is based on mountains, fields and sky. Everything that exists has
its own reason and beauty. Making something with clay with the hands and
then painting white over the surface is an expression of my dream. I am
alive at this minute.’21 Lee Kang-hyo and his wife, Son Kyung Hee, work
together at his studio and kiln site near Ochang, North Chungcheong
Province, south of Seoul, making a range of wares. Lee is known above all

for monumental onggi pots that are dramatically splashed and wiped with
slip to create large-scale jars with a haunting presence.22 Other vessels and
sculptural ceramics are also made from the clays he sources all around the
country. A likeable, genial man, Lee has travelled widely, demonstrating his
forming skills and performing the application of slip to leather-hard body to
the accompaniment of drumming and song. The tall cylindrical jar (illus.
158) made in the 1980s heralds the later decades of Lee’s practice, when he
created enormous onggi jars that bear witness to Korea’s food culture of
storing and using fermented vegetable and fish condiments. On Lee’s onggi
jars, pale liquid slip is dynamically painted, splashed and finger-drawn on
the dark body of the vessel, creating a furious energy as the rising curves of
one movement sweep upwards, in contrast to the horizontal bands covering
most of the walls.23
    Working both in buncheong and in white porcelain is Ree Soo-jong (b.
1948), who is widely recognized as a pre-eminent artist of his generation.
Ree is known as a maker of vessels, but his life as an artist has also
encompassed ceramic sculpture and a lively engagement with painting and
drawing. His work is powerful and elemental: his moon jars bear spare,
dramatic brushstrokes of iron brown; for Ree, the moon jar form celebrates
rather than conceals the joint between sections, drawing attention to the
making process and its intimate connection to the physical properties of
clay. In his buncheong practice, Ree creates abstract patterns by tracing
lines into the drying slip (illus. 159). Trained at Hongik University, and
working mainly independently, Ree has exhibited his work inside and
outside Korea.
    Choi Sung-jae (b. 1962) trained at Hongik University and is a
professor in traditional arts and crafts at the Korea National University of
Cultural Heritage in Buyeo, which trains students in ‘creative inheritance
and development of traditional culture and preservation, management and
utilization of cultural properties’.24 He is known for his powerful
buncheong work, where a thick white slip is applied over grey stoneware
clay, using brushes or hands. When the slip is partly dried, he uses his
fingers to wipe it away to create meditative designs of plants and waterfowl,
often so minimalist as to be a mere flourish (illus. 161). The artist has said
of his flat vessels and rounded jars that ‘the form and surface aim to express
the traces of impromptu passing actions conducted by an artist, as well as
abstraction and contemplative landscape of a comfortable mind reminiscent

of the natural image.’25 Choi’s tranquil pictorial compositions on the clay
are known for including ducks, moving in harmony with watery reeds and
grasses.

stoneware, height 68.5 cm.

   A Seoul-based buncheong artist who teaches ceramics at Kookmin
University and works in the sgraffito technique is Huh Sang-wook (b.
1970). Huh uses the coarse clay and pale slip of the historical buncheong
potters, but his practice is to prepare the surface while the clay is damp,
resulting in a soft, natural texture. Huh Sang-wook is known for jars and
bowls decorated with powerful flower-heads. Firmly rooted in the Joseon
tradition, his pieces are recognized for the subtlety and interest of their
surface decoration, achieved when the artist repeatedly scrapes away the
clay and applies coatings of slip, giving a three-dimensional effect (illus.
160).

    Lee Jeong-Do (b. 1953) is a potter who has focused primarily on
reviving the beauty of stamped buncheong ware in the modern manner. His
pine-ash glaze has a distinctive blue-grey tone, which renders his pots
rather bright and elegant.26 His stamped and inlaid designs have a direct
and natural appeal, often incorporating stylized bird, fish and flower motifs
demarcated by dividing lines inlaid into the vessel. Lee resides in Ontario,
Canada, where he continues to show work actively (illus. 162).27
    Lee In Chin (b. 1957) brings an international perspective to his
practice. Educated in Korea and California, he is a Hongik University

alumnus who continues to teach ceramics there. Accomplished in diverse
styles of ceramic production, Lee In Chin travels widely, including to Japan
and China. His output includes installation assemblies where the rich
variety of clay colours, textures and lustre draw the eye over stacked groups
of vessels.28 He celebrates the functional, practical nature of ceramics. His
early red jars and onggi-style containers bear visible marks of the potter’s
shaping hand and of the kiln’s transforming heat (illus. 163).
    Jeon Seong-keun (1959–2015) produced remarkable double-layered
porcelain with organic designs spanning the entire vessel. Originally
working as a wood carver, he developed remarkable skill in carving the
outer layer of his porcelain vessels with diverse patterns. He is known for
integrating the Korean script, Hangeul, into his vases and for the three-
dimensional quality of his carving in porcelain, a truly virtuoso style of
ceramics. Despite his technical skill, his work has a poetic quality that
encourages reflection on Korea’s long history as a producer of openwork
ceramics (see illus. 70). His remarkable vase with lacquer varnish playfully
simulates the appearance of a vessel encased in a continuous wooden
covering of carved flowers (illus. 164). In fact, the vase consists of a double
layer of porcelain, with the outer skin covered in the Korean lacquer known
as otchil (illus. 165).

Kim Kee-chul (b. 1935) is an English teacher who turned to ceramics
as a vocation. He reconstructed a traditional wood-fired dragon kiln, where
he fires a variety of wares including unglazed porcelain. Kim controls the
kiln atmosphere to produce effects such as the pink colour of the tall bowl
of flower-petal form (illus. 166). Kim also produces elegant white glazed
porcelain vessels.
   Kim Syyoung (b. 1958) is unusual in his devotion to black ceramics.
As a child, living in Japan, he prepared ink for his calligrapher foster-father,
who also taught him about the black tea bowls made in Song China (960–
1279) and about Goryeo black wares. He retained a curiosity about the
allure of black ceramics and made comparisons between Korean and
Chinese glazes. An engineer by training, he changed direction in his thirties,
learning clay preparation, throwing and firing from Icheon master potters.
Later he established his own kiln in Hongcheon County, Gangwon
Province, in the mountainous centre of Korea. By researching clay qualities
and firing conditions, and by collecting organic materials to make ash
glazes, Kim Syyoung and his talented daughters, who promote his work in
Korea and internationally, have brought dark, iron-rich clay to collectors’
attention.29 The starting point for black-glazed work is, of course, the
treasured tea bowls used to serve whipped green tea in Buddhist ritual
(illus. 167). Kim has devoted much energy to the visual effects of these
remarkable small vessels with their thick, unctuous glazes, which impart a
wide range of colour tones to his vessels. Song dynasty black-glazed bowls
are known as Tenmoku tea bowls and are viewed with great reverence in
Japan. (Tenmoku is the Japanese pronunciation of the Chinese mountain
Tianmu, location of the temple from where the Japanese Buddhist monks
obtained black-glazed tea bowls and took them home.) Black-glazed bowls
were considered perfect for the aesthetic and spiritual appreciation of
whipped tea, matcha, because they accentuated the pale colour of the liquid,
seen against the darkness of the bowl.
    Over long periods of test firing at different temperatures and with
various levels of atmospheric oxygen, Kim Syyoung has produced glazes
composed of pine wood and of local soils, each resulting in specific
coloration. Kim’s output encompasses most tableware and tea ceramics, but
his most striking, large-scale pieces include rugged installations of glazed
clay, wall-mounted and free standing. His black moon jars (illus. 168) are
also a surprising and powerful set of vessels: their asymmetrical shapes and

curvaceous forms seem to fit naturally with the complex glaze spectrum,
achieved through control of the atmosphere inside the kerosene-fired kiln.
Kim’s scientific background and interest in exploring the mountainous areas
near his residence have enabled him to mix iridescent glazes that showcase
the diverse mineral components of Korea’s earth. Kim’s life has been a
quest to match the renowned tea vessels made by Song dynasty potters in
China’s Fujian Province, since they inspired his decision to dedicate his life
to pottery. His is a meditative practice, steeped in a ceramic tradition that
blends connoisseurship with a spirit of scientific inquiry.





166 Kim Kee-chul, vase, 1994, porcelain, unglazed, height 36 cm.

Another single-minded potter who has devoted a lifetime to the
creation of ceramics inspired by earlier times is Kwon Dae Sup (b. 1952).
Kwon abandoned his painting studies at Hongik University to pursue the art
of making pots after falling in love with a Joseon porcelain jar he had
chanced upon in a Seoul antique shop. Years of study and practice followed,
including a period in Japan where he learned the strict discipline needed to
follow the calling of the potter – clay collection and preparation, kiln
building and maintenance, firing regimes. Eventually he felt ready to
establish his own kiln, in the Gwangju area southeast of Seoul, and to start
producing ‘work that needs nothing added and nothing subtracted’.30 Kwon
prepares his clay personally, before throwing the jars on a foot-turned wheel
in the classic Korean fashion, in two parts. When the vessels have dried off
in carefully controlled conditions, the upper and lower parts are joined
together at the belly, forming a spherical shape. Kwon’s firing is done in a
small kiln chamber, with only a few vessels at a time. There are two firings:
after a biscuit firing at 850°C, which leaves the vessel porous, the vessel is
glazed and fired a second time at around 1250°C, for about 24 hours. ‘This
is a process that cannot be fulfilled without the help of nature,’ according to
Kwon.31 In a typical year of production, only half a dozen successful moon
jars will be made. He discards any finished jars that fall below his exacting
standards for shape and glaze colour. Fuel quality, clay properties and
changes in kiln atmosphere all affect the finished work (illus. 169). Kwon
Dae Sup’s rigorous pursuit of artistic perfection exemplifies modern Korean
potters’ ability to bridge tradition and modernity: his pots are collected
around the world and seen as perfect additions to modern urban design, yet
his methods and place of work situate Kwon firmly in the tradition of the
porcelain producers of the Joseon period.
167 Unknown potter, bowl, 1127–1279 (Song), stoneware, black glaze, height 7 cm.

168 Kim Syyoung, jar, 2019, stoneware, black glaze, height 42 cm.

     Resident in Germany since 1972, Lee Young-Jae (b. 1951) is a leading
ceramic artist in her adopted country. She studied in Seoul before pursuing
ceramics and design in Wiesbaden, setting up a studio near Heidelberg, and
since 1987 has worked at Margarethenhöhe, Essen, a garden city
established for Krupps workers. Lee’s minimalist bowls, vases and jars are
a fitting continuation of the Bauhaus philosophy of ‘form follows function’:
before the Second World War a Bauhaus-inspired community of artists and
designers had lived at the Zeche Zollverein coal mine complex where Lee’s
ceramics workshop operates. Lee has presented one-person exhibitions in
Munich, Cologne and Berlin showing series of bowls, each unique, in
museum settings. One exhibition, in 2006, showed 1,111 bowls in a single

installation: its title can be read as ‘one, one, one, one’, thus drawing
attention to the unique qualities of each bowl.32 Her work has also been
seen in the United States, in Boston and in Los Angeles (illus. 170). Her
bowls and jars refer both to Joseon white porcelain and to the design
philosophy of the Bauhaus school, bringing together the notions of art and
use, elegance and practicality.33 In addition to her bowls, jars and vases,
Lee Young-Jae’s workshop in Essen produces tableware for commercial
distribution.

    Also based in Europe for much of his professional life was the
porcelain artist Suku Park (Suck-Woo Park; b. 1947). After studies at Seoul
National University and the Swedish State School of Art and Design, Park
worked for many years in Finland. He was artistic director at the design
company Pentik, in Posio, in the snowy north of the country, where he
found the cold climate conducive to good concentration.34 Park has also
taught ceramics at university level in Korea, moving between Scandinavia
and his native country in the 2000s. His white porcelain is elegant and
restrained in design and execution, achieving bright white forms that are

cast, joined, pierced and glazed (illus. 171). Park has written that his
language of form ‘is not Korean, but a reaction inside myself to form things
with my own hands in order to give an object its own character. When I’m
designing I’m thinking function, but I’m thinking humour too.’35

Ceramics in South Korea: Younger-Generation Artists
Yun Jucheol (b. 1972) makes what he describes as ‘pointed decoration,
cheomjang’ ceramics (illus. 173), the origins of which he has described:





171 Suku Park, vessel, 2004, porcelain,
glazed, height 15 cm.

      I think that many of clay artists in Korea try to succeed to our tradition
     in more creative and functional way, and at the same time, we strive to
    develop its design with modern sensibility of our era. ‘Cheomjang
    Technique’ stems from Korean traditional buncheong which is almost
      all about brushstrokes with varying consistencies of slip-engobe [the
     mixture of clay and water that also contains deflocculants and fluxes] .
        . . Cheomjang technique came out of its process while applying thick
     slips of varying consistencies with Hakeme brush on the surface. The
    outcome of my study and experiments in Cheomjang has been
    accomplished and completed on my ceramic pieces evoking rustic and
    simple sentiment toward Korean traditional ceramics. I have been
     eager to reinterpret about our tradition within ceramics in my own way
     of Cheomjang.36

Experimenting with digital technology to form vessels of iron-rich
clay, Ahn Seong Man (b. 1974) uses innovative construction techniques
(illus. 172). His blue-glazed vase was formed not on the wheel, and not
with slab building, but by designing the shape on the computer and printing
with a specially adapted 3D printer, which reads the design and renders it in
clay.
    Yoo Euijeong (b. 1981) makes startling, cross-cultural ceramics that
comment on the advent of mass consumer brand culture and
hyperconnectivity in modern Korea. He creates garishly coloured
confections in which cartoon characters, commercial logos and @ symbols
are jarringly juxtaposed with traditional decorative motifs. Encapsulations
of the longings, excesses and failures of contemporary Korean society,
Yoo’s transfer-printed vessels are quirky assemblages of hand-thrown and
mass-produced components. The sense of parody is further enhanced by the
use of overglaze silver and gold (illus. 164). Western and Eastern imagery is
intermingled in a technically impressive assembly of elements whose
playful exuberance masks a serious underlying purpose.
    Yu Sangduk (b. 1973) designs the moulds for his beautiful
architectural tiles using computer-aided technology (illus. 175). Ceramic in
buildings and ceramics made for special purposes are important branches of
the art of working with clay. Yu’s method of making requires careful
attention to the slip being cast and to the application of glaze, here sprayed
rather than dipped. Yu, who trained in North America after his studies in
Korea, is known for his beautiful, intense surfaces:

     [Yu] is interested in a particularly meticulous method of creating
     porcelain tiles. He derived the idea from functional plate forms but his
     intention is to move away from function to create something purely
     aesthetic. Creating flat porcelain shapes is not easy technically; he has
     struggled to resolve technique and concept. He focused on creating his
     concepts as computer programs and then processed them using three-
    dimensional printing.37
