    The ‘Variation of Space’ series by Yoon Sol (b. 1976) takes spheres of
clay, cutting them back and reassembling them to form complex, abstract
forms (illus. 176). Yoon studied ceramics at Seoul National University and
is now a professor of ceramics himself. He has had wide international
exposure in London and Munich. He slip-casts spherical forms,
deconstructing and grouping them in restful, undulating compositions that
are neither functional nor non-functional: individuals viewing the work are
left to make their own judgement.38 The son of a painter, Yoon Sol has
chosen to work in three dimensions. His impressive body of work

demonstrates a restrained use of colour, and a highly disciplined, clean and
uncluttered style.
    Cho Shinhyun (b. 1970) works in a highly unusual way, using
contrasting colours of porcelain slip to build up marble-effect walls on his
vessels (illus. 177). Each layer of coloured clay must dry before the next is
poured. The work is sanded to a smooth, soft surface, which blurs the
distinction between two- and three-dimensional design. Trained at Dankook
University, Cho works in the ceramic centre of Icheon.39





175 Yu Sangduk, architectural tile, 2010, embossed,
coloured ceramic, height 42 cm.

   Kim Juree (b. 1980) describes her ceramic sculpture practice as being
about ‘impermanence and the changing nature of our environment, both in
its natural form and in the urban settings surrounding us’.40 Her work is
time-based and involves unfired clay installations that are placed in a tray
of water so that they gradually sink, in a manner controlled by the artist
through the introduction of more or less water. Kim is a sculptor who has
turned to clay, a material that alters over time, as part of a practice engaging
with ephemerality. Kim’s ‘Hwigeong’ series quietly presents a narrative of
decay and dilapidation in the urban environment, one that arose from the
artist’s life in fast-changing Seoul (illus. 178). Kim’s thoughtful practice as
a sculptor and a ceramic artist has brought her international success, despite
the challenges inherent in collecting unfired clay works, which are certain
to alter and disappear in the course of time. Kim’s clay scale models,
intricately created to depict buildings in Seoul, reflect on the disappearance
of things and have titles that refer to real places.

An artist who has worked in ceramics in a way that interrogates
memory and identity is Ju Sekyun (b. 1980). As part of a practice that
encompasses installation, sculpture, drawing and video, Ju has produced the
series ‘Tracing Drawing’ (illus. 179). Ju throws a porcelain vessel on the
wheel and leaves it unglazed after firing. He then draws pencilled
decoration on the plain clay, using imperfect memories of museum exhibits
or published images he has seen throughout his life. Complicating the
appearance of a well-known, iconic treasure, he draws attention to the
emotional and physical spaces that familiar objects occupy in personal
consciousness. Pencil is a transitory medium, very different from the fixed,
fired decoration found on the original Goryeo-period vase. Ju trained in
sculpture at Kookmin University but was sufficiently drawn to ceramics
that he spent time apprenticed to different master potters, learning to handle
clay. His work playfully reflects on the relationship between modern viewer
and heritage object, questioning the reality of the past as we understand it in
the modern world.41

    The photographer Koo Bohnchang (b. 1953) approaches Joseon white
porcelain from an unusual creative perspective (illus. 180). Koo initially
trained in business studies before turning to photography. He has visited
museum collections of Korean white porcelain and photographed them
individually or in assemblages, placed against white textured Japanese
paper and softly lit. Koo’s long-exposure images, white on white, are a
meditative response to ceramics from a bygone age, a quiet tribute to the
virtuous Confucians who shaped Koreans’ outlook on life. Koo uses a 4 × 5
film camera and then prints images with delicate whispers of pigment. Plain
and undecorated, the ceramics Koo chooses to depict are peaceful and
comforting.42
    The poetic and perplexing ceramic sculptures of Yeesookyung (b.
1963) are an instance of a modern sensibility at play in the realm of Korea’s
ceramic heritage. Yeesookyung is a conceptual artist, trained at Seoul
National University and active internationally since the 1990s; she works in
sculpture, painting and video. Her ‘Translated Vase’ series, initiated in

2002, takes sherds and wasters from the potters’ studios around Icheon,
Yeoju, Gwangju, Gangjin, Buan and other places. From their fractured
forms Yeesookyung builds forms that suggest the volumes once occupied
by the broken pieces (illus. 181, 182).43 The sculptural assemblages are
joined with a gold-leaf bond, a metaphor for the precious nature of fragility
and rupture in the human condition. In a recent installation in Naples, Yee’s
work appeared to create narratives that start from existing objects, as the
exhibition website explains:

179 Ju Sekyun, Tracing Drawing 68, 2012, ceramic with pencil, height 44.5 cm.

    [Yeesookyung] aims at restoring dignity to the vulnerability of the
     object and the experience of the individual, between fact and
     hypothesis, history and narration. The fragmentation of the experience
    and the attempt to recover it are translated into the restoration of the
     shattered vase through welding, [in the way that consciousness can be
     recovered through] analysis.44

Yeesookyung brings a Buddhist sensibility to her work, with notions of
incarnation and embodiment present in her paintings, moving images and
ceramic assemblages. Interested in presenting her work in dialogue with
particular places and times, Yeesookyung has intervened in the ceramic
realm in a haunting manner.

    Lee Bul (b. 1964), a conceptual artist known for installation and
performance art, also made a brief foray into ceramics in the course of her
diverse practice (illus. 183). She has performed and built her work in ways
that explore her position as a woman in Korea, as a human person in
society. The ‘Cyborg’ series, begun in the late 1990s, addressed

contemporary Japanese animation with its fetishization of female breasts
and buttocks. Made sometimes of cast plastics, sometimes of porcelain, the
cyborg sculptures express Lee Bul’s powerful rejection of male-dominated
depictions of the female form, pushing ‘the logic of the largely masculine
fantasy of the cyborg to its darkest extremes, to the point of convulsion’.45
    Ceramic art in South Korea has grown dynamically in scale and
ambition since the early post-war years. The American artist Mei-ling Hom
conducted in-depth interviews with dozens of ceramic artists in 2007–8 in
Seoul and throughout South Korea, supported by a Fulbright grant. She
noted the contrast between Korea’s substantial investment in ceramics as an
art practice specialism and the situation in the United States. According to
Hom, in Seoul at that time there were 37 universities offering programmes
in ceramics. One of these schools produced two hundred graduates per
year.46 In addition to education, ceramics has a strong profile in Korea as a
heritage subject, as a consumer product, and as an active part of the
contemporary art scene, accessible to practitioners in diverse disciplines.
After the decline of the Joseon kilns and production model in the early
twentieth century, the position of ceramics and public understanding of the
subject has emerged revitalized, leading to a flourishing, competitive and
internationally prominent scene in the twenty-first century’s early decades.

Ceramics in North Korea
To turn from South Korean ceramics in the twenty-first century and
consider the qualities of ceramics made in North Korea since the division of

the country is a startling shift, one that reflects both the common cultural
heritage of the two modern Koreas and the mutually antagonistic social and
political structures of the two states. In the Korean Workers’ Party-led
socialist society of North Korea, artistic production and cultural
participation are viewed as part of an ideological project, one that requires
all citizens to strive for and celebrate common prosperity. Following the
theories of Lenin, Stalin, Mao and above all Kim Il-sung (1912–1994), the
Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) has shaped the arts to serve
its political messages and aims. Public art and architecture have presented a
consistent narrative of heroic triumph over adversity, with monumental
arches, sculpture and wall mosaics adorning outdoor urban spaces. A
mosaic mural produced in 2009, Work Team Contest, was designed by the
artist Kim Hung Il (b. 1965) and produced in collaboration with mosaic
artist Kang Yong Sam (b. 1956) and a team of six male and two female
artists from the Mansudae Art Studio in Pyongyang (illus. 184). Work Team
Contest is a tribute to the industriousness of workers in various sites of
production in the DPRK. In this scene, the work team from one of the furnaces
has won a productivity contest. The efficiency targets are indicated by the
chart on the left and a brass band nearby joins the celebrations. The scene is
rigorously planned; a border of magnolias (North Korea’s national flower)
frames the scene. A warm glow from a distant furnace bathes the
background, illuminating the industrial setting. The workers themselves are
decorated with flower garlands or hold bouquets; beaming, jubilant and
curiously uniform in their demeanour, they appear radiant in their moment
of glory. Designed and produced in Pyongyang, Work Team Contest was
commissioned for the 2009 Asia Pacific Triennial of Contemporary Art in
Brisbane, Australia, offering a rare opportunity for non-Koreans to
experience the scale and ambition of North Korean mosaic art.47 Citizens of
North Korea are required to participate in communal cultural endeavours,
such as the well-known Arirang mass games, mass dancing events and
performing arts. Artists and performers enjoy prestige in a society that
proclaims itself to be an earthly paradise (as reflected in the name of a
Pyongyang Metro station, Ragwon).
     In the visual arts, the shaping hand of Soviet education is apparent, a
legacy of the period between 1945 and 1989 when North Korea was a
member of the international family of socialist states, benefiting from
financial support and consultancy provided by Moscow, East Germany and

the other members of the Soviet bloc. Many North Korean artists of the
post-division period visited or trained in Russia or in Eastern Europe.
Education and training in the arts, including ceramics, was influenced by
the Soviet Russian model. It would be a mistake, however, to imagine that
all North Korean artistic production is derivative and characterless. Kim Il-
sung, the founding president of the Democratic People’s Republic,
encouraged artists to develop ‘national form with socialist content’, while
his son Kim Jong-il (1941?–2011) spoke out against abstraction, ruling that
‘if the people who see a picture cannot grasp its meaning, no matter what a
talented artist may have painted it, they cannot say it is a good picture.’48
State funding of the arts, along with the universally understood principle
that all works of art must serve a political purpose, led to a remarkably
stable and recognizable North Korean style, evident in ceramics as in other
media. Ceramics were included in the products and artistic forms
reproduced in state media, such as the illustrated periodical Joseon Hwabo.
Issues from the 1960s, when North Korea enjoyed friendly relations with
and economic support from the Soviet bloc, included displays of factory-
made china, as well as reports of artistic ceramics such as an artist carving
openwork decoration on a celadon vase, or a blue-and-white vessel whose
decoration celebrated romantic socialism by depicting agricultural scenes
and the famous ‘Thousand-league horse, Chollima’, which was designed to
embody the ambition and success of the socialist nation.49

184 Kim Hung Il and Kang Yong Sam, Work Team Contest, 2009, glass tessera tiles, 3.5 × 5.7 m.





185 Yonggwang station mosaic, Pyongyang, opened in 1987.

Pyongyang University of Fine Arts has been the top school, with a
highly competitive process for recruiting students. After graduation, and
allocation to a workplace, visual artists would work in a collaborative
manner, since individuality was not seen as a desirable trait. Some artists
and makers would be paid a salary to work in government-run workshops,
producing paintings, designs, sculpture and ceramics to commission. In
cities and landscapes around the country, monumental installations such as
sculpture praising the alliance of workers, peasants and intellectuals, or
encouraging high levels of output from factories and farms, or honouring
the two Kims, father and son, define the public realm. North Koreans
generally take pride in the monumental buildings and sculptures that their
country’s artists make, including the grandiose mosaic murals that decorate
the Pyongyang subway and prestigious building interiors and exteriors
(illus. 185). The Mansudae Art Studio is the premier centre for works of art
available to be purchased by international clients (illus. 186). Occupying a
large site in central Pyongyang and employing several thousand artists,
technicians and managers, Mansudae is organized in departments devoted
to oil painting, ink painting, sculpture, printmaking, embroidery, poster art,
jewel painting (a discipline using pulverized gemstones), embroidery and
applied arts, including ceramics. Mansudae produces official art for sites
around North Korea as well as commissions from overseas countries.
Among the famous public art commissions executed by Mansudae are the
large mosaics in the Pyongyang City Metro50 and the 52-metre-tall bronze
sculpture African Renaissance Monument (2009) in Dakar, Senegal. Other
studios are also authorized for visits and sales to international clients,
including Paekho, Minye and Koryo art studios. In the 2000s Mansudae
collaborated with the entrepreneur Pier Luigi Ceccioni to sell artwork
through Italy, in an attempt to reach customers otherwise prevented by
international sanctions from acquiring North Korean works of art.
Mansudae studios have also operated a gallery in 798, the contemporary art
district in northeast Beijing, China.
    The works discussed here were collected in Pyongyang in March 2001
and June 2002, in the course of two official visits made by the authors,
accompanied by British Museum Director Dr Robert Anderson, to mark the
opening of the Embassy of the United Kingdom in Pyongyang. The works
illustrated were acquired at Mansudae and Minye studios and hand-carried
to London at that time.51 Immediately after the first visit, a change in

international relations following the events of 9/11 made continuing contact
with North Korean cultural professionals more challenging. At the time of
writing, sanctions (imposed on the DPRK by the international community
following the country’s test-firing of nuclear missiles) make it all but
impossible to collect art produced in North Korea in most European and
North American countries. There is an ongoing, unofficial flow of North
Korean work into South Korea and China in particular, but in collecting and
museum practice, as in many spheres of economic and cultural activity,
relationships with North Korea are tightly controlled by international law.
As a result, international gallery audiences and creative arts researchers face
significant challenges to understanding the nature of North Korean artistic
life and the ways in which artists and makers train, live and work there.
This small selection of works, acquired and viewed through personal
introductions, may shed light on the particular qualities and genesis of
studio ceramics and mosaics for the public realm in late twentieth and early
twenty-first centuries in North Korea.
    North Korea’s most senior, accomplished artists in different media are
associated with Mansudae studios.52 Famous as ‘the incarnation of clay and
fire’53 was the prodigiously productive U Chi Son (O Chi-seon; 1919–
2003), who first exhibited his ceramic works as an eighteen-year-old and
focused on celadon making from 1981 until his death. U was a People’s
Artist and a winner of the Kim Il Sung Prize, both marks of distinction in
the artistic environment of North Korea. The ceramic showroom at
Mansudae was for years dominated by a striking, life-size wax model of U
Chi Son examining a large double-gourd inlaid celadon bottle, presumably
of his own making (illus. 187).54 Im Sa-jun (1927–2007) was also
renowned as a maker of celadon. Celadon had been singled out for praise
by Kim Il-sung, who said that Goryeo people ‘manufactured the Koryo
ceramics which the world values as treasures because of their distinctive
colours, patterns and models’.55 With the approval of the Great Leader,
celadon artists were encouraged to produce green-glazed wares in
traditional and more experimental styles. Im Sa-jun trained in Nampo, his
birthplace, during the Japanese colonial period and lectured at Pyongyang
University of Fine Arts after 1957, gaining the title of People’s Artist in
1985. Im was also a Mansudae artist, and the studio displayed and sold his
work along with pieces made by his three sons, Kyong-ik, Kwan-ik, Kun-
ik, and his daughter, Hye-ok. Following the trend of early twentieth-century

potters exploring technical aspects of celadon decoration, Im Sa-jun created
varied styles of celadon vessel, with inlaid, painted and pierced decoration.
He was also famous for creating gigantic vases and praised for ‘his own
unique method that combines the traditional taste with the modern
beauty’.56 Two vases in the British Museum collection illustrate his
confident, well-designed mastery of the celadon style (illus. 188, 189).

CHAPTER FIVE
CURRENT
DIRECTIONS
IN CERAMIC
RESEARCH

In the late twentieth century, new, interdisciplinary scholarship on the
ceramics of Korea gathered pace. Art historians, collectors, curators and
cultural studies researchers began to look at the production, technical and
material qualities, aesthetics, social uses, international circulation and
collecting history of Korean ceramics. South Korean university arts and
humanities departments produced highly qualified researchers who
questioned received narratives and chronologies and who laid the
foundations for a new era of ceramic studies. In North Korea too, during the
period of close cooperation with the Soviet bloc, universities and art
schools re-examined the ceramic past, in the context of Juche (self-reliance)
philosophy and the teachings of President Kim Il-sung. Much of the
literature from the period of division, naturally, is written in the Korean
language for Koreans who are already familiar with their country’s history
and geography.
    Around the world, ceramic enthusiasts who were not familiar with the
Korean peninsula’s cultural history started to encounter displays of Korean
art in the world’s great museums, often sponsored by the South Korean
government, and to access high-quality studies of Korea’s decorative and
fine arts. Particularly since its move to the new Yongsan site in 2005, the
National Museum of Korea has made enormous contributions to Korea’s
profile by mounting exhibitions and publishing catalogues and journals in
English, the language of international exchange.1 Other government-funded
agencies, such as the Korea Foundation, the Academy of Korean Studies
and the National Research Institute for Cultural Heritage, have also actively
driven cultural and historical projects in international universities and
museums. Korea’s pioneering, creative spirit in the digital realm has
generated excellent online resources for studying ceramics. In addition to
catalogues of national, private and university museums, published surveys
of museum collections around the world have been organized and funded
by the National Research Institute of Cultural Heritage.2 In the early
twentieth century, understanding of Korea’s ceramic history was very
rudimentary. In the twenty-first century, however, the situation is entirely
different and Korea’s porcelain, stoneware and early funerary and ritual
ceramics are well published and increasingly appreciated and discussed. In
this chapter, we review selected topics in Korean ceramics research,
highlighting the context in which scholars, collectors and curators work
today.

Terminology
Ceramic researchers in different academic communities have developed a
set of terms to describe the bodies, glazes and shapes of vessels. The
terminology of ceramics studies can appear daunting to general readers. In
the case of East Asian ceramics, we noted earlier that Western and Asian
authors have different words for white ceramics (Korean baekja) and green
ceramics (Korean cheongja). In the West, white ceramics, made of high-
fired purified clay and covered with a milky or transparent glaze, are known
as porcelain, while green-glazed wares, which usually have more impurities
in the clay body and are fired at a slightly lower temperature, have long
been described as ‘celadon’.





197 Pieter de Bailliu, after Anthony van Dyck, Honoré d’Urfé, 1645–55, engraving.

    The etymology of the term ‘celadon’ in particular has intrigued
scholars. If we disregard the possibility that it originates in the Middle East
or in Sanskrit,3 we can focus on the surprising story of a fictional shepherd,
Céladon, who made his way into a 1694 French dictionary, where his name
was defined as ‘a colour between blue and green’. At the time, fashionable
ladies associated colours with characters in a popular play, L’Astrée (The
Story of Astrea). In addition to celadon, these ladies named other colours,
including ‘colour of Astrea, colour of the sick Spaniard, of Amaranthe, of

an excited girl, of Neptune’s beard’.4 L’Astrée, a romance about love affairs
among shepherds, was written by Honoré d’Urfé and was adapted for the
theatre before 1650 (illus. 197). Its convoluted plot recounts the amorous
exploits of hundreds of characters, with shepherds and Druids interacting
through disguises and ruses. D’Urfé wrote his novel – one edition runs to
5,500 pages – over more than ten years. The first part appeared in 1607,
with further instalments in 1610 and 1619. He died in 1625, leaving his
masterpiece to be completed by two collaborators in 1627 (illus. 198).
   Many accounts of the term ‘celadon’ in ceramic studies refer to a
passage in Albert Jacquemart’s pioneering work on the history of porcelain,
published in 1862. Jacquemart, who coined terms that are still widely used
in ceramic studies, wrote disparagingly about L’Astrée and its influence on
French society. In his view, in the seventeenth century L’Astrée became

     a kind of manual of the court and the bourgeoisie, people read it and
     reread it and it was normal to introduce phrases borrowed from the
     sentimental language of its pages into one’s conversation. The
     shepherds of Lignon [protagonists in L’Astrée] were the models for
    French high society; distinguished men abased themselves, when
     speaking to women, by repeating the kinds of declarations typical of
     [d’Urfé’s] amorous philosophy. Astonishingly, the fashion lasted a long
    time . . . in the eighteenth century people lived still in this artificial
     atmosphere; serious people sat for Jean-Baptiste Pater [1695–1736]
    and Nicolas Lancret [1690–1743] to be portrayed in celadon colours,
     dressed up in silk robes with numerous rosettes, holding pipes and
     shepherds’ crooks . . . In order to fit in with the pastoral craze, these
     courtier-shepherds chose tender, vague colours: water-green, lilac, pale
     rose, sky blue or the changeable silk known as pigeon’s throat were the
     acceptable materials, and the paintings of [Jean-Antoine] Watteau
    [1684–1721], particularly the Departure for the Isle of Cythera leave
    no doubt in this regard’ (illus. 199). Language felt the influence of
     fashion and from 1690 the Dictionnaire universel, compiled by
    Antoine Furetière (1619–1688) and published posthumously, brought
     the term into existence by defining it as ‘green colour, pale, mixed
    with white, with a whitish tinge’. In 1694 and 1695 the Académie
     Française accepted more or less the same definition.5

198 Daniel Rabel, plate engraving in Honoré d’Urfé’s L’Astrée (1632).

    Céladon the shepherd, whose name must derive from that of the Lapith
in Ovid’s Metamorphoses, or from the river Keladon mentioned in Homer’s
Iliad, retained his association with the colour green throughout the
eighteenth century. We find the term used by the writer and critic Louis
Petit de Bachaumont (1690–1771) in an inventory describing a pair of green
vases that were embellished with mounts by the Parisian craftsman Pierre
Gouthière (illus. 200).6 No contemporary illustration or account of the
portrayal of Céladon on the stage has been identified that could confirm the
assertion that his robes were pale green in colour (nor indeed that the
association of the colour with the character arises in the play rather than in
the romance).7 Nonetheless, the connection between calm, jade green and

the sensual, noble character of Céladon, whose exploits include cross-
dressing and wearing the garments of his estranged beloved Astrée, persists
in refined European appreciation for East Asian green-glazed ceramics.
    Before the nineteenth century all Korean ceramics, including celadons,
were a domestic rather than a commercially traded product. They reached
the European market in the late nineteenth century, about three hundred
years after Chinese ware. When early twentieth-century Western
connoisseurs began to add Goryeo green-glazed ceramics to their
collections, they called them ‘celadon’, influenced by the similarities
between Chinese (Yue, Yaozhou and Ru) and Korean green ceramics. The
amorous exploits of Céladon and Astrée and their companions were by then
seen as ‘the product of a civilization, of an epoch’,8 and left a legacy of
depictions of the lovers (illus. 201), as well as the evocative word ‘celadon’,
which gradually extended in usage beyond the world of ceramic
connoisseurship, as a signifier for pale green.

   A further example of assimilation of Korean ceramics into Western
taste is the practice of applying metalwork mounts to ceramics. European
collectors often commissioned elaborate stands, covers and handles for
Chinese and Japanese ceramics in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries,
so when Korean vases and bowls began to appear on the international
market in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, they too were
very occasionally embellished with silver or gilded bronze mounts. To
modern eyes, the resulting ensemble may appear disconcerting, but the
practice of mounting Asian ceramics in European mounts, marrying clay

and metal, is nonetheless a remarkable example of cultural transfer. The
Honolulu Art Museum bottle (illus. 202) was formerly in the collection of
Robert P. Griffing Jr, an art historian and museum director. Similar
examples are rare but do survive in various collections.9

Japanese Archaeology
In Korea, ceramic historians working in the late twentieth century revisited
sites that had first been surveyed and published by Japanese specialists
during the colonial period. Between 1905 and 1940 archaeological surveys
of historical sites were systematically undertaken in typical colonial style.10
The architectural historian Tadashi Sekino (1868–1935) of Tokyo Imperial
University regularly travelled around the country for several months each
autumn, recording and photographing with prodigious energy and
discipline.11 The sites Tadashi and others visited were often connected with
Japan’s empire-building project, including railway construction and
development of ports and other strategically important places. At the time,
the (Western) disciplines of art history, archaeology and ethnography were
gaining ground in Japan’s universities. Japanese historians and
archaeologists naturally turned to Korea to apply their pioneering
methodologies. The results of these early investigations were mixed.
Valuable records of antiquities, buildings and sites that would later be
destroyed were published, and archived, in Japan. These constitute an
unrivalled resource for the investigation of the built environment, and of
excavated sites, in the decades after the fall of Joseon. Many Koreans
regard these studies as tainted, since they were closely associated with
notions of Japan’s superiority to other peoples. The ideology of the time
presented Japan as the leader and the fulcrum of Asian peoples and
interpreted the past to support Japan’s contemporary imperial ambitions.
Furthermore, the scale and methodology of some investigations by Japanese
researchers has been criticized by modern Korean scholars, who
understandably regret the disturbance to sites, and obstacles to
understanding, caused by poorly controlled digging and (in some cases)
pilfering and looting.
   An example is the kiln complex near Gyeryongsan, which produced
buncheong ware between 1400 and 1600. The free, vigorous dark brown
designs on Gyeryongsan vessels attracted collectors and scavengers who
removed finds from the site over many decades. A short excavation by

Japanese archaeologists led by Nomori Ken in 1927 found that by that date
the site had already been seriously disturbed by unsupervised digging.12
Excavations by two Korean museums in 1992 and 1993 were followed in
2007 by an exhibition at the National Museum of Korea, whose catalogue
introduced the 1927 and the 1990s excavations to the wider community.
Such extended delays in systematizing knowledge are unfortunately rather
common.
   A major cultural centre where ceramics are among the burial objects is
the Nangnang (Chinese: Lelang) Commandery in northwestern Korea.
Situated around Pyongyang, capital of modern North Korea, sites were
excavated during the colonial period and published then to considerable
international excitement. Between 108 BC and AD 313, Chinese military
commanderies, of which Nangnang was one, ruled the northern part of the
Korean peninsula. Excavations revealed burials with fine jades,
lacquerware, metalwork and earthenware vessels, funerary models and
inscribed tomb bricks. These remarkable sites of cultural interaction,
between Han and Six Dynasties China on the one side, and Goguryeo and
other early Korean states on the other, offer rich possibilities for
investigation but have been problematic in terms of access for the
international research community.
    The narratives built around the discovery of Nangnang artefacts during
and after the Japanese colonial period are fraught with nationalistic
distortions and polarized interpretations. For some Japanese historians, the
Chinese commandery sites were evidence of early Korea’s weakness and
inability to control the territory of the peninsula. For North Korean
historians, Nangnang was a lie perpetrated by cheating Japanese
colonialists. The North Koreans claimed that Nangnang was an invention
and that the objects described in the site reports were fraudulently shipped
by the Japanese from China to create the impression of past Chinese rule on
the Korean peninsula. South Korean historians have not gone so far as to
accuse the Japanese archaeologists of cheating, but their interpretation of
Nangnang is coloured by disagreement with the Japanese assessment of
early Korean history. Some South Korean historians have viewed Nangnang
and the other commanderies as hostile invaders who provoked resistance by
native Korean communities. More recently, Hyung-il Pai has argued that
Nangnang and local Goguryeo culture enriched and changed each other.
Fundamental lack of consensus among Korean scholars about what

constitutes ‘early Korean material culture’ has been a major barrier to
understanding the history of ceramics before the Unified Silla.13 The
relationships between Three Kingdoms Korea and pre-Tang Chinese states
were complex and varied: much research lies ahead in demonstrating how
ideas and cultural forms were transferred eastwards and westwards between
eastern China and the Korean peninsula.

Maritime Archaeology
Shipwreck excavations have been an exciting and fast-moving specialism in
late twentieth-century Korean ceramic research. The experience of
excavating the Sinan wreck, a Chinese ship heading to Japan with
thousands of ceramics in its cargo, in the territorial waters of South Korea
was transformational. As previously mentioned, the Sinan wreck was
accidentally discovered by a fisherman in 1976, off the southwest coast of
Korea. It attracted huge international attention, with its tens of thousands of
Chinese ceramics as well as seven Goryeo pieces (illus. 203). It kicked off
the discipline of maritime archaeology in Korea. Since its excavation, a
research institute and museum have been founded in Mokpo, Jeolla
Province. Numerous finds have been investigated, often bringing up
Goryeo-period ceramics in large numbers. At around 34 metres long, the
Chinese ship that sank at Sinan was much larger than the Korean junks that
carried celadons from the official kilns near the coast of modern Jeolla and
Chungcheong provinces northwards to the Goryeo capital, Gaeseong.14
    The Sibidongpado ship, the Wando ship discovered in 1984, the
Daebudo ship, the Dalido ship, the Taean ship and the Anjwa ship are
among the vessels that have been excavated and reported.15 More wrecks
were discovered over time, with fourteen already recorded.16 Until recently
all the shipwrecks containing ceramics that had been reported dated from
the Goryeo, but in 2014 a Joseon-period wreck was discovered near Mado
Island, Chungcheong Province.17 Among the Goryeo shipwreck discoveries
are tags bearing the names of clients, known court officials named in the
dynastic historical record, who commissioned individual bottles and
vessels, as well as coins that allow particular shipments to be dated. The
growth of maritime archaeology in the treacherous waters off Korea’s
southwest coast provides valuable information that complements the textual
and material evidence that survives on land. As evidence of a high-level

network of production and consumption, shipwreck archaeology
discoveries offer a valuable addition to material evidence, allowing Goryeo
ceramics to be traced from kiln to customer.18

Technical Studies
Technical studies of the material qualities of Korean ceramics have also
answered some questions and raised some new ones since the 1980s.
Laboratory analysis including magnification under the microscope and
colour spectography have enabled researchers to identify the elements used
in glazes and inlays and to explain their visual effects. Inlaid decoration is
one of the glories of the Korean ceramic tradition, rarely found on other
countries’ ceramics, and likely to connect to the taste for inlaid silver and
bronze metalwares and fine mother-of-pearl inlaid lacquers during the high
Goryeo period (illus. 204, 205, 206). Early collectors and writers believed
that inlaid decoration on ceramics was achieved simply by incising designs
into the partially dried clay using a sharp tool and then filling the depression
with liquid clay, or slip, of contrasting colours: light to produce white and
dark to produce black.
     Since the 1990s, when conservation scientists began to examine large
sample sets of Goryeo period inlaid ceramics, it has become clear that the
process of creating multicoloured inlaid designs on celadon was more
complex. Using magnification and light spectography, scientific researchers
have analysed the composition of the contrasting materials that were
introduced into the clay before glazing. White inlays are composed of
quartz particles, sintered together with small amounts of glass and
potassium-rich clay, which produces mullite (a mineral consisting of

aluminium silicate) during firing. Interaction between the glaze and the
inlay material during firing is the key to successful contrast between
brilliant, light and dense, dark inlay colours in the finished piece. Black
inlay material is similar to the glaze composition, rather dense and richer in
iron oxide, along with oxides of calcium, phosphorus and manganese, all of
which are found in wood ash. Black inlay material seems to consist of a
clay rich in black biotite, a kind of mica often found in igneous and
metamorphic rocks.19 It seems likely that inlay materials were deliberately
modified in order to achieve a desired visual effect.

To end this study of Korean ceramics, it is worth reflecting on the
international collecting, presentation and reception of Korean works of art,
including ceramics, before and after the Korean War. By that time, a
number of ceramic collectors and scholars outside Korea had already built
collections based on the advice and contacts of dealers and agents. An
example is the American industrialist Charles Freer, who bought through

Yamanaka & Co.20 In Britain, George Eumorfopoulos, the first president of
the Oriental Ceramic Society, collected Goryeo celadons, and pieces from
his collection can be found in the British Museum and the V&A.21 Neither
man ever visited Korea. Other early Western collectors had bought ceramics
while touring the world by steamship and train in the early twentieth
century.22 They include Aubrey Le Blond and his wife Elizabeth (née
Hawkins-Whitshed), whose collection of celadons was donated to the
V&A,23 and the well-connected Oxford professor Archibald Sayce, whose
lively account of his world travels includes a description of visiting Seoul in
1912. Korean ceramics were among Sayce’s bequest of Egyptian and Asian
antiquities to the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford (illus. 207).24 During the
Japanese colonial period, Western collecting taste was strongly shaped by
relationships between European and American specialists and Japanese
scholars and collectors such as Yanagi Sōetsu, Koyama Fujio (1900–1975)
and Nomori Ken (dates unknown).
     Later in the twentieth century the close relationship between the
governments of the United States and the Republic of Korea in the post-war
period led to programmes like the Peace Corps sending young American
graduates to live and work in Korea. Some of these people, along with
diplomats, missionaries, teachers, businesspeople and military officers,
developed interests in the arts of Korea and later in life donated collections
to U.S. museums.25 The late twentieth-century galleries of Korean art that
have appeared in European and North American museums present
collections that were assembled through purchases and donations from
some of these figures, and also from knowledgeable dealers like Kang
Collection Korean Art in New York City26 and auction house experts like
Haekyum Kim, who was for many years the Christie’s specialist for Korean
art. An alumnus of the Peace Corps, Robert Mowry, developed an interest in
Asian art while serving in Korea; he went on to curate collections at
Harvard and at the Asia Society, New York, and is currently a senior
consultant at Christie’s.

       It is not surprising that, while dealing with classical Korean art, issues
of restitution, provenance and good title have arisen from time to time, but
these often relate to paintings and religious objects, rather than to ceramics.
As museum curators become more connected through professional

networks, international regulation of the market in antiquities naturally
becomes a routine aspect of collection building and management, for
Korean collections as much as in other fields.
     In ceramic studies, the international museum-going public has enjoyed
enhanced opportunities to learn about Korean ceramics and to engage with
their technical, aesthetic and historical contexts. This is an outcome of
strategic investment of attention and resources by the South Korean
government, leading to opportunities for institutions and individuals to
focus on Korean works of art. With the raising of Korea’s cultural profile,
ceramics research has been transformed since about the 1980s. Historic
pieces and collections have been surveyed and published, in print and
online. In Korea, numerous new museums devoted to traditional and
contemporary ceramics have been founded,27 and ceramics displays in
major historical museums have been upgraded and expanded. Around the
world, gallery spaces for Korean arts in major museums have played a big
part in building appreciation for Korea’s ceramics (illus. 208). The arrival in
Western art schools and colleges of Korean students also built links
between specialists in different parts of the globe. When the Korea
Foundation was established in 1991 to promote Korea to the world and to
support public diplomacy, a thoughtful programme of nurturing expertise in
a community of international museums was initiated that encouraged
collaboration and creativity. Despite the many cultural differences that exist
between institutions in Asia, the Americas, Europe and Australasia, these
intensive curatorial meetings fostered professional links between dispersed
colleagues, which have produced research and raised the standard of
museum practice in Korean curatorial affairs.28 With growing numbers of
makers, students and collectors engaging with Korean historic ceramics, the
future looks promising for academic research into Korean ceramics and
their display in museums. At the same time, living artists in Korea and
around the world are taking inspiration from Korea’s ceramic past, with
styles and techniques that demonstrate how clay in Korea has not only a
distinguished past but a dynamic future too.
